Title: Opening Remarks For The 3Rd Financial Forum
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: OPENING REMARKS FOR THE 3rd FINANCIAL FORUM CBBH MILESTONES By Governor Peter W. Nicholl Wednesday, 2nd June 1999 Holiday Inn Hotel Sarajevo, BIH When I addressed this forum last year, the Central Bank of Bosnia & Herzegovina, and I believe ALL of Bosnia & Herzegovina stood at the brink of a new era of financial security, possibilities and cooperation. That was because the CBBH was just about to introduce a new currency, the Convertible Marka, or KM. Since that time, the KM has moved into practically ever corner of this country, and even beyond as it is now accepted in or will be very soon at banks in a half dozen countries. The release of the first ever BiH coins in modern history! The KM currency has been in circulation almost a year and on the whole it has been well accepted. This is illustrated by the fact that the CBBH balance sheet has doubled in size from KM 150 million to over KM 300 million since it went into circulation. More importantly, the KM is also now used in all parts of the country. However, its use still varies throughout the country. The DEM, Croatian kuna and Yugoslavian dinar are still used to varying degrees. The KMs use has risen strongly in the Republika Srpska over the last six months and it is now the dominant currency in that entity! That is very pleasing. The use of the KM in Herzegovina is beginning to improve also. I visited Livno last week for discussions with county officials. They said that people there were very willing to accept and use the KM but the major problem was that many federation government payments were still being made in the other currencies. Impending changes to Federation government laws to promote the use of the KM and changes in the operations of the Payments Bureaus to make the KM the only currency they use for domestic transactions should lead to increased use of the KM in the Herzegovina region in the near future. People should have no doubt about the Currency Board. The Currency Board has been strictly maintained over the last year. Our foreign exchange reserves are currently about 111% of our KM liabilities and have been around that ratio over the past year. So we more than meet the statutory requirement of full backing for all our KM liabilities. More recently, we have reached agreements with some banks in other countries to deal the KM. Banks in Austria, Germany and Switzerland are already doing so. Some banks in Hungary will start within a week or so. We are currently completing discussions with some Croatian banks. I think this dealing in the KM outside of BiH is an important sign of its stability and growing acceptance. The KM is also playing an increasing role in non-cash payments and in bank deposits. For example, commercial bank deposits denominated in KM were 118-million in October 1998. By May 1999 they had risen to KM 227-million, growth of 92 percent. KM. KM bank deposits are rising in all three parts of this country. So the CBBH is very pleased with the way in which KM acceptance and use has risen in the year since the last Bosnian Financial Forum. We will do all we can to ensure that progress continues next year. WE WONT BE CHANGING!  BUT ALMOST ALL OF THE REST OF THE BIH FINANCIAL SYSTEM DOES HAVE TO CHANGE. The second major issue I want to talk about today is the integration and reform of the financial sector in BiH. The financial sector in BiH is currently very fragmented and weak. As a consequence, the level of financial inter-mediation is very low and the financial sector is incapable of playing roles it should in the growth and development of the economy. BIH needs to attract private foreign investments. One of the things that will be necessary for this is to reform the banking sector and payments systems in BIH so that it is structured and works like the financial systems in Western Europe. A more efficient and strong financial sector will also have a positive impact on local investment. The problems have been diagnosed and I think they are well known and understood by policy-makers. The year ahead should therefore be one of implementation rather than one of further analysis. The key changes fall into three areas: The transfer of the roles currently carried out by the payments bureaus The strengthening of the commercial banking sector through privatization of solvent publicly owned banks, merging or closure of weak or insolvent banks, an extension of the functions commercial banks can carry out by removing the monopolies the Payments Bureaus have, further development of the inter-bank settlement system via the CBBH, and I hope foreign investment into the BiH commercial banking sector. The development of financial markets and instruments that dont currently exist in BIH. The reform process will need the cooperation of all levels of government, the Payments Bureaus, the Banking Agencies, the commercial banks, the CBBH and, the international community. The strategy for the reform process has already been largely developed at the political and institutional level. WHAT IS NEEDED NOW? Two things are needed now. First, the political will to carry out the reforms. International assistance with advice and funding to implement the reforms. At the recent Donors Conference many donors recognized the importance of financial sector reform and pledged support to carry it out. The CBBH will do all it can to promote and assist with these important reforms over the year ahead. They are a critical part of the development strategy for the BiH. If the BIH economy is to develop and progress it needs a stronger financial sector. Financial Forums such as this are an important part of getting that message across and I congratulate the organizers for the splendid job they have done and wish them every success for this 3rd Bosnian Financial Forum. Title: Peace Seminar On Bosnia And Herzegovina - Building Institutions In A Market Economy
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: The following speech was delivered at an international conference on BiH in Stockholm earlier this year, but is particularly relevant now that BiH is entering a very critical phase of its economic maturity. Building the institutions of the market economyd1 Stockholm, March 3, 2000d1All international representatives agree that Bosnia and Herzegovina must become a private sector market economy if it is to gain sustainable economic growth and eventually integrate into Europe. Most politicians as well as policymakers inBIH also say that is their goal. Many are truly sincered1on some theoretical and abstract level. In practice, however, there are two main problems. First, most have never lived in an environment where private sector markets have played a big ormining role. They have little idea of how fundamental there must be changes in many of their institutions, ways of thinking and behaviour to shift from state-controlled markets to private markets. That's why they prefer to tamper withme instead of making fundamental changes. Second, the enhanced role of private markets means a loss of political and financial power. The document circulated before this Seminar clearly showed how this leads to resistance to change. So there are problems both those in understanding and political ones that have to be overcome. At the moment, the middle ground in BiH is very hostile to private investment and private markets. There are problems in the legal system, the regulatory system, the financial system and mosteco-nom sectors still have government companies that manage them. I wanted to talk first about the general mistake that I think the international community is making regarding economic reform in BiH. The mistake is that every issue in BiH is treated as a political issue. Little has been made in convincing politicians that some issues are purely economic and fluid and should be decided on the basis of these criteria. The main reason for this is that we've never tried it. We play their game. One consequence of this is that although BiH is a small country and although the trend is everywhere to create larger financial institutions, four years after Dayton, the Bosnian financial system is still divided into two or even three relatively separate systems. For example, there is only one bank operating on the territory of the whole country, CBBH. None of the 59 so-called commercial banks still operate across the country. I'll give you another example. There are now international consultants in BiH helping BOssan authorities establish the stock exchange. They came to me for help and support. The first two sentences in their letter say: * BiH is a very small country and there are doubts that a sustainable stock exchange can be created in BiH. * For political reasons, however, it will be necessary to organise two exchanges, one in each entity. I told them these two statements were completely inconsistent. The stock market is not a political institution. It's an economic institution. And it only works if there are products that will be sold on it and evenpeople are willing to trade. You can always establish an institution called the stock exchange and maybe politicians will feel good when they say they have one in Banja Luka and one in Sarajevo. But you can't force people to use them and they won't use weak and neliquid institutions. If we want to build a market economy in BiH, we need to create institutions that will work, not just institutions, to say that we have built them. I don't want to say much about CBBH, but it's an example, one of the few, of the constitution ofa nation that works. Why? "Targeted economic conditioning" and "Intensive institution building" are some of the reasons, but there are other fundamental characteristics that are also important. First, the CBBH has a clear objective and can be held responsible for it. Most other institutions have very general goals. Secondly, the CBBH is structured more or less along a line that would be proposed by well-corporated governance principles that have been developed during the last 10 to 20 years in our countrya. All other state ministries are set up as reflections in the mirror of the political structure: three presidents rotating, decision-making by consensus, etc. Instead of keeping politics in political institutions, we created a set of political ministries. These ministries should implement the policies adopted by their political mastersd1and should be held accountable for this implementation. Instead, they often repeat political discussions instead of applying but makingno decisions. The third key element of CBBH is that we operate under a very clear and good law. He says what we have to do. It also gives a list of things we can't do. Being a foreigner helped, but if I didn't have the support and strength that he gave med obar legal framework, I don't think I would have succeeded. This fact is also very important for the creation of private markets. Private investors need a clear, strong, legal structure and court system that will protect and uphold their rights given to them by law. Without it, private investment is very risky. This applies to both local and foreign investors.?
text_original: Govor koji slijedi je odran na meunarodnoj konferernciji o BiH u tokholmu, poetkom ove godine, ali je posebno relevantan sada kada BiH ulazi u jako kritinu fazu svoje ekonomske zrelosti. Izgradnja institucija trine ekonomije tokholm, 3 mart, 2000Svi meunarodni predstavnici se slau da Bosna i Hercegovina mora postati trina ekonomija privatnog sektora ako eli da stekne odriv ekonomski rast i na kraju se integrie u Evropu. Veina politiara kao i kreatora politke u BIH isto tako kae da je to i njihov cilj. Mnogi su zaista iskrenina nekom teoretskom i abstraktnom nivou. U praksi, meutim, postoje dva glavna problema. Prvo, veina ih nikada nije ivjela u sredini gdje su trita privatnog sektora igrala veliku ili dominantnu ulogu. Malo imaju predstave o tome koliko fundamentalne moraju biti promjene u mnogim njihovim institucijama, nainima miljenja i ponaanja da bi se prebacili sa trita koje kontrolie drava na privatna trita. Zato oni radije akaju probleme umjesto da prave fundamentalne promjene. Drugo, pojaana uloga privatnih trita znai gubitak politike i financijske moi. Dokument koji je cirkulisao pred ovaj Seminar jasno je pokazao kako to vodi ka otporu promjenama. Tako da postoje problemi i oni u razumjevanju i oni politiki koji se moraju prevazii. U ovom momentu, sredina u BIH je jako neprijateljska prema privatnom ulaganju i privatnim tritima. Postoje problemi u zakonskom sistemu, regulativnom sistemu, financijskom sistemu i veina ekonomskih sektora jo uvijek ima dravna preduzea koja njima upravljaju. Htio sam prvo da govorim o generalnoj greci za koju mislim da pravi meunarodna zajednica u vezi sa ekonomskom reformom u BiH. Greka je u tome to se svako pitanje u BIH tretira kao Politiko pitanje. Malo je napravljeno uspjeha u ubjeivanju politiara da su neka pitanja isto ekonomska i tenika i da bi se o njima trebalo odluivati na osnovu ovih kriterija. Glavni razlog za ovo je da to nikada nismo pokuali. Mi igramo njihovu igru. Jedna posljedica toga je da, iako je BIH mala zemlja i iako je trend svugdje da se stvaraju vee financijske institucije, etiri godine nakon Daytona, bosanski financijski sistem je jo uvijek podijeljen u dva ili ak tri relativno odvojena sistema. Na primjer, postoji samo jedna banka koja djeluje na podruju cijele zemlje, CBBH. Nijedna od 59 takozvanih komercijalnih banaka jo uvijek ne djeluje na podruju cijele zemlje. Dau vam drugi primjer. U BIH su sada meunarodni konsultanti koji pomau bosanskim vlastima u uspostavljanju berze. Obratili su mi se za pomo i podrku. Prve dvije reenice u njihovom pismu kau: BiH je jako mala zemlja i postoje sumnje da se moe kreirati odriva berza u BIH. Meutim, zbog politikih razloga bie neophodno da se organizuju dvije berze, po jedna u svakom entitetu. Rekao sam im da su ove dvije konstatacije potpuno nedosljedne. Berza nije politika institucija. To je ekonomska institucija. I funkcionie samo ako ima proizvoda koji e se prodavati na njoj i ako su ljudi voljni da trguju. Uvijek moete osnovati jednu instituciju zvanu berza i moda e se politiari dobro osjeati kad kau da imaju jednu u Banja Luci i jednu u Sarajevu. Ali ne moete natjerati ljude da ih koriste i oni nee koristiti slabe i nelikvidne institucije. Ako elimo da izgradimo trinu ekonomiju u BiH treba da napravimo institucije koje e funkcionisati, a ne samo institucije da bismo rekli da smo ih izgradili. Ne elim da kaem puno o CBBH, ali je primjer, jedan od rijetkih, institucije koja funkcionie. Zato? Ciljana ekonomska uslovljenost i Intenzivna izgradnja institucija su neki od razloga, ali postoje i druge fundamentalne karakteristike koje su takoer vane. Prvo CBBH ima jasan cilj i moe se smatrati odgovornom za njega. Veina drugih institucija ima vrlo generalne ciljeve. Drugo, CBBH je struktuirana manje ili vie po liniji koju bi predloili dobro korporisani principi upravljanja koji su razvijeni u toku posljednjih 10 do 20 godina u naim zemljama. Sva druga dravna ministarstva su postavljena kao odrazi u ogledalu politike strukture: tri predsjednika koja se rotiraju, donoenje odluka koncenzusom, itd. Umjesto da se politika zadri u politikim institucijama, mi smo kreirali komplet politikih ministarstava. Ova ministarstva bi trebala implementirati politike koje donose njihovi politiki gospodarii trebali bi se smatrati odgovornim za tu implementaciju. Umjesto toga, oni esto ponavljaju politike diskusije umjesto da primjenjuju ve donesene odluke. Trei kljuni element CBBH je da mi djelujemo po vrlo jasnom i dobrom zakonu. On kae ta moramo raditi. Takoer daje spisak stvari koje ne smijemo uraditi. To to sam stranac je pomoglo, ali da nisam imao podrku i snagu koju mi je davao dobar zakonski okvir, ne vjerujem da bih uspio. Ova injenica je takoer jako vana za stvaranje privatnih trita. Privatni investitori trebaju jasnu, jaku, zakonsku strukturu i sudski sistem koji e zatititi i podrati njihova prava koja im daje zakon. Bez toga, privatno ulaganje je vrlo rizino. Ovo se odnosi i na lokalne i na strane investitore.

Title: Chamber Of Commerce Speech
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: DISCUSSION AT THE ROUND TABLE ON "DIRECT FOREIGN INVESTMENT IN BIH" ORGANIZED BY THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE SARAJEVO, 8 FEBRUARY 2000 GOVOR PETER-A NICHOLL-A GOVERNOR BIH CENTRAL BANK I am pleased to join this palnell discussion today as its subject is critical to the further development of biH's economy. Although I probably don't have to convince any of you here at this roundtable about this fact, I will briefly explain to you why this is such an important issue for BiH. The latest data on payment transactions shows that in both entities, export accounts currently cover only about 20% of import payments. This means imports are five times higher than exports. This is clearly not sustainable. Current economic growth and import rates in BiH are only maintained by high levels of official capital entering the country. We all know this can't last. It is not clear whether the slowdowns in official capital flows will begin this year or next year. But it's certainly going to start soon and for BiH it's better to betoo late to face it. What can BiH do in this situation? - Policymakers can bury their heads in the sand and hope nothing happens. That would be the worst political reaction possible. Policymakers can embrace policies and try tomake exports and domestic production of goods that are a substitute for imported goods. This has to be done. Industries built in this way must be internationally competitive to avoid further problems, but it will take time for exports to grow significantly even if BiH implements even the most correct policies. Their implementation in many political spaces has been utterly undecided. The need to attract private direct investment in BiH is very clear. The uneasy truth that we all have to do at this roundtableis that the environment in BiH is still far from being attractive and supporting private investment. Attracting direct private investment in BiH is more than a struggle and it must be if sensitive policies and procedures are accepted. Some of the policies that have begun have been applied with more urgency and strength. The discussion on increasing private investment in BiH often focuses on what needs to be done to attract foreign private investment. But it's also important to create an environment thatencourages local private investment. The kind of political changes that will improve the environment for local private investment will also make BiH a more attractive place for old-fashioned investments. Second, many policymakers and officials in BiH still do notsee how fundamental changes encouraged by private investment are. There are problems in the system, which is not complete, licensing and regulatory system, which are very bureaucratic and arduous, and in the financial system - which is weak or not existingand. The importance of a good legal and financial system cannot be overstated. These systems are pillars for a market-based private sector economy. While progress is under way in some of these areas, the country is still moving too slowly to changethe la orientation of economies towards the private sector d0 and time is running out. The organizers asked me to look at the financial system first . This is one of the areas of the main problem holding back private investment. The financial system in BiH is currently veryweak and evaporative. Many of the markets and instruments relied on by private sector investors in developed areas do not yet exist. One positive feature for foreign investors , especially those from Europe , is that tying the Convertible Brand to the Euro through a strict curency board means that for investors from the Euro area investing in BiH, there is no risk of a course difference. Also, the CBBH law requires CBBH to maintain the full convertibility of KM in DEM and EURO. These characteristics of the kusus exchange regime are very significant for foreign direct investments, and should be emphasized by potential foreign investors at every opportunity. The monopoly that payment agencies have on domestic without cash payments has been a serious hindrance to foreign direct investment. Anyone who does not come from the territory of the former Yugoslavia simply does not understand these institutes and the need for the business community to make all the domestic payments through them. Their legal monologue was abolished last year in both entities. That's very positive. The process of moving domestic payment transactions from the institute to commercial banks is under way. It's also positive. But this transmission is still at an early stage. Banking agencies, in co-operation with the CBBH, have developed criteria that they will use to allow banks toperform these payment services. In the Federation, 20 banks have applied so far and the first permits should be issued in a few weeks. I don't think any bank in RS has applied so far, but I expect that to happen soon. The need to develop a modern payment system in BiH is critical to economic development. Payment institutes provided a safe form of payment transactions but they are the antithesis of market-based systems because their role is based on regulationand monopoly powers more than the client's choice. Aganja. It is the general structure of domestic payment systems in all developed countries, but a sign of the weakness of the Banking Sector in BiH is that this transfer must be done in phases and that all banks will not get approval to conduct these payment functions. CBBH will do everything it can to ensure that this transformation of the BiH payment system goes smoothly and that the end result is a modern, market-oriented system. Our goal is to complete this transformation this year. But banking reform has to go muchfurther than transferring the domestic payment system to commercial banks. There are two main problems with biH's banking sector. The first is that it is not actually one banking sector, there are actually three banking sectors in BiH. BiH is a small country. They will have a difficulttime creating financial institutions with enough strength and foundation to play a major role in financing the development of the first sector. But if it continues to share its small financial space in three separate markets, it will never create the financial institutionsit needs to boost development. In the rest of the world, the growing trend of financial institutions is uniting to create larger, more highly capitalised and often outside the border institution. But we in BiH still don't have one bank operatingin both entities d0 apart from CBBH! Another important problem, partly caused by the former, is that BiH banks are generally very small and undercapitalized to be capable of any significant role in attracting savings and financing investments inthe p rivat sector. Change is beginning to unfold. For example, the Federation Banking Agency does a good job of closing insolvent banks and encouraging small but solvent banks to unite. As a consequence, the number of banks licensedin the Federation dropped from 55 to 42 during last year. But much more reforms need to be done - and quickly, a host of small weak banks are not helping development. They can play a small direct role and the problems they have can lead to a loss of confidence in sVE banks, including those that are solid. I reviewed the KM deposit figures of BiH banks recently. I know that many banks will have deposits in currencies other than KM so these KM figures are not an indicator of its actual size. But their KM deposits became mleg for most of their total deposits in the course of last year. The figures that speak of the size of a bank based on KM deposits are surprising, in the sense that most banks are incredibly small: deposit level (KM million) Number of registered banks over 100mil. 0 50-100mil. 2 30-50mil. 3 20-30mil. 4 10-20mil. 6 5-10mil. 7 1-5mil. 14 under 1mil. 22 The organizer asked me to also talk about the development of other financial markets and instruments such as t ricemoney, value paper market, stock exchange, etc. business starts around this. It is important that these markets are developed in BiH so that people and businesses have a whole range of savings financial variants that are open to them. The development of a well-developed, progressive and modern banking and payment system is more fundamental and important. This is the base on which these other markets were developed. They are not an alternative to facing some difficult choices in the reform of the banking sector, such as the privatisation of a large number ofstate-owned banks, the closure of insolvent banks, and the development of banks operating on the territory of the whole of BiH. Also, I am concerned that in many new markets the same mistakes that have already occurred in the banking sector look like they are being repeated. This means that these issueswill be seen as a primary political issue more than as an economic one and BiH will create two or maybe three of each market. I repeat what I said earlier: BiH is a small country , financial institutions and markets all over the world are uniting tocreate larger, much more liquid markets. It would be a mistake for BiH to move in the opposite direction to this trend. Money markets, securities markets, stock markets, etc. need to be made that can be tied up across the country and which can also beone-stranded tied to markets in neighbouring countries and finally with a broad European market. In creating these new markets, BiH needs to look forward to the future, not back in time. country
text_original: DISKUSIJA ZA OKRUGLIM STOLOM O DIREKTNOM STRANOM ULAGANJU U BIH ORGANIZOVANO OD STRANE PRIVREDNE KOMORE SARAJEVO, 8 FEBRUAR 2000 GOVOR PETER-A NICHOLL-A GUVERNER CENTRALNA BANKA BIH Drago mi je to mogu da se pridruim ovoj palnel diskusiji danas poto je njen predmet od kritine vanosti za dalji razvoj BiH ekonomije. Mada vjerovatno ne moram da ubjeujem bilo koga od vas ovdje za ovim okruglim stolom o ovoj injenici, kratko u vam objasniti zato je to toliko vano pitanje za BiH. Posljednji podaci o platnim transakcijama pokazuju da u oba entiteta, izvozni rauni trenutno pokrivaju samo oko 20% uvoznih plaanja. To znai da je uvoz 5 puta vei nego izvoz. Ovo jasno nije odrivo. Trenutna stope ekonomskog rasta i uvoza u BIH su samo odravane velikim nivoima zvaninog kapitala koji ulazi u zemlju. Svi znamo da ovo ne moe trajati. Nije jasno da li e usporavanja u slubenim tokovima kapitala poeti ove godine ili sljedee godine. Ali sigurno je da e poeti uskoro i za BIH je bolje da bude spremna da se s tim suoi. ta BiH moe uraditi u ovoj situaciji? -tvorci politike mogu zakopati glave u pijesak i nadati se da se nita nee desiti. To bi bila najgora mogua politika reakcija. -stvaraoci politike mogu prihvatiti politike i pokuati da povaaju izvoz i domau proizvodnju robe koja je zamjena za uvoznu. Ovo se mora uraditi. Industrije koje su napravljene na ovaj nain moraju biti meunarodno konkurentne da bi se izbjegli dalji problemi, ali e potrajati dok izvoz znaajno poraste ak ako BiH implementira i najpravilnije politike. Njihova implementacija u mnogim politikim prostorima bila je krajnje neodluna. Potreba da se privuku privatna direktna ulaganja u BiH je vrlo jasna. Nelagodna istina koju svi za ovim okruglim stolom moramo shaviti da je okruenje u BIH jo uvjiek daleko od toga da bude privlano i da podrava privatna ulaganja. Privlaenje direktnih privatnih ulaganja u BIH je vie od borbe a to mora biti ako su osjetljive politike i procedure prihvaene. Neke od politika koje su poele su primjenjene sa vie hitnosti i snage. Diskusija o poveanju privatnog ulaganja u BiH se esto fokusira na onome ta se treba uraditi da bi se privukla strana privatna ulaganja. Ali , isto tako je vano da se stvori okolina koja ohrabruje lokalna privatna ulaganja. Vrsta politikih promjena koja e unaprijediti ambijent za lokalna privatna ulaganja e takoer napraviti od BiH atraktivinije mjesto i za starana ulaganja. Drugo, mnogi kreatori politike i zvaninici u BiH jo uvijek ne shvataju kako su fundamentalne promjene koje ohrabruju privatno ulaganje. Postoje problemi u zakoskom sistemu, koji nije potpun, licenciranju i regulatornom sistemu, koja su vrlo birokratina i naporna, i u financijskom sistemu , koji je slab ili ne postojei. Vanost dobrog zakonskog i financijskog sistema ne moe bit prenaglaena. Ovi sistemi su stubovi za trino baziranu ekonomiju privatnog sektora. Dok je progres u toku u nekima od ovih podruja, zemlja se jo uvijek kree suvie sporo da bi se promjenila orijentacija ekonomija prema privatnom sektoru  a vrijeme istie. Organizatori su me zamolili da se prvo osvrnem na financijski sistem . To je jedno od podruja glavnog problema koji koi privatna ulaganja. Financijski sistem u BiH je trenutno vrlo slab i isparan. Mnoga trita i instrumenti na koje se oslanjaju investitori u privatnom sektoru u razvijenim zamljama jo uvijek ne postoje. Jedna pozitivna osobina za strane ulagae , naruito one iz Evrope je da je vezivanje Konvertibilne marke za Euro kroz striktan curency board znai da za investitore iz Euro podruja koji investiraju u BIH ne postoji rizik kursne razlike. Takoer, CBBH zakon zahtjeva od CBBH da odri punu konvertibilnost KM-a u DEM i EURO. Ove osobine reima kusne razmjene su vrlo znaajne za direktna strana ulaganjai trebaju biti naglaena potencijalnim stranim investitorima u svakoj prilici. Monopol koji zavodi za platni promet imaju na domae bez gotovinsko plaanje je bila ozbiljna smetnja za direktna strana ulaganja. Svako ko ne dolazi iz podruja bive Jugoslavije jednostavno ne razumije ove zavode i potrebu da poslovna zajednica obavlja sva domaa plaanja preko njih. Njihov zakonski monoplol je ukinut prole godine u oba entiteta.To je vrlo pozitivno . Proces pomjeranja domaih platnih transakcija iz zavoda na komercijalne banke je u toku. To je takoer pozitivno . Ali ovaj prenos je jo vijek u jednoj ranoj fazi. Bankarske agencije, u saradnji sa CBBH su razvile kriterije koje e koristiti da bi se odobrile bankama dozvole za obavljanje ovih usluga platnog prometa. U Federaciji, 20 banaka je apliciralo do sada i prve dozvole bi se trebale izdati za nekoliko sedmica. Ne mislim da je ijedna banka u RS aplicirala do sada, ali oekujem da e se to desiti uskoro. Potreba da se razvije moderan platni sistem u BiH je od kritine vanosti za ekonomski razvoj. Zavodi za platni promet su obezbjeivali siguran oblik platnih transakcija ali oni su antiteza trino baziranih sistema jer je njihova uloga bazirana na regulacijskim i monopolskim moima vie nego na klijentovom izboru. injenica da platne funkcije trebaju da ponu svoj transfer na komercijalne banke koje e regulisati njihove transakcije kroz njihove rezervne raune kod CBBH bie od pomoi da se privuku strana ulaganja. To je opta struktura domaih platnih sistema u svim razvijenim zemljama, ali znak slabosti bankarskog sektora u BiH je to ovaj transfer mora biti obavljen u fazama a i da sve banke nee dobiti odobrenje za obavljenje ovih platnih funkcija. CBBH e uiniti sve to moe da bi obezbijedila da ova transformacija BiH platnog sistema ide glatko i da je krajnji rezultat moderan, trino orijetisan sistem. Na cilj je da se ova transformacija obavi ove godine. Ali reforma bankarstva mora da ide mnogo dalje od prenoenja domaeg platnog sistema na komercijalne banke. Postoje dva glavna problema sa BIH bankarskim sektorom. Prvi je da on u stvari nije jedan bankarski sektor, postoje u stvari tri bankarska sektora u BiH . BiH je mala zemlja . Imae tekoa u kreiranju financijskih institucija sa dovoljno snage i osnove da bi igrale glavnu ulogu u finansiranju razvoja prvatnog sektora . Ali ako nastavi da dijeli svoj mali financijski prostor u tri odvojena trita nee nikad kreirati financijske institucije koje su joj potrebne da bi pospjeila razvoj. U ostatku svijeta rastui trend financijskih institucija je sjedinjavanje da bi se stvorile vee, vie visoko kapitalizirane i esto van granine institucije. Ali mi u BIH jo nemamao jednu banku koja posluje u oba entiteta  sem CBBH! Drugi vaan problem, koji je djelimino uzrokovan prvim, je da su BIH banke uglavnom jako male i podkapitalizirane da bi bile sposobne za bilo kakvu znaajniju ulogu u privlaenju uteevina i financiranju ulaganja u privatni sektor. Promjena poinje da se odvija. Na primjer, Federacijska Bankarska Agencija obavlja dobar posao u zatvaranju nesolventnih banaka i ohrabrivanju malih ali solventnih banaka da se ujedinjuju. Kao posljedica toga, broj banaka koji je licenciran u Federaciji je opao sa 55 na 42 u toku prole godine. Ali mnogo vie reformi treba da se obavi  i to brzo, mnotvo malih slabih banaka ne pomae razvoj. One mogu igrati malu direktnu ulogu a problemi koji imaju moe dovesti do gubljenja povjerenja u sve banke, ukljuujui one koju su vrste. Pregledao sam cifre KM depozita BiH banaka nedavno. Znam da e mnoge banke imati depozite u valutama drugim od KM-a tako da ove KM cifre nisu indikator njene stvarne veliine. Ali njihovi KM depoziti su postali mnogo vei dio njihovih ukupnih depozita u toku prole godine. Cifre koje govore o veliini banke bazirane na KM depozitima su iznenaujue, u smislu da je veina banak nevjerovatno mala: nivo depozita (KM miliona) Broj registrovanih banaka preko 100mil. 0 50-100mil. 2 30-50mil. 3 20-30mil. 4 10-20mil. 6 5-10mil. 7 1-5mil. 14 ispod 1mil. 22 Organizator me je pitao da takoer razgovaramo o razvoju drugih financijskih trita i instrumenata kao to su trite novca, trite vrjednosnim papirima, burza itd. Posao poinje oko ovoga. Vano je da su ova trita razvijena u BiH tako da ljudi i poslovanja imaju itav niz tednih financijskih varijanti koje su im otvorene. Razvoj dobro razvijenog, progresivnog i modernog bankarskog i platnog sistema je fundamentalniji i vaniji. To je baza na kojoj su ova druga trita razvijena. One nisu alternativa suoavanju sa nekim tekim izborima u reformi bankarskog sektora, kao to je privatizacija velikog broja dravnih banaka, zatvaranje nesolventnih banaka, i razvoj banaka koje djeluju na teritoriju cijele BiH. Takoer, zabrinut sam da u mnogim novim tritima iste greke koje su se ve desile u bankarskom sektoru izgledaju kao da se ponavljaju. To znai, ovo pitanje bie vieno kao primarno politiko pitanje vie nego kao ekonomsko i BiH e kreirati dva ili moda tri svakog trita. Ponavljam ono to sam rekao ranije: BiH je mala zemlja , financijske institucije i trita u cijelom svijetu se ujedinuju da bi se stvorila vea, mnogo likvidnija trita. Bila bi greka za BiH da krene u suprotnom pravcu od ovog trenda. Trebaju se napraviti trita novca, trita vrijednosnim papirima, berza itd koja se moe uvezati preko cijele zemlje i koja takoer moe biti jednostavno vezana sa tritima u susjednim zemljama i konano sa irokim evropskim tritom. U kreiranju ovih novih trita, BiH treba da gleda naprijed u budunost, ne unazad u prolost. kraj

Title: Presentation for the students of the economic faculties in Brcko and Banja Luka
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: ' THE ROLE OF THE CENTRAL BANK OF BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA' LECTURE TO STUDENTS OF THE FACULTY OF ECONOMICS, BANJA LUKA UNIVERSITY. 13 DECEMBER 2001 PETER NICHOLL GOVERNOR CBBH I am very pleased to have this opportunity to talk to you today. The subject of my lecture is the roles of the central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina (CBBH). I will leave plenty of time at the end of the session for you to ask any questions you have. The CBBH commenced its operations on 11 August 1997 so it is just over four years old  very young by central banking standards. It is interesting to remember what the financial system in BH looked like in 1997. There were four currencies being used. There were over 70 commercial banks but most of them were very small, none of them operated over the whole country, and in the main, citizens did not use the banks. There were three payments bureaus each of which had a monopoly on non-cash payments in the territory they covered. In short, it was a very weak and fragmented financial system. The CBBH is a state-level institution. Its mandate covers the whole country. It operates under its own law. The law is a very good one. In saying that, I am not praising myself as the law was developed and passed before I came to Bosnia to be governor. The CBBH reports to the presidency of BH, and through them, to the parliament of BH. The law is a very detailed one and sets out very precisely what the CBBH has to do and also what we cannot do. Subject to the requirements of our law, the CBBH is an independent institution. The law says specifically that the CBBH 'shall be entirely independent... In the pursuit of its objectives and the performance of its tasks.' This operational independence is very important. The strategic direction of the CBBH is set by a governing board of four members. The governor is the chairman of the board and there are three local members. All of them have been involved from the beginning of the CBBH. So we have had good continuity, which has also been important. The day-to-day management is in the hands of the governor, who is also the chief executive officer, and three local vice governors. The CBBH has five offices. The head office is in Sarajevo. There are three main units, in Banja Luka, Mostar and Sarajevo, and two branches, in Brcko and pale. We have 240 staff. I am the only full-time staff member of the CBBH who is not a Bosnian citizen. So it is very much a Bosnian institution. Monetary policy: The most important function of the CBBH is to 'formulate, adopt and control the monetary policy of BH.' the CBBH operates monetary policy through a currency board arrangement. This is stipulated in the CBBH law and in the Dayton agreement. The choice of a currency board had two main motivations. First, it provides a firm nominal anchor in the form of a fixed exchange rate. This was considered critical for the very uncertain post-war economic situation in BH. Second, it took into account the difficulty there would be in establishing institutions and making political decisions in the complex political environment that existed in BH. The three essential features of the currency board, all of which are specified in the CBBH law, are: The BH currency, the convertible mark (KM) is tied to the Deutscmark (DEM) at a fixed exchange rate. The fixed exchange rate is 1KM 1DEM. It is now also tied to the euro at the same rate as the DEM (1 KM 0.51129 euro). It has been tied to the euro at this rate ever since the euro was introduced on 1 January 1999. This KM/euro exchange rate will shortly be put in to the CBBH law as the DEM will soon cease to exist as a currency; The KM liabilities of the CBBH have to be fully backed with convertible foreign assets. At the end of November 2001 our KM liabilities were KM 1,55 billion and our foreign assets were KM 1,62 billion so we had more than 100% coverage; The CBBH has to be prepared to convert KM for DEM at any time for any amount. Since we started in 1997 we have issued KM 5,43 billion and we have converted back KM 4,11 billion. So it has been a fully convertible currency. Linking the KM to the DEM through a currency board was an easy choice for BH because the DEM was already extensively used in the country and was the currency people trusted. It has been a successful choice too: The KM has been a stable currency against the DEM and the euro since it was introduced; Inflation in BH is low and stable. The latest figures are below 1% per annum in both entities; KM use has risen rapidly within BH and it is now the dominant transactions currency in all parts of the country. Our KM liabilities have risen from KM 132 million when we started in August 1997 to KM 1,55 billion at the end of November 2001.; The KM can even be traded in a number of other countries in Europe; I do not think there is any other type of monetary policy, except the adoption of the DEM as the currency of BH, that could have given a country like BH a stable and trusted currency and low inflation this quickly. Why has the currency board worked in BH? I think there are four main reasons: First, people have faced many financial traumas. They therefore value a stable currency. The currency board consequently has a high level of public support within BH; Second, people had complete trust in the anchor currency, the DEM. A strict currency board has allowed the CBBH, a new institution with no track record, to gain some of the credibility of the DEM and the Bundesbank; Third, some people say it is because the CBBH has a foreign governor. I think that is only a small part of the reason. In my view, the major reason it has worked is the very good legal and institutional framework the CBBH operates under: The goal of the CBBH is simple, clear and specified in the law; The law limits our activities where there would be any potential conflict with the currency board requirements; Within these statutory goals and limitations, the CBBH is independent of political direction; We have sensible and sound internal decision-making processes; We are easily and firmly held accountable. A breach of the currency board requirements would be quickly obvious to all. Within the current economic jargon, it is a very transparent form of policy implementation. Some economists and others argue that a currency board has disadvantages because of the limitations it places on the economic roles of the CBBH. For example: The CBBH can not play a role in providing liquidity to the banking sector (i.e., it can not act as lender of last resort); The CBBH can not finance the government; The CBBH can not play any direct role in financing economic development; The exchange rate cannot be used as a tool to adjust to economic shocks or poor economic performance. These areas of policy discretion, if used wisely and in moderation, could be of advantage to economic development in BH. There are lots of projects in BH for which a little bit of CBBH finance may be helpful. But the problem would be in keeping the CBBH credit to a little bit. the experience of the region is that excess central bank credit has usually been created and the result is inflation. That does not help business, employment or confidence in BH. So in my view, the strict currency board is the best approach for BH and that to change it would have very adverse economic and social impacts. I fully understand the concerns about the state of the economy and the high level of unemployment that are causing people to examine all the policy options BH has to try and address these problems. But to change the currency board would be the wrong option and would make things worse rather than improve them. Some people are saying that to adopt a currency board is to give up monetary policy as an instrument of macro-economic policy. That view is wrong. Deciding to adopt a currency board is as much a monetary policy choice as adopting any other type of monetary policy. It is a rule-based rather than a discretionary form of monetary policy, thats true. But that is a major reason why it was chosen and is one of its strengths rather than a weakness. By choosing to adopt a currency board, BH decided that the aim of monetary policy will be to achieve stability  stability in the value of the local currency against the anchor currency and stability in the rate of inflation. The desire for stability has led to a revival of interest in currency boards in the 1990s when 6 or 7 were established, including the one in BH. During the 1990s a number of countries took the desire for currency stability further by fully adopting the currency of another country (so-called dollarisation) or introducing a new common currency over a number of countries (the euro zone). Such areas have taken the currency board principle of the importance of currency stability to their furthest extent by adopting someone else's currency or a common currency. Once one adds to these countries all the countries that have during the 1990s adopted some form of inflation targeting, the overwhelming direction that monetary policy around the world has been taking over the last fifteen years is to make stability the objective of monetary policy. So the monetary policy being implemented in BH through the currency board is not unusual at all. What would be unusual, and would have a very adverse effect on potential foreign investors, would be a return in BH to the old discretionary type of monetary policies that have failed in many countries  and failed spectacularly in this region. I think a more apt name for that type of monetary policy would be indiscretionary rather than discretionary. I believe therefore that the BH currency board must be continued for the following reasons: There is widespread public support for it because it has provided one of the few elements of stability the people of BH have had for some time; It would be risky to change it. Confidence in the KM would drop as people waited to see how any alternative monetary policy would work; Currency boards have worked well in other eastern European countries such as Latvia and Bulgaria. Currency boards and joint currencies are becoming acceptable, even fashionable; The long-term goal of BH policy is to take the economy closer to Europe. The KM is already tied to the euro. It would therefore seem sensible to maintain this link; Alternative types of monetary policy are much more likely to generate inflation rather than economic growth. There is one academic in BH who has said publicly recently that an inflation rate of around 20% would be good for economic growth and employment in BH. I have not seen any evidence from anywhere to support such a claim. Most countries in the world are aiming for inflation in the low single figures  because they believe that is the best inflation rate to promote investment and economic growth. Also, it would be impossible to maintain an inflation rate at around 20%. All the pressures would be for it to rise further. Stability in a country's exchange rate and inflation rate are extremely important economic benefits. They allow people to plan their economic decisions ahead with more confidence. This is particularly important for investment as the economic return from any investment is spread over many years. Stability in inflation and the exchange rate are therefore critically important for investment. A small country like BH needs substantial private foreign investment. Foreign investors don't need to come to BH. They can supply the small BH market from a neighbouring country or even from their home country. Stability in inflation and the exchange rate are also extremely important for financial sector development. At present, the main risk the banks need to focus on is the credit risk of their borrowers. This is still a major problem in BH but as it is the main area of risk, it is possible to develop policies to progressively reduce it. As a consequence, we are seeing the banking sector in BH becoming more normal. But if the banks also had to worry about inflation risk and exchange rate risk, I am sure we would not have seen any significant improvements in the banking sector. Stability is also an important social benefit because it is more frequently the poor who suffer from the adverse affects of devaluation or inflation. The rich or well-connected can often finds ways around it or even ways to benefit from it. Other CBBH roles: One other important role of the CBBH is our role in the payments system. We issue the KM and that has become the dominant means of cash payments in BH. Three of the four currencies that were in use in BH back in 1997, the Bosnian dinar, the Yugoslavian dinar and the Kuna, have either completely or largely disappeared from BH. The fourth one, the DEM, is still in use but it too has been substantially replaced by the KM over the last three years. This trend has accelerated over the last few months because of the impending replacement of the DEM by the euro. We sent 935 million of DEM currency back to Germany in 1999, 842 million in 2000 and so far we have sent over DEM 1.9 billion back this year. That is a grand total so far of DEM 3.7 billion. The CBBH also played a major role in reform of the domestic non-cash payments system. Banking sector: The country has an improving banking sector. The reform in the banking sector has gone further and faster than reform in any other sector. Confidence is coming back, depositors are beginning to return to banks and banks are beginning to lend on more reasonable terms. Competition is real, helped by the arrival of some good foreign banks. Proportionately, foreign investment in the banking sector has been higher than in any other sector in BH. Yet we have politicians criticising banks for not lending enough and for holding so much of their liquidity outside BH. These politicians need to ask themselves why banks are still reluctant to lend more in BH. After all, banks are in the business of lending, as that is how they earn their income. But they will only lend if they can be confident that the customer will pay back the loan or, if he does not, they can go to the courts. So the key need is to get these banking risks down. The worst thing to do would be to pressure banks to ignore the real commercial risks that still exist in BH. Conclusion: Unless the regulatory, legal and tax systems are changed, and changed quickly and substantially, BH will have a very difficult future. These problems are interrelated and have a common core  a lack of understanding of the way in which a private sector economy works and what the investment environment needs to be like to attract the level of investment that BH needs. This is where the attention of BH politicians and international consultants and advisors needs to be directed. It is this basic regulatory and microeconomic reform that will determine the future of BH. There is not one, quick policy fix that BH can adopt to get themselves out of the difficult economic situation that has built up over a long period of time. It is not that simple. Continued banking reform, accelerated regulatory reform, legal and court reform, reduction of bureaucracy, lowering of the tax burden, privatisation  there is a long list of things that need to be done. And time is running out to do them. In the meantime, the stability of the currency board is the most positive attribute BH has for attracting foreign investment. Given the fragility of the economic and balance of payments situations in BH at present, undermining the stability of the KM by adopting some other discretionary form of monetary policy would be the best way I can think of to guarantee that BH will have an economic crisis. Macro-economic sustainability in BH. While I believe strongly that BH should maintain its currency board, there will need to be changes made in other areas if BH is to have macro-economic sustainability over the medium term. The currency board requirement means that the CBBH cannot issue KM currency in any quantity it chooses or the economy needs. The amount that can be issued is tied to the net position of Bosnia and Herzegovina's external accounts. This is the currency board arithmetic. What does this currency board arithmetic mean for a central bank and a country? If the net position on a countrys external accounts is positive, the central banks foreign reserves will increase as the foreign inflows are changed into the domestic currency. There is nothing to stop a currency board having more than 100% backing for its domestic currency liabilities. (Indeed, at present the CBBH has foreign reserves equal to 106% of our KM liabilities.) So if the overall foreign accounts are in good shape, there will be no pressure on the currency board and medium term economic sustainability will be easy. But, if the countrys overall foreign accounts are negative, the situation is very different. If people wish to buy foreign exchange with their KM currency, the CBBH has to do so without limit. That is what full convertibility means. The level of the CBBHs foreign reserves will fall as will the volume of the domestic money supply. The currency board rules will still be met, but the balance sheet of the CBBH will decline and could continue to decline until there were no more foreign reserves. At that stage, BH could only meet foreign expenditures as they earned or gained foreign exchange. The current position of the balance of payments of BH are a cause for concern. The trade deficit is very high. The amount of foreign private capital coming into the country is still very low. The flows that have made the situation work are the large amounts of official capital and repatriations by Bosnians living abroad. Looking ahead: We know the level of official capital flows will slow, the only uncertainty being exactly when this will occur: It will be difficult to rapidly increase export receipts, though more could be done than has so far occurred; The country is very heavily dependent on imports. A slowdown in reconstruction will slow imports to some extent. But a rapid slowdown in imports would also hurt consumption and living standards; It is difficult to predict or rely on repatriations; The item that has the most potential to change rapidly is foreign private investment. But for BH to attract more foreign private investment the environment for private investment will have to change substantially. If BH does not attract large quantities of private foreign investment, pressure will come on the level of foreign reserves as the official capital flows slow down. This in turn will decrease the domestic money supply and put upward pressure on interest rates. Monetary policy as implemented through a currency board arrangement is pro-cyclical when the economy has a foreign exchange problem i.e. it will increase the contractionary pressure on the economy The situation facing the BH economy is critical and urgent. Most of the policy-makers have some understanding of the foreign exchange problems. But they still seem to think they have policy choices and a sense of urgency is lacking. In my view the only choice is to make BH an attractive place for private investment and to do everything necessary to attract foreign private capital. If that does not happen, the BH economy will have major foreign exchange problems and the currency board will be unable to protect the country from those shocks. Indeed, it could become one of the victims of those shocks as politicians look for scapegoats to explain the countrys economic problems to the people. Foreign investment is increasing. In 1999 for example, direct foreign investment was 50% higher than in 1998 and though we do not yet have figures for 2000, I am sure it has risen strongly again. But while this growth rate sounds spectacular, it is from a very low base. Direct foreign investment into BH in 1999 is estimated to have been KM 170 million. The current account deficit for that year was KM 1.4 billion. So private foreign investment financed just 12% of the current account deficit. That year. BH needs to be increasing private foreign investment by around 200% a year over the next two years rather than 50% a year if the current economic growth rates are to be sustainable when the official aid flows slow down. This target is possible. The arrival here of foreign banks from Austria and Croatia shows that there is increased interest from foreign investors. But the climate for private investment in BH is still far from supportive. This applies to local investment as well as foreign investment. There are still problems in the legal system, which is incomplete, the licensing and regulatory systems, which are far too bureaucratic, intrusive and multi-level, and in the financial system, which is still relatively weak. Improving the environment for private investment, both local and foreign, is the key economic issue facing this country. It is this that will determine whether BH has a sustainable economy  and whether it is a country in which good students like yourselves should stay to be a part of its future. The second statement is that the banking sector in BH has been through many significant changes over the last year and it is in better shape today than it was when we held our last conference. Indeed, the improvements have been even more rapid over the last year than they were in the preceding year. Thats very positive. I will briefly list some of the most significant changes over the last year: The payments system has been reformed and now matches best European practice; There have been significant increases in a bank's minimum capital imposed by the banking agencies; Deposit insurance has started and is having an impact on citizens confidence in banks; More foreign banks have started operations in BH; Five banks now have branches in both entities; And so on. But the third thing I have said in past years and have to repeat this year is that there is still a long way to go before BH has a banking sector that can play the major economic role that the banking sector plays in most other economies in Europe. We are still at an early stage in the bank reform process. At our two past conferences I have spoken mainly about bank reform and payments reform rather than about the central bank and the BH currency board arrangements. There were two reasons for this. The first was that there was so much happening in bank reform and payments reform. The second was that I thought that the currency board arrangements were well-understood and accepted and I didn't need to say too much about them.

Title: The Reform Of The Banking System In Bih
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: Comments of the Governor of the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Peter W. Nicholl, at the Peace Implementation Council Meeting, 23 & 24 May, 2000 Brussels Belgium Mr. Chairman, Excellencies, I appreciate the opportunity to speak at this meeting. I speak primarily as a Bosnian official. I want to make three points that are related to two of the themes proposed for this Peace Implementation Council document, Economic Reform and Institution Building. Payments Systems: The payments system has to be reformed in BiH and the Payments Bureaus closed. This was an objective set by the Madrid PIC meeting. A deadline of 31st December 2000 was set. After a slow start, good progress is now being made. For example, the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina, (CBBH) has recently signed a contract with a foreign supplier for a Real Time Clearing System for high value transactions to be introduced in BiH. It will be in place by the end of this year. But the reform task is far from finished. It is critically important that the international community continues to provide technical and financial assistance and political pressure to ensure this job is completed. Please dont reduce your focus on this issue. Single Economic spaces: The second issue I want to comment on is the creation of a single economic space in BiH. BiH is a small country. Being a small country can be an economic handicapI know, I come from a small country, New Zealand. But BiH compounds this problem by subdividing its economic and financial space into two or even three. This frankly is economic nonsense. It is critical for the development of a viable economy in BiH that political and economic issued become less entwined. Economic decisions must begin to be taken on sensible, economic criteria, not political criteria. While this comment is addressed mainly to my Bosnian colleagues, it is also addressed to the International Community (IC). The IC frequently aids and abets the BiH authorities to subdivide its economic and financial space by helping them to build institutions and markets at the entity level that should be state-wide. In my view, two such examples are deposit insurance and the stock exchange. On this issue of creating a single economic space there are often inconsistencies between the rhetoric of the IC and their actions. State Institutions: Most speakers at this meeting have been critical of the performance of the state institutions in BiH. It is possible to build successful state institutions in BiH. The CBBH is a state institution. It works successfully. In my view, the major reason it works successfully is not that it has a foreigner as its head, but because of the way it is structured. The CBBH has: Clear and unambiguous goals A good legal framework Good internal decision making processes A sensible degree of independence. The politicians have set the goals for the CBBH but they do not have any role in the day to day operations of the bank In other words, the legal and operational structure of the CBBH is much the same as that of central banks in other countriesand it works. But most other state institutions, and particularly the ministries, are constructed in a way that we would never use in our countries. They are built on political criteria rather than effective operational criteria. We should not therefore be surprised by their relatively poor performance. I believe the design of the state institutions and particularly the ministries, is an issue the BiH authorities and the IC need to pay much more attention to. Making the ministries political also undermines the responsibility and effectiveness of the institutions that should deal with the political issues in BiHThe Presidency, The Council of Ministers and the Parliament.

Title: Managing Foreign Exchange Risks In Bosnia And Herzegovina
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: MANAGING FOREIGN EXCHANGE RISKS IN BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA. COMMENTS BY PETER NICHOLL GOVERNOR CENTRAL BANK OF BIH AT A CONFERENCE ON FOUNDING PRIVATISATION INVESTMENT FUNDS IN BIH ORGANISED BY IFC, USAID AND THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE OF CANTON SARAJEVO. SARAJEVO, BIH 14-15 OCTOBER, 1999 INTRODUCTION THE AIMS OF THIS CONFERENCE ARE TO HELP PROMOTE THE PRIVATISATION OF STATE-OWNED ASSETS AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF A VIGOROUS PRIVATE SECTOR IN THE BIH ECONOMY. THESE ARE VERY IMPORTANT POLICY GOALS FOR BIH. IT IS CLEAR THAT THE MAIN DRIVER OF ECONOMIC GROWTH IN BIH IN THE FUTURE IS GOING TO BE THE PRIVATE SECTOR. FOR THE PRIVATE SECTOR TO DEVELOP AND PROSPER, AN ECONOMIC CLIMATE THAT IS SYMPATHERTIC TO AND ENCOURAGES PRIVATE INVESTMENT NEEDS TO BE CREATED. THIS IS A KEY ELEMENT OF THE ECONOMIC POLICIES OF ALL THE LEVELS OF GOVERNMENT IN BIH. I JUST WANT TO MAKE TWO GENERAL COMMENTS ABOUT THIS BEFORE MOVING ON TO THE TOPIC I WAS ASKED TO ADDRESS FOR THIS CONFERENCE. THE FIRST IS THAT DISCUSSION ON INCREASING PRIVATE SECTOR INVESTMENT IN BIH OFTEN FOCUSES ON WHAT NEEDS TO BE DONE TO ATTRACT FOREIGN PRIVATE INVESTMENT. IT IS VERY IMPORTANT THAT BIH ATTRACTS FOREIGN PRIVATE INVESTMENT. BUT IT IS JUST AS IMPORTANT, POSSIBLY EVEN MORE IMPORTANT, TO CREATE AN ENVIRONMENT THAT ENCOURAGES LOCAL PRIVATE INVESTMENT. THE FOUNDING OF PRIVATISATION INVESTMENT FUNDS IN BIH IS ONE POLICY THAT WILL HELP IN PROMOTING LOCAL PRIVATE INVESTMENT. SECOND, I THINK MANY POLICY MAKERS AND OFFICIALS IN BIH DO NOT YET REALISE HOW FUNDAMENTAL THE CHANGES TO MANY OF THEIR PROCESSES AND INSTITUTIONS NEED TO BE IF THEY ARE REALLY TO CREATE AN ENVIRONMENT THAT DOES ENCOURAGE PRIVATE INVESTMENT. AT PRESENT THE ENVIRONMENT IN BIH IS STILL VERY UNFRIENDLY TO PRIVATE INVESTMENT. THERE ARE PROBLEMS IN THE LEGAL SYSTEM, THE REGULATORY SYSTEM AND IN THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM. MOST OF THIS IS A LEGACY OF THE COUNTRYS PAST BUT THE COUNTRY IS MOVING MUCH TOO SLOWLY TO CHANGE THINGS. I FEEL THAT THE MIND-SET THAT DOSENT REALLY TRUST THE PRIVATE SECTOR IS STILL QUITE DEEPLY ENTRENCHED IN SOME POLITICIANS AND BUREAUCRATS. THE BIH CURRENCY BOARD. THE TOPIC OF MY ADDRESS TO YOU IS MANAGING FOREIGN EXCHANGE RISK IN BIH. I WANT TO START BY BRIEFLY EXPLAINING THE NATURE OF THE BIH CURRENCY BOARD AS IT IS HIGHLY RELEVANT FOR THE TYPE AND DEGREE OF RISK THAT IS FACED BY DEALING IN BIHS LEGAL TENDER CURRENCY, THE CONVERTIBLE MARKA (KM). UNDER THE BIH CONSTITUTION, THE CBBH IS THE SOLE AUTHORITY FOR MONETARY POLICY AND ISSUING CURRENCY IN BIH. THE CBBH LAW PROVIDES THAT THE CBBH WILL OPERATE AS A CURRENCY BOARD. WHAT DOES OPERATING AS A CURRENCY BOARD MEAN? FIRST, YOU PEG YOUR DOMESTIC CURRENCY TO AN EXTERNAL CURRENCY THAT YOU CONSIDER TO BE SOUND AND STABLE. FOR BIH THE CHOICE OF THE EXTERNAL CURRENCY TO PEG TO WAS AN EASY ONE. THE DEUTSCHEMARK HAS BEEN A SOUND AND STABLE CURRENCY FOR A LONG TIME; THE CENTRAL BANK THAT ISSUED IT, THE BUNDESBANK, HAS AN UNPARRALLELED REPUTATION FOR STRENGTH AND STABILITY; AND THE DM WAS ALREADY WIDELY USED IN BIH BECAUSE PEOPLE HAD CONFIDENCE IN IT. SECOND, THE PEG IS FIXED IN THE LAW SO THAT IT CANNOT BE CHANGED. IT IS SET AT 1 KM 1 DM (ARTICLE 32). THIRD, THE CBBH HAS TO MAINTAIN AT LEAST 100% BACKING IN FOREIGN EXCHANGE RESERVES FOR ALL OF ITS KM LIABILITIES (ARTICLE 31). THIS REQUIREMENT MEANS THAT WE CAN ONLY ISSUE KMS IF WE OBTAIN FOREIGN CURRENCY IN RETURN. WE CANT PRINT MONEY. THIS IS A KEY ELEMENT OF THE CURRENCY BOARD AND ENSURES A SOUND CURRENCY AND LOW INFLATION. AS AT 10 SEPTEMBER 1999 WE HAD MONETARY LIABILITIES OF KM 375 MILLION AND WE HAD KM 405 MILLION FOREIGN RESERVE ASSETS BACKING THOSE LIABILITIES. SO IN FACT WE HAVE MORE THAN 100% BACKING AT PRESENT. FOURTH, WE HAVE TO MAINTAIN FULL CONVERTIBILITY OF THE KM INTO DM WITHIN BIH (ARTICLE 33). THIS MEANS THAT IF YOU HAVE KM AND WANT TO CHANGE IT INTO DEM YOU CAN DO IT WITHOUT RESTRICTION. FIFTH, SINCE THE INTRODUCTION OF THE EURO ON 1 JANUARY 1999, THE KM HAS BEEN TIED TO THE EURO THROUGH THE DM. THAT IS, THE KM IS FIXED BY LAW TO THE DM, THE DM IS FIXED BY LAW TO THE EURO, SO THE KM IS ALSO EFFECTIVELY TIED TO THE EURO, AND TO THE ELEVEN COMPONENT CURRENCIES THAT ARE NOW SUB-UNITS OF THE EURO. THE CBBH WILL NOW BUY AND SELL THE KM AT FIXED EXCHANGE RATES AGAINST ANY OF THE ELEVEN EURO CURRENCIES. SIXTH, THE CBBH LAW SAYS THAT THE CBBH CAN NOT EXTEND CREDIT TO ANYONE, INCLUDING THE GOVERNMENT AND THE COMMERCIAL BANKS. (ARTCICLE 67) THIS CLAUSE MEANS THAT THE CBBH CANT PLAY ANY DIRECT ROLE IN FUNDING ECONOMIC RECONSTRCUTION IN BIH OR IN PROVIDING LIQUIDITY TO THE COMMERCIAL BANKING SYSTEM. BUT WHAT THE CBBH DOES PROVIDE IS A STABLE ENVIRONMENT WHERE PEOPLE HAVE CONFIDENCE IN THE MONEY AND WHERE INFLATION IS LOW. THAT IS THE BEST CONTRIBUTION THE CBBH CAN MAKE TO ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND A SOUND FINANCIAL SYSTEM IN BIH. IT ALSO MEANS TWO THINGS FOR MANAGING FOREIGN EXCHANGE RISK IN BIH OPERATIONS. FIRST, THERE WERE PRIOR TO THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE CBBH, FOUR CURRENCIES THAT WERE USED WITHIN BIH. THAT IS STILL THE CASE. THE DM, THE CROATIAN KUNA AND THE YUGOSLAVIAN DINAR ARE ALL STILL IN USE IN BIH. THEY ARE ALL CURRENCIES ISSUED BY FOREIGN CENTRAL BANKS AND THEIR EXCHANGE RATE IS NOT UNDER THE CONTROL OR EVEN THE INFLUENCE OF THE CBBH. IN THE PAST, THE EXISTENCE OF THESE MULTIPLE CURRENCIES IN USE IN BIH MEANT THAT PEOPLE AND FIRMS FACED EXCAHNGE RATE RISKS EVEN ON DOMESTIC TRANSACTIONS. FOR EXAMPLE, THEIR INCOME COULD BE IN ONE CURRENCY AND THEIR COSTS IN ANOTHER AND THE EXCHANGE RATE BETWEEN THOSE TWO CURRENCIES COULD, AND DOES MOVE. NOW THERE IS A FIXED LINK BETWEEN TWO OF THE CURENCIES IN USE IN BIH, THE KM AND THE DM, AND THE KM IS INCREASINGLY BECOMING THE DOMINANT CURRENCY FOR TRANSACTIONS. SO THE AMOUNT OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE RATE RISK WITHIN THE BIH FINANCIAL SYSTEM HAS BEEN SUBSTANTIALLY REDUCED. SECOND, THE KM CURRENCY HAS BEEN STRONG AND STABLE SINCE IT FIRST APPEARED IN AUGUST 1997. IT HAS REMAINED STABLE THROUGHOUT A PERIOD OF SEVERE TURMOIL IN MANY OF THE WORLDS FINANCIAL MARKETS, DURING AN ELECTION CAMPAIGN IN BIH, AND DURING A WAR IN A NEIGHBORING COUNTRY. THESE EVENTS COULD, IN OTHER CIRCUMSTANCES, HAVE UNSETTLED THE KM CURRENCY. BUT WITH THE CURRENCY BOARD STRUCTURE WE HAVE, CONFIDENCE IN THE KM HAS BEEN MAINTAINED. THIS MEANS THAT THE MANAGEMENT OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE RISK IN BIH IS ESSENTIALLY THE SAME AS MANAGING FOREIGN EXCHANGE RISK OF ANY OF THE EURO CURRENCIES. THE KM IS FIXED TO THE EURO AND ITS COMPONENT CURRENCY. THE CURRENCY BOARD IS A VERY STRICT ONE AND IT IS BEING FOLLOWED RIGIDLY. THE CURRENCY BOARD ARRANGEMENT HAS WIDESPREAD POLITICAL AND PUBLIC SUPPORT IN BIH. I BELIEVE THEREFORE THAT PEOPLE OPERATING IN THE BIH ECONOMY CAN HAVE COMPLETE CONFIDENCE THAT THE VALUE OF THE KM WILL REMAIN FIXED AGAINST ITS ANCHOR CURRENCY, THE EURO.

Title: Opening Remarks Grand Opening Of New Banja Luka Premises Of The Central Bank Of Bosnia And Herzegovina
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: Speech Notes of Peter W. Nicholl Governor of the Central Bank of Bosnia & Herzegovina Peace Seminar on Bosnia and Herzegovina Stockholm Sweden, March 3, 2000 Building Institutions in a Market Economy Stockholm, March 3, 2000  All internationals agree that Bosnia and Herzegovina has to become a private sector market economy if it is to get sustainable economic growth and eventually become integrated into Europe. Most politicians and policy makers in BiH also say that this is their aim. Many of them are actually sincereat a sort of theoretical or abstract level. In practice though there are two major problems. First, most of them have never lived in an environment where private sector markets have played a major or dominant role. They have little idea of how fundamental the changes to many of their institutions and ways of thinking and behaving have to be to make their switch from state control to private markets. They are therefore tinkering with issues rather than making fundamental changes. Second, an increased role for private markets means a loss of political and financial power. The paper circulated prior to this seminar clearly showed how this leads to resistance to change. So there are problems of both understanding and of politics to overcome. At present the environment in BiH is very unfriendly to private investment and private markets. There are problems in the legal system, the regulatory system, the financial system and most economic sectors still have state-owned enterprises operating them. I want to first talk about a general mistake I think that the International Community is making in dealing with economic reform in BiH. The mistake is that every issue in BiH is treated as a Political Issue. There has been little success in persuading the politicians that some issues are purely economic and technical and should be decided on those criteria. The main reason for this I believe is that we never try. We play their game. One consequence of this is that even though BiH is a very small country and the trend everywhere else is to create larger financial institutions, four years after Dayton, the Bosnian financial system is still divided into two or even three relatively distinct systems. For example, there is only one bank that operates over the whole country, the CBBH. Not one of the 59 so-called commercial banks yet operates over the whole country. I will give you another example. There are international consultants assisting the Bosnian authorities in setting up a stock exchange. They came to seek my support and help. Two early sentences in their paper read: BiH is a very small country and there is some doubt that a viable stock exchange can be created in BiH. However, for political reasons it will be necessary to create two stock exchanges, one in each entity. I said that those two statements are totally inconsistent. A stock exchange isnt a political institution. It is an economic institution. It only works if there are things to sell on it and people are willing to trade. You can always set up an institution called a stock exchange and it may make the politicians feel good to say they have one in Banja Luka and one in Sarajevo. But you cant make people use them and people wont use weak or non-liquid institutions. If we want to build a market economy in BiH we have to create institutions that will work, not just institutions for the sake of saying we have built one. I do not want to say a lot about the CBBH but it is an example, one of the few, of an institution that works. Why does it work? The paper says Targeted Economic Conditionality and Intensive Institution Building have done it. Those are important aspects but there are a few other fundamental characteristics that have been important too. First, the CBBH has a clear goal and can be held accountable against that goal. Most other state institutions have very general goals. Second, the CBBH is structured more or less along the lines that good corporate governance principles developed over the last 10 to 20 years in our countries would suggest. All other state ministries are set up as mirror images of the political structure: 3 heads that rotate, consensus decision-making, etc. Instead of keeping politics in the political institutions, we have created a set of political ministries. These ministries should be implementing the policies decided by their political mastersand be held accountable for their implementation performance. Instead, they frequently repeat the political discussion instead of implementing already taken decisions. The third key element of the CBBH is that we operate under a very clear and good law. It says what we have to do. It also lists a number of things we cant do. Being a foreigner has been helpful but if I had not had the support and strength provided by a good legal framework, I do not think I could have succeeded. This point is also highly relevant for creating private markets. Private investors need a clear, strong legal structure and a court system that will protect and back up their rights that the law gives them. Without that, private investment is very risky. This applies to local investors as well as foreigners.

Title: Speech Notes For The Ceremony On The Signing Of Agreements To Deal In The Km Prague
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: SPEECH NOTES FOR THE CEREMONY ON THE SIGNING OF AGREEMENTS TO DEAL IN THE KM. PRAGUE, FRIDAY 18 FEBRUARY 2000. PETER NICHOLL GOVERNOR CENTRAL BANK OF BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA. Thank you all for joining us here this morning in marking another step in the expansion of the economic relationships between Bosnia & Herzegovina and the Czech Republic. In particular I would like to welcome Vice Governor Oldrich Dedek from the Czech National Bank and thank him and his staff for all of the assistance they have given to our team when they were in Prague last November. I also want to thank the management and staff of Ceskoslovenka Obchodni Banka, Bank Austria and Volksbank Brno for their cooperation in bringing the Konvertible Marka to the Czech Republic and Slovakia. The two countries have a long history of economic and political cooperation and this cooperation has continued through to today. There are Czech peace-keepers in Bosnia Herzegovina, Czech consumer goods on the store shelves and the Skoda factory in Sarajevo is now producing hundreds of Felicias and Octavias every month and soon will start to produce a new model for the Skoda line. These automobiles fit into Skodas overall distribution plan for southeastern Europe and Turkey. Negotiations are ongoing and positive for an agreement for the bilateral promotion of trade and investments between our two countries, and this should be signed in the coming months. There are also many Bosnians here in the Czech Republic, some who have lived here for decades, others are more recent arrivals. They help to contribute to the 80 million D-mark of trade between our two countries. I believe that the acceptance of the KM at these three commercial banks here in Prague, Brno and Bratislava will serve to help foster further growth in our economic partnership as well as boost tourism and trade between the two countries. I want to tell you a few things about Bosnia and Herzegovinas Konvertible Marka currency. The KM is a young currency. It was placed into circulation in June 1998, less than two years ago. It has become the dominant currency in Bosnia and Herzegovina and it is now accepted at banks in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Hungary, Croatia, Slovenia and after March 1st, here in the Czech Republic and Slovakia. The main reason for the stability of the KM and its growing acceptance in a short period of time is that the Central Bank of BiH operates as a Currency Board. What does this mean? First, the exchange rate of the KM is fixed in the CBBH Law. It is fixed at 1KM 1DM. Since the introduction of the euro, it is also fixed through the DM exchange rate against the euro and its 11 component currencies. Second, every KM in circulation by law must be backed by at least one German Mark. This means the CBBH can not print money. It can only issue KMs if it receives an equivalent amount of foreign exchange. At present the CBBH has more than 100% backing in foreign exchange for all our KM liabilities, predominantly in euro assets Third, the Law prohibits the CBBH from making loans to the government, or from acting as a lender of last resort to the banking system. So we can not undermine the currency board by providing credit. Fourth, the Law also requires the CBBH to maintain full convertibilty of the KM into DM at all times and for any amounts. We have been in operation for 29 months and have made very good progress during this time gaining the confidence of the people and institutions that use our services and currency. The KM is now used as the dominant cash instrument in all areas of Bosnia & Herzegovina. The KM has increasingly displaced the other three currencies that were in widespread use in BiH when the CBBH was established, the DEM, the Croatian kuna and the Yugoslavian dinar. As a consequence, there has been very strong growth in the Central Banks assets since we started operation in August of 1997. Foreign reserves managed by the CBBH have trebled during 1999, from DEM 283.3 million at the beginning of 1999 to DEM 867.4 million by years end. We are still quite a small central bank but the growth rate of our reserves has been very pleasing. Our program to make the KM tradeable outside of Bosnia & Herzegovina at first glance may not seem that practical or important, since BiH is a small country and the KM is not a major currency. But it has been a very important part of stabilizing the economic climate in BiH and increasing peoples confidence in their new state and its new money. Money does little for you unless it can grant you freedom of choice. The ability to exchange their domestic currency abroad give the citizens of BiH increased mobility as they can take their own currency with them and change that currency on site and on demand at partner banks. There are also very important symbolic effects that go along with the prestige of having a convertible currency to call your own. In closing I would like to thank members of my own staff for helping to make this milestone for the KM possible. In particular, I would like to thank two people. First, my Vice Governor for International and Domestic Banking, Mr. Ljubisa Vladusic, who is here with me today, and his staff who have worked hard with our three partner banks in the Czech Republic to put into operation all of the technical and practical aspects of this cooperation. Second, Mr. Chris Simon, our Public Relations Manager, who is also here with us today, for his untiring efforts in promoting these currency arrangements and in helping to arrange this ceremony today. Thank you for coming.
