Title: Presentation of RTGS and Giro Clearing Systems
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: Speech of Governor Peter Nicholl at the Presentation of RTGS and Giro Clearing Systems in the CBBH Main Office Sarajevo on December 20, 2000 I would like to welcome all of you to the CBBH for this presentation today. I would particularly like to welcome Ambassador Tom Miller and Edward Kadunc from USAID, who will be joining me in this presentation today, and all our other distinguished guests. The purpose of todays presentation is to bring you up-to-date on progress in developing the new payments and clearing system for BiH and to show you what the new hardware for the clearing houses looks like. In that sense it can be regarded as the first appearance in public of the new system  a coming-out. The CBBH plans to open the new clearing houses for business on 5 january 2001  thats 16 days from today. All authorised commercial banks will be able to submit payment transactions to both the RTGS system and the Giro system from that day. The CBBH and the commercial banks have been testing parts of the systems for the last several weeks and those tests will continue. We will test the complete systems on 3 January 2001, fine tune them on 4 January and open them on 5 January. Will it go completely smoothly from day one? Probably not and we will need to fix any problems that arise as they occur. But the new payments system is a major step for BH that takes the BH financial system closer to a modern, financial system. The benefits of the new payments system will quickly become evident to all its users. The RTGS system is installed in the Headquarters of the CBBH. There are four Giro Clearing Centers: one in Headquarters and one in each of our Main Units in Banja Luka, Mostar and Sarajevo. The reserve accounts of the commercial banks will continue to be maintained in our Main Units as at present. Each commercial bank is connected to both the RTGS system in our Headquarters and to the GCS in the Main Unit where their reserve account is maintained. Since early December, all commercial banks have been sending payment orders to the RTGS system without any difficulties. We plan to duplicate a complete business day for the RTGS system on 23 December. (Yes , we do know that is a Saturday!!) we do not foresee any difficulties with the RTGS system based on our experience to date. We began testing the GCS with commercial banks on 18 december. We started with tests on 12 commercial banks. From tomorrow we will test another 10 banks. Next week we will test all the rest of the banks that are connected to the Giro Clearing Center. We are pleased with the way the first set of tests are going. The CBBH is confident that both systems will be ready to operate on 5 January 2001 and that most of the commercial banks will also be ready to process payments transactions. We have been very pleased with the enthusiasm shown by the commercial banks. This is a major opportunity for them to start to establish normal banking relationships with their customers. Most banks have recognised that and are eager to be involved. I have only one concern about the banks and that relates to fees. The new payments system should be substantially cheaper than the current system. For example, the CBBH will be charging banks a flat, per transaction fee of just KM 1.2 for an RTGS transaction and KM 0.05 for a Giro transaction. Commercial banks are entitled to charge their customers more than that. But I have been worried by some of the fees people have told me their banks are quoting. Banks should base their fees on the new charges they will face from the CBBH and not on the fees that have been charged by the payments bureaus in the past. Their fees should be per transaction and not a percentage of the value and they should be substantially lower than payments bureau fees. I hope competition amongst banks will ensure that this happens. If after a short period we find that all bank fees are unreasonably high, the CBBH will intervene to bring them down. Because of the efficiency of the new systems and the generosity of USAID in funding their establishment, it is possible for everyone to be a winner. Payments services can become a profit center rather than a cost center for banks, but at the same time, customers of the payments system should get substantially lower costs, especially for high value transactions. The other important element of the new payments system is the customers. Most legal entities have a deposit account in a commercial bank. They also need to open a payments account in a bank. They can open accounts in more than one bank if they wish. I urge legal entities to do this before 5 january. It will be in their own interest to do so as it is not certain that payments will be able to be made through a payments bureau after that date. If a period of transition is allowed, it will be relatively short and putting a transaction through a payments bureau will be more expensive and slower. USAID is the sole source of financing for all the hardware and software for the new clearing houses. USAID donated KM 11 million and with that we have purchased the two software systems, hardware systems and workstations from IBM, a swift software system for the messaging and terminals for the RTGS operations. From the US donation, we also supplied all authorised banks with a network server and installation of the telecommunications lines to connect to the GCS. In other words, the US funding has allowed us to move quickly and to take a comprehensive approach to software and hardware issues. I want to thank them for their generous support which has been instrumental in enabling BH to build these new clearing houses so quickly. I hope that the US authorities feel they have got good value for this investment in the future of BH. Lastly, I want to thank my own staff who are involved in this project. They have worked extremely hard; they have worked extremely well. Initially our suppliers doubted that the system could be established anywhere within the timetable that we had. It has been done. It involved the Governing Board and staff of the CBBH, the management and staff of commercial banks, telephone companies, computer consultants and lots of others. It proves that large, complex projects can be implemented quickly and smoothhly in BH if all parties work together. With the introduction of this new payments system early next year and with all the other positive changes that are now occurring in the BH banking sector, BH is finally on the way to getting a banking system that will provide its customers with the range and quality of banking services that are taken for granted in developed economies.There is still a long way to go but the signs of progress in the banking sector are now very real.

Title: Comments at the Peace Implementation Council Meeting
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: Governors Welcome and Opening Remarks The Transformation of the Payments System in BiH A joint conference presented by the Central Bank of Bosnia & Herzegovina and the BiH Chamber of Commerce The Central Bank of BiH Governor Peter Nicholl Tuesday, 28 March, 2000 10:00 As Co-Host of this conference, I would like to welcome you to the Central Bank this morning, and wish all of the participants in this historic process the best success as we undertake together a very critical project in the overall Financial Reform of BiH. All of you will be aware that the Government of BiH has accepted a strategy for fundamental reform of the BiH payments system proposed by the international community. The core of this strategy is to shift the domestic non-cash payments from the Payments Bureaus to the commercial banks and, once that is done, to close the Payments Bureaus. This is to be completed by the 31 December this year. The process of transferring domestic payments to commercial banks has already begun. The legal monopoly on such payments the Payments Bureaus had was removed last year, the Banking Agencies have developed criteria they will use to authorise banks to carry out these payments, and the Federation Banking Agency has announced the first list of authorisations. The settlement of domestic payments will be done through the accounts the commercial banks have at the CBBH. That system of commercial bank accounts at the CBBH already exists. The piece of the new system that is not yet established is the clearing system or systems that will be used to transfer the payments information generated at commercial banks to the settlement accounts those banks have at the CBBH. The Governing Board of the CBBH decided at a meeting it held on 16th February that the CBBH would take the lead in determining the future clearing systems in BiH. There were three main reasons for that: It is necessary for the CBBH to be able to control and determine the entries to the commercial banks settlement accounts at the CBBH in order to be able to ensure the Currency Board principles are protected at all times; The CBBH law lists as one of the basic tasks of the CBBH, is the duty to promote or to establish and maintain appropriate payment and settlement systems; In order to meet the deadline of 31, December 2000 to complete this transfer of payments to commercial banks, it is necessary to move speedily and in a coordinated manner. The CBBH believes it is in the best position to meet the needs for speed and coordination. This decision by the CBBH to take the lead in designing and establishing the clearing systems that will be used in the reformed payments system in BiH was endorsed by the National Payments Council at their ninth meeting on the 24th of February. It has also been supported in other meetings we have held with commercial banks and is supported by the international community. As a first step ion the establishment of a new clearing system in BiH, the Governing Board of the CBBH last Friday (24th March2000) adopted a draft plan for the implementation of an RTGS System. RTGS stands for Real Time Gross Settlement System. This decision has two important implications for the future clearing system in BiH. First, it will mean that there will be a two-tier payments system in BiH. There will be a state-wide RTGS system operated by the CBBH through which large value transactions will be settled. Below that there would be a bulk clearing system (or possibly systems as there could be more than one) that will handle the large volume of small value transactions. Transactions through this system will also be settled in the same bank accounts at the CBBH but the settlement would be on a net basis and made only once (or possibly a few) times a day. The second major implication is that BiH will be moving in one step to an advanced RTGS system even though the volume of large volume transactions in BiH at present is not high. There are several reasons why the CBBH has adopted this approach: It is the system that will ensure the best protection for the Currency Board; It is the system that will best enable commercial banks to move quickly to carry out all domestic payments including what have been called high risk transactions; We believe it is better to make one system change rather than introduce a less advanced system now and have to change to RTGS in one or two years time; We hope that the economic changes underway in BiH will lead to a quite rapid increase in market volumes of high value transactions and we wish to be ready for that; It is supported by the commercial banks, who will be the users of the systems; It is a system widely used in other countries and is once of the necessary conditions for BiH to enter Europe The CBBH will put out a tender advertisement for this RTGS system very soon, probably this week. The Governing Board will decide on the successful tenderer in April and they will start the introduction and testing of the system soon after that. We will need some banks to volunteer to take part in the testing. But there are no shortage of volunteers. Once the testing is complete, which may take 3 to 4 months, the system will start live operations and additional banks will be added to the system. The aim is to have it fully operational by 31, December 2000. My CBBH collegues who will speak to this seminar today will give you more of the technical details of the RTGS system during this seminar. The CBBH is very pleased that on a highly visiable level, reform of the payments system is moving ahead. 11 banks in the Federation out of 20 who initially applied have received licenses for various low risk and medium risk transactions. Congratulations to those banks. I expect the first banks to receive authorisations in the RS soon. This shows the public that there is an interest amongst commercial banks to take over domestic payments. We need to remember that in most other countries, domestic non cash payments are one of the basic roles of commercial banks. So what we are doing is far from new or novel. The announcement today that the CBBH will establish an RTGS system for the clearing of large value transactions in BiH is another important step in the reform process. Its my hope and that of the CBBH Board, management and staff that through this forum today and future ones like it as we progress through this very important year of transition, that answers are found to the outstanding questions and the experiances and advise we receive from the experts and colleagues aid, in a very practical sense, the reform process. The reform of the payments system in BiH is no longer a theoretical proposal, it is a practical reality and is being implemented. We will need the support and cooperation of all of you to complete the reform process smoothly. I believe the benefits to the users of the payments system and to the BiH economy will be substancial. Again, as Governor of the CBBH, I welcome you once again, and look forward to your active participation in todays conference and hope you find it beneficial.

Title: Rebuilding The Domestic Economies Of The Balkan Region And Facilitating Economic Ties Within The Region And The International Economy
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: REBUILDING THE DOMESTIC ECONOMIES OF THE BALKAN REGION AND FACILITATING ECONOMIC TIES WITHIN THE REGION AND THE INTERNATIONAL ECONOMY. Comments by PETER NICHOLL GOVERNOR CENTRAL BANK OF BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA CONFERENCE ON ECONOMIC RECONSTRUCTION IN SOUTH EASTERN EUROPE SPONSORED BY THE WORLD BANK AND THE GEORGE C. MARSHALL FOUNDATION. WASHINGTON D.C., U.S.A. 24 SEPTEMBER 1999 I WANT TO THANK THE ORGANISERS OF THIS CONFERENCE, THE WORLD BANK AND THE GEORGE C. MARSHALL FOUNDATION FOR THEIR INITIATIVE IN ORGANISING THIS CONFERENCE AND FOR INVITING ME TO PARTICIPATE. THE TOPIC FOR THIS PANEL IS VERY BROAD. I WILL CONCENTRATE MY COMMENTS ON FINANCIAL SECTOR ISSUES. IT IS THE AREA I AM WORKING IN. I ALSO BELIEVE CREATING STRONG AND FLEXIBLE FINANCIAL SECTORS IN THESE COUNTRIES IS ONE KEY REQUIREMENT FOR REBUILDING THE DOMESTIC ECONOMIES OF THE BALKAN REGION. MANY OF THE COUNTRIES IN THE REGION ARE GOING THROUGH THREE DIFFICULT TRANSITITONS SIMULTANEOUSLY: - THE TRANSITION FROM WAR TO PEACE; - THE TRANSITION FROM BEING CENTRALLY-CONTROLLED ECONOMIES DOMINATED BY THE STATE TO BECOME MARKET-ORIENTED, PRIVATE SECTOR ECONOMIES; - THE TRANSITION FROM BEING PART OF ONE NATION STATE TO BEING A NEWLY-INDEPENDENT STATE. THE CHALLENGES ARE ENORMOUS. THERE IS A NEED WITHIN THIS AVALANCHE OF CHANGE TO PROVIDE SOME ANCHORS OR AREAS OF ECONOMIC STABILITY AT AN EARLY STAGE OF THE REFORM PROCESS. THE COUNTRIES HAVE HAD A SURFEIT OF INSTABILITY, BOTH POLITICAL AND ECONOMIC. ONE SUCH ANCHOR WHICH I BELIEVE THE EXPERIENCE OF BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA (BIH) SHOWS CAN BE ATTAINED SUCCESSFULLY AND RELATIVELY QUICKLY IS A STABLE CURRENCY. BIH CHOSE TO ADOPT A CURRENCY BOARD. THEY COULD HAVE CHOSEN TO SIMPLY ADOPT THE DEUTSCHEMARK (DEM) AS THEIR CURRENCY. IT WAS ALREADY BEING USED EXTENSIVELY IN BIH, IT WAS THE ONLY CURRENCY BEING USED IN ALL PARTS OF THE COUNTRY, AND IT WAS THE CURRENCY PEOPLE HAD THE MOST TRUST IN. HOWEVER, BIH CHOSE TO HAVE ITS OWN CURRENCY BUT TIE IT 1:1 TO THE DEM THROUGH A STRICT CURRENCY BOARD. THE MAIN REASON WAS THAT THE NEW COUNTRY NEEDED SYMBOLS OF ITS EXISTENCE AND UNITY. HAVING ITS OWN CURRENCY IS ONE SUCH SYMBOL. THE CURRENCY BOARD POLICY HAS WORKED IN BIH: THE CONVERTIBLE MARKA (KM) IS STABLE; INFLATION IS RELATIVELY LOW; THE KM IS USED IN ALL PARTS OF THE COUNTRY; KM USE HAS RISEN RAPIDLY WITHIN BIH. FOR EXAMPLE, THE CBBH BALANCE SHEET WAS JUST KM 140 MILLION IN JUNE 1998 WHEN THE KM BANKNOTES WERE FIRST PUT INTO CIRCULATION. FIFTEEN MONTHS LATER, OUR BALANCE SHEET HAS JUST PASSED KM 500 MILLION; THE KM IS NOW TRADED IN SIX OTHER EUROPEAN COUNTRIES. WHY HAS THE CURRENCY BOARD WORKED IN BIH? FIRST, PEOPLE HAVE FACED MANY FINANCIAL TRAUMAS IN THE PAST. THEY THEREFORE NOW VALUE A STABLE CURRENCY. THE CURRENCY BOARD HAS A HIGH LEVEL OF POLITICAL AND PUBLIC SUPPORT WITHIN BIH. SECOND, PEOPLE HAD COMPLETE TRUST IN THE ANCHOR CURRENCY, THE DEM. A STRICT CURRENCY BOARD HAS ALLOWED THE CENTRAL BANK OF BIH (CBBH), A NEW INSTITUTION WITH NO TRACK RECORD, TO GAIN SOME OF THE CREDIBILITY OF THE ANCHOR CURRENCY. I BELIEVE THE REST OF THE REGION COULD GAIN SIMILARLY BY EITHER USING THE DEM OR THE EURO OR BY TYING THEIR OWN CURRENCIES TO THEM BY A CURRENCY BOARD. THIRD, SOME PEOPLE HAVE SAID AN IMPORTANT REASON IS THAT THE CBBH HAS A FOREIGN GOVERNOR. ( THE CBBH LAW REQUIRES THAT FOR THE FIRST SIX YEARS THE GOVERNOR BE A FOREIGNOR. I AM A NEW ZEALANDER) I THINK THAT IS A PART OF THE ANSWER, BUT NOT THE KEY PART. WE SHOULD NOT RUSH TO THE CONCLUSION THAT THE ONLY WAY TO GET SOUND INSTITUTIONS IN THE REGION IS TO PUT A FOREIGNOR IN CHARGE OF THE INSTITUTION. IN MY VIEW, THE MAIN REASON THE CURRENCY BOARD HAS WORKED IN BIH IS THE VERY CLEAR MANDATE OF THE CBBH AND THE CLEARLY SPECIFIED LAW WE OPERATE UNDER: THE GOAL OF THE CBBH IS SIMPLE AND CLEAR; THE LAW LIMITS OUR ACTIVITIES WHERE THERE COULD BE ANY CONFLICT WITH THE CURRENCY BOARD REQUIREMENTS; WITHIN THESE LIMITATIONS, THE CBBH IS INDEPENDENT OF POLITICAL DIRECTION; WE ARE EASILY HELD ACCOUNTABLE. A BREACH OF THE CURRENCY BOARD REQUIREMENTS WOULD BE QUICKLY OBVIOUS TO ALL. WITHIN THE CURRENT JARGON, IT IS A VERY TRANSPARENT FORM OF MONETARY POLICY. I AM SURE STEVE HANKE, WHO SPEAKS NEXT, WILL SAY MORE ABOUT CURRENCY BOARDS. I WANT TO DRAW A MORE GENERAL CONCLUSION FROM THE SUCCESS OF THE CENTRAL BANK IN BIH. THAT CONCLUSION IS THAT IT IS POSSIBLE TO BUILD EFFECTIVE POLICY INSTITUTIONS IN THE REGION. THE KEYS TO DO SO ARE: KEEP IT SIMPLE. INSTITUTIONAL CAPACITY IN THESE COUNTRIES IS NOT HIGH SO THE GOALS AN INSTITUTION IS GIVEN NEED TO BE STRAIGHT-FORWARD AND ATTAINABLE. KEEP IT CLEAR. IN COUNTRIES WHERE INSTITUTIONS GENERALLY AREN'T TRUSTED, AMBIGUITY AND VAGUENESS WILL BE COSTLY AND WILL MAKE IT MUCH HARDER FOR THE INSTITUTION TO GAIN PEOPLES CONFIDENCE. THE IMPORTANCE OF THE CLEAR AND COMPREHENSIVE LEGAL FRAMEWORK THE CBBH OPERATES UNDER FOR THE SUCCESS OF THE CURRENCY BOARD LEADS IN TO MY SECOND MAJOR ISSUE. THE NEED TO ESTABLISH A STRONG LEGAL AND COURT SYSTEM THAT WILL BE TRUSTED AND USED IS FUNDAMENTAL FOR THE CREATION OF BOTH DEMOCRACY AND A PRIVATE-SECTOR, MARKET ECONOMY. IN BIH, A CLEAR AND COMPLETE LEGAL AND COURT SYSTEM STILL DOES NOT EXIST FIVE YEARS AFTER DAYTON. A LOT OF LAWS HAVE BEEN WRITTEN AND PASSED BUT THE OVERALL STRUCTURE OF LAW IS STILL NOT COMPLETE. I BELIEVE IT SHOULD HAVE BEEN GIVEN A HIGHER PRIORITY IN THE SEQUENCING OF INSTITUTION BUILDING. PART OF THE PROBLEM COULD BE THAT IT IS NOT CLEAR WHO IS LEADING THE REFORM OF THE LEGAL AND COURT SYSTEM. MAYBE THERE IS A GAP IN THE INTERNATIONAL LEADERSHIP IN THIS AREA OF THE REFORM PROCESS. THE LACK OF A SOUND LEGAL AND COURT SYSTEM IS HINDERING FINANCIAL SECTOR DEVELOIPMENTS IN BIH. FOR EXAMPLE, IT IS ONE FACTOR THAT STILL DISCOURAGES FOREIGN BANKS FROM ENTERING THE BIH MARKET. IT ALSO DISCOURAGES THE LOCAL BANKS FROM LENDING. A WOULD-BE BORROWER OFTEN HAS DIFFICULTY ESTABLISHING A CLEAR LEGAL CLAIM TO ANY ASSETS THEY WOULD USE AS COLLATERAL. EVEN IF THEY CAN ESTABLISH THIS CLAIM, BANKS ARE UNCERTAIN THAT THE COURTS WOULD SUPPORT ANY CLAIM THE BANK MADE AGAINST THAT COLLATERAL. SO THE LOCAL BANKS HOLD A LARGE PROPORTION OF THEIR ASSETS ON DEPOSIT AT THE CBBH OR IN DEM ACCOUNTS ABROAD. I SUSPECT A SIMILAR STORY COULD BE TOLD ABOUT OTHER COUNTRIES IN THE REGION. ANOTHER MAJOR PROBLEM THE REGION FACES IS CHRONICALLY WEAK FINANCIAL SECTORS. THIS IS A LEGACY OF THE LONG PERIOD OF STATE CONTROL AND OF THE EXTREME INSTABILITY THE REGION HAS SUFFERED. I WILL GIVE YOU A FEW EXAMPLES FROM BIH THAT I AM SURE WILL HAVE THEIR PARALLELS IN MOST BALKAN COUNTRIES: THERE ARE CURRENTLY 63 LICENSED BANKS IN BIH. MOST OF THEM ARE INCREDIBLY SMALL. NONE OF THEM OPERATE OVER THE WHOLE COUNTRY. EXTENDING THIS TO THE WHOLE REGION, THERE ARE NO BALKAN BANKS THAT OPERATE OVER THE WHOLE REGION THAT COULD ACT AS A CATYLYST FOR THE ECONOMIC INTEGRATION OF THE REGION. PEOPLE DO NOT TRUST THE BANKING SECTOR. THEY HAVE MANY GOOD HISTORICAL REASONS FOR THAT ATTITUDE. IT IS NOT IRRATIONAL. SO THE LEVEL OF SAVINGS HELD IN THE BANKING SECTOR IS VERY LOW. FOR EXAMPLE, IN NEW ZEALAND, A COUNTRY WITH A SIMILAR POPULATION LEVEL TO BIH, BANK SAVINGS PER CAPITA ARE 250 TIMES HIGHER THAN IN BIH. (INCOME LEVELS IN NZ ARE ABOUT 20 TIMES HIGHER THAN IN BIH SO THAT ONLY ACCOUNTS FOR A SMALL PROPORTION OF THE HUGE DIFFERENCE.) THE BANKING SECTOR SHOULD BE A IMPORTANT DRIVER OF ECONOMIC GROWTH AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE PRIVATE SECTOR. BUT AT PRESENT THEY EXTEND LITTLE CREDIT AND ARE RELATIVELY INSIGNIFICANT. ONE OTHER ISSUE THAT IS SIGNIFICANT IN ALL OF THE COUNTRIES OF FORMER YUGOSLAVIA IS THAT A SYSTEM OF STATE-CONTROLLED PAYMENTS BUREUAS STILL EXIST AND PLAY A MAJOR ROLE IN THE LOCAL FINANCIAL SYSTEM. I DONT THINK ANYTHING QUITE LIKE THESE INSTITUTIONS EXISTS ANYWHERE ELSE. I DONT HAVE TIME TO GO INTO A DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THEIR OPERATIONS. THEY DO PROVIDE A SECURE PAYMENTS SYSTEM BUT THEY IMPOSE HIGH COSTS ON BANKS AND ENTERPRISES. IN BIH THEY HAVE UNTIL VERY RECENTLY HAD A MONOPOLY ON DOMESTIC NON-CASH PAYMENTS SO THEY HAVE STIFLED THE DEVELOPMENT OF A VIABLE COMMERCIAL BANKING SECTOR. IN SHORT, THEY ARE VERY INTRUSIVE, VERY EXPENSIVE, VERY POLITICAL AND THE ANTITHESIS OF A FREE-MARKET FINANCIAL SYSTEM. PAYMENTS BUREAU REFORM IS NOW UNDERWAY IN BIH. THE AIM IS TO COMPLETE THE TRANSFORMATION BY THE END OF Y2000. THE SUCCESSFUL COMPLETION OF THIS REFORM IS CRITICAL IF A VIABLE, PRIVATE SECTOR FINANCIAL SYSTEM IS TO DEVELOP IN BIH. THE OTHER COUNTRIES OF FORMER YUGOSLAVIA FACE A SIMILAR CHALLENGE. BUT THE REFORM IN THIS AREA IS UNDERWAY PRIMARILY BECAUSE THE IMF, THE WORLD BANK, AND OTHER DONORS HAVE MADE IT A KEY PART OF THEIR CONDITIONALITY FOR FURTHER FUNDING FOR BIH. THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY SHOULD CONTINUE TO USE CONDITIONALITY TO HASTEN THE SPEED AND DEPTH OF THE REFORMS IN THESE COUNTRIES AS THE REFORMS ARE NOT MOVING WITH THE URGENCY THAT IS REQUIRED. THE KEY STEPS TO TRANSFORM THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM IN BIH AND THE REGION ARE AS FOLLOWS: CREATE IN EACH COUNTRY A SOUND CORE INSTITUTION AND A STABLE CURRENCY. BIH HAS DONE THAT WITH THE CBBH- BUT IT HAS TO BE MAINTAINED. FOSTER STRONGER DOMESTIC BANKING SECTORS THROUGH THE PRIVATISATION OR CLOSURE OF THE MANY STATE-OWNED BANKS, THE MERGING OR CLOSURE OF THOSE PRIVATELY-OWNED BANKS THAT ARE WEAK OR INSOLVENT, CHANGES TO THE BANK LICENSING SYSTEM THAT MAKE IT HARDER FOR SMALL OR WEAK BANKS TO BE ESTABLISHED, AND THE ATTRACTION OF A FEW GOOD FOREIGN BANKS INTO THE LOCAL MARKET. THIS LATTER STEP WOULD DO MORE TO TRANSFORM THE REGIONS FINANCIAL MARKETS THAN ANY NUMBER OF EXPERT REPORTS. THE GRADUAL DEVELOPMENT OF OTHER FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND MARKETS THAT EXIST IN DEVELOPED ECONOMIES. THE DEVELOPMENT OF REGIONAL FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS, BOTH PUBLIC AND PRIVATE. THIS HASNT STARTED AT ALL. THIS CONFERENCE COULD PROVIDE AN IMPETUS TO THE REGION AND THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY TO START THIS PROCESS. IN SUMMARY, THE REGION NEEDS SOME STRONG, SOUND FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS IF IT IS TO DEVELOP AND PROSPER. IN MY VIEW IT IS NOT IMPORTANT WHETHER THEY ARE LOCALLY-OWNED OR FOREIGN OWNED. WHAT IS IMPORTANT IS THAT THEY NEED TO BE DEVELOPED URGENTLY IF THE BALKAN ECONOMIES ARE TO ADVANCE. GETTING GOOD FOREIGN BANKS TO START OPERATIONS IS LIKELY TO GIVE A QUICKER AND MORE DEFINITE RESULT THAN RELYING SOLELY ON DEVELOPING LOCALLY-OWNED INSTITUTIONS. REFORM DRIVE, REAL COMPETITION AND GENUINE USER CHOICE WILL COME FROM THE ENTRY OF FOREIGN INSTITUTIONS INTO THESE UNDEVELOPED MARKETS. THEREFORE, FOREIGN GOVERNMENTS SHOULD ENCOURAGE THEIR ENTERPRISES, SUCH AS BANKS AND COMPANIES, TO START OPERATING IN OR TRADING WITH THE BALKAN COUNTRIES NOW. INTERNATIONAL ADVICE AND FUNDING ARE VERY IMPORTANT FOR THE REFORM PROCESS. BUT THEY WILL NOT ACHIEVE THEIR GOALS UNLESS INTERNATIONAL BUSINESSES FOLLOW. THE BALKAN COUNTRIES ALL NEED ASSISTANCE IN CREATING OR ATTRACTING THESE INSTITUTIONS. THE THIRD GENERAL ISSUE I WANT TO TALK ABOUT IS THE IMPORTANCE OF CREATING AN ENVIRONMENT THAT IS SYMPATHETIC TO AND ENCOURAGES PRIVATE INVESTMENT. MOST GOVERNMENTS IN THE REGION, INCLUDING THE GOVERNMENT IN BIH, SAY THAT A KEY ELEMENT OF THEIR ECONOMIC STRATEGY IS TO ATTRACT AND FOSTER PRIVATE INVESTMENT. I THINK IN MOST CASES THEIR STATEMENTS ARE SINCERE. THE PROBLEM IS THAT FOR MOST OF THEM, THEY HAVE NEVER LIVED IN AN ENVIRONMENT WHERE THE PRIVATE SECTOR PLAYED A MAJOR ROLE. THEY HAVE LITTLE IDEA OF HOW FUNDAMENTAL THE CHANGES TO MANY OF THEIR INSTITUTIONS AND WAYS OF DOING THINGS HAVE TO BE IF THEY ARE REALLY GOING TO ACHIEVE THIS OBJECTIVE. THE DISCUSSION OFTEN FOCUSES ON WHAT THEY MUST DO TO ATTRACT FOREIGN PRIVATE INVESTMENT. THIS IS CRITICALLY IMPORTANT FOR ALL OF THE COUNTRIES. BUT IT IS JUST AS IMPORTANT TO CREATE AN ENVIRONMENT THAT ENCOURAGES LOCAL PRIVATE INVESTMENT. SOME OF THE POLICIES TO DO THIS ARE THE SAME BUT NOT ALL OF THEM. AT PRESENT THE ENVIRONMENT IN BIH, AND I SUSPECT IN MOST OF THE REST OF THE REGION, IS VERY UNFRIENDLY TO PRIVATE INVESTMENT. THERE ARE PROBLEMS IN THE LEGAL SYSTEM, THE REGULATORY SYSTEM AND THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM. MOST OF THEM ARE A LEGACY OF THE PAST BUT THE MIND-SET THAT DOESNT REALLY TRUST THE PRIVATE SECTOR IS STILL ENTRENCHED IN SOME POLICY-MAKERS AND MOST BUREAUCRATS. PROGRESS IS BEING MADE IN ALL THESE AREAS TO IMPROVE THE ECONOMIC ENVIRONMENT BUT THE REFORMS ARE STILL MOVING MUCH TOO SLOWLY.

Title: "Currency, inflation, interest rates and the banking system." Prsentation to the 'Economist' Roundtable with the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: ' Currency, inflation, interest rates and the banking system.' Presentation to the 'Economist' Roundtable with the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sarajevo, 22nd February, 2002 Peter Nicholl Governor Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina INTRODUCTION: I am very pleased to have this opportunity to talk to you today. It is critical that private investment in BiH, and particularly private foreign investment, increase at a faster rate than has occurred in the last four years if the BiH economy is going to continue to grow in a smooth and sustainable manner. I believe that BiH has a reasonably positive story to tell potential foreign investors. You need to remember that BiH is going through three difficult transitions at the same time: from war to peace, from socialism to a market-economy; and from being a part of a larger country to establishing its own democratic and administrative institutions. Many people judge BiH by how far they still have to go to complete these transitions and on this basis they are very critical of progress in BiH. But given the extreme nature of these simultaneous challenges, if you judge BiH by the progress they have so far made the picture is much more optimisitic. THE CBBH: I will talk to you about two main areas this morning: The Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the commercial banking sector. The Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina (CBBH). The CBBH commenced its operations on 11 August, 1997 so it is just over four years old  very young by central banking standards. I would like to briefly describe to you what the financial system in bih looked like in 1997 when the CBBH commenced its operations. There were four currencies being used in the country. There were around 75 commercial banks, but most of them were very small, none of them operated over the whole country, and in the main, citizens did not use the banks. There were three payments bureaus, each of which had a monopoly on non-cash payments in the territory they covered. In short, it was a very weak and fragmented financial system. The CBBH is a state-level institution. Its mandate covers the whole country. It operates under its own Law. The Law is a very good. The Law is a very detailed one and sets out very precisely what the CBBH has to do and also what we cannot do. The CBBH reports to the Presidency of BiH, and through them, to the Parliament of BiH. Subject to the requirements of our law, the CBBH is an independent institution. This operational independence is very important. The CBBH is also self-financing so that we have financial independence as well. The strategic direction of the CBBH is set by a Governing Board of four members. As Governor I am the Chairman of the Board and there are three local members. The day-to-day management is in the hands of the Governor and three local Vice Governors. We have had very good continuity at both Board and Management level since the CBBH started and this has also been important for our successful operations. The CBBH has five offices. The Head Office is in Sarajevo. There are three Main Units, in Banja luka, Mostar and Sarajevo, and two branches, in Brcko and Pale. We have 240 staff. I am the only full-time staff member of the CBBH who is not a Bosnian citizen. So it is very much a Bosnian institution. MONETARY POLICY: The most important function of the CBBH is to 'formulate, adopt and control the monetary policy of BiH. The CBBH operates monetary policy through a 'Currency Board arrangement'. This is stipulated in the CBBH Law and in the Dayton Agreement. The choice of a Currency Board had two main motivations. First, it provides a firm nominal anchor in the form of a fixed exchange rate. This was considered critical for the very uncertain post-war economic situation in BiH. Second, it is a rule-based approach to monetary policy that took into account the difficulty there would be in establishing insitutions and making political decisions in the complex poltical environmment that existed in BiH after the war. The three essential features of the Currency Board, all of which are specified in the CBBH Law, are: Fixed exchange rate: the BiH currency, the Convertible Mark (KM) was tied to the Deutscmark (DM) at a fixed exchange rate of 1KM 1DM. This exchange rate allowed the two currencies to be used together during the period in which citizens were building up their trust in the KM. The KM is now tied to the euro at the same rate as the DM was (1 euro 1.95583 KM). It has in fact been tied to the euro at this rate ever since the euro was introduced on 1 January 1999. We did not alter the exchange rate at the time of the euro changeover as we believed it was very important that citizens of BiH (and potential foreign investors) continue to have complete confidence that the exchange rate will remain fixed against our anchor currency. Full foreign exchange backing: the KM liabilities of the CBBH have to be fully backed with convertible foreign assets. At the end of December 2001 our KM liabilities were KM 2.623 billion and our foreign assets were KM 2.697 billion so we had more than 100% coverage; Full convertibility: the CBBH had to be prepared to convert KM for DM at any time for any amount. Now the KM is convertible into a euro. Since we started in 1997, we have issued KM 8.1 billion and we have converted back KM 5.9 billion. So it has been a fully convertible currency in practice as well as in name. THE CURRENCY BOARD IN OPERATION: Linking the KM to the DM through a Currency Board was an easy choice for BiH because the DM was already extensively used in the country and was the currency people trusted. It has been a successful choice: The KM has been a stable currency against the DM and the euro since it was introduced; Inflation in BiH is low and stable. The latest figure is around 2 % per annum and it is similar in both entities; KM use has risen rapidly within BiH and it is now the dominant transactions currency in all parts of the country. Our KM liabilities rose from KM 132 million when we started in August 1997 to KM 1.166 billion at the end of September 2001. During the final four months of the euro introduction they more than doubled. The citizens of BiH took the large amounts of DM banknotes they had been keeping under their mattress to the banks and converted a lot of them either to KM banknotes or put them on deposit in a BiH bank. By 31 December our KM liabilities had reached DM 2.623 billion and they have stayed around that level during 2002 so far. This is a clear sign that the citizens of BiH trust the KM and are beginning to trust the banking system also ; The KM can now be traded in specified banks in a number of other countries in Europe. I do not think there is any other type of monetary policy, except the adoption of the KM as the currency of BiH, that could have given a country like BiH a stable and trusted currency and low inflation this quickly. WHY HAS THE CURRENCY BOARD WORKED BiH? I think there are four main reasons: First, people have faced many financial traumas. They therefore value a stable currency. The Currency Board consequently has a high level of public support within BiH; Second, people had complete trust in the anchor currency, the DM. A strict Currency board has allowed the CBBH, a new institution with no track record, to gain some of the credibility of the DM and the Bundesbank. The changeover to the euro as the anchor currency does not appear to have weakened the credibility of the Currency Board in BiH; Third, the CBBH has a foreign Governor. I think that has been important for establishing the independence of the CBBH; But the major thing that has helped my job as Governor and is the major reason why the CBBH works well is the very good legal and institutional framework the CBBH operates under: The goal of the CBBH is simple, clear and specified in the law; The Law limits our activities where there would be any potential conflict with the Currency Board requirements; Within these statutory goals and limitations, the CBBH is independent of political direction; We have sensible and sound internal decision-making processes; We are easily and firmly held accountable. A breach of the Currency Board requirements would be quickly obvious to all. Within the current economic jargon, it is a very transparent form of policy implementation. Some economists and others argue that a Currency Board has disadvantages because of the limitations it places on the economic roles of the CBBH. For example: The CBBH can not play a role in providing liquidity to the banking sector ( i.e., it can not act as lender of last resort); The CBBH can not finance the Government; The CBBH can not play any direct role in financing economic development; The exchange rate can not be used as a tool to adjust to economic shocks or poor economic performance. These areas of policy discretion, if used wisely and in moderation, could be of advantage to economic development in BiH. There are lots of projects in BiH for which a little bit of CBBH finance may be helpful. But the problem would be in keeping the CBBH credit to a little bit. the experience of the region is that excess Central Bank credit has usually been created and the result is inflation, and sometimes hyper-inflation. That does not help business, employment or confidence in BiH. So in my view, the strict Currency Board is the best approach for BiH. To change it would have very adverse economic and social impacts. A Currency Board is a rule-based rather than a discretionary form of monetary policy. But that is a major reason why it was chosen and is one of its strengths rather than a weakness. By choosing to adopt a Currency Board, BiH decided that the aim of monetary policy will be to achieve stability  stability in the value of the local currency against the anchor currency and, because of this, stability in the rate of inflation. The overwhelming direction that monetary policy around the world has been taking over the last fifteen years is to make stability, particulalrly of inflation, the objective of monetary policy. So the monetary policy being implemented in BiH through the Currency Board is not unusual. What would be unusual, and would have a very adverse effect on potential foreign investors, would be a return in BiH to the old discretionary type of monetary policies that have failed in many countries  and failed spectacularly in this region. I think a more apt name for that type of monetary policy would be indiscretionary rather than discretionary. WILL THE CURRENCY BOARD CONTINUE: I believe therefore that the BiH Currency Board must be and will be continued for the following reasons: Stability in a country's exchange rate and inflation rate are extremely important economic and social benefits. They allow people to plan their economic decisions ahead with more confidence. This is particularly important for investment as the economic return from any investment is spread over many years. Stability in inflation and the exchange rate are also extremely important for financial sector development. We are seeing the banking sector in BiH becoming more normal and interest rates are gradually being reduced as credit risk is reduced. But if the banks also had to worry about inflation risk and exchange rate risk, I am sure we would not have seen any significant improvements in the banking sector over the past few years. - Stability is also an important social benefit because it is more frequently the poor who suffer from the adverse affects of devaluation or inflation. The rich or well-connected can often finds ways around it - or even ways to benefit from it. - So the main reasons why the Currency Board should be retained is that it is producing real economic and social benefits for BiH. The citizens can see this. There is widespread public support for it because it has provided one of the few elements of stability the people of BiH have had for some time. Surveys suggest that the citizens of BiH still have only a low level of trust in their institutions. The survey also says that the CBBBH, operating as a Currency Board, is an exception and has a high level of trust from the citizens ; The second main reason why the Currency Board should be retained is that there is no sensible alternative given the present state of the BiH economy and its institutions. It would be risky to change it. Confidence in the KM would drop as people waited to see how any alternative monetary policy would work. It is not clear to me what type of monetary policy BiH would adopt as an alternative. There are some people advocating change but none of them have made their alternative clear. I do not see how a discretionary form of monetary policy would work in BiH. The politicians are unlikely to be prepared to give the discretionary powers to an official. But given that there is still a lack of trust among political groups, I do not see how politicians would be able to make these decisions. Any alternative types of monetary policy are much more likely to generate inflation rather than economic growth or to lead to little action but a lot of confusion and uncertainty. The one thing that financial markets hate the most is uncertainty. The Currency Board gives them and the people certainty. The final reason why the Currency Board should be retained is that the long-term goal of BiH policy is to take the economy closer to Europe. The KM is already tied to the euro. It would therefore seem sensible to maintain this link. The exit strategy for BiH from the Currency Board should therefore be the eventual adoption of the euro. BANKING SECTOR: The second area I want to focus on in my address is the commercial banking sector. BiH has an improving banking sector. The reform in the banking sector has gone further and faster than reform in any other sector of the economy. Confidence is coming back, depositors are beginning to return to banks and banks are beginning to lend on more reasonable terms. Competition is real, helped by the arrival of some good foreign banks. Proportionately, foreign investment in the banking sector has been higher than in any other sector in BiH. I will briefly list the main changes that have brought this improvement about: Payments system reform: the cash payments system has been unified with the KM becoming the dominant, and almost the sole, currency in use in BiH. In the non-cash payments area, the old state-owned centralised system that had a monopoly was closed. BiH is the only country in former Yugoslavia where this has so far happened. It has been replaced with a modern European-type system with two clearing houses, an RTGS one and a Giro one, owned and operated by the Central Bank. Payments are being conducted by the commercial banks. The suppliers we used had put similar systems into place in nine other European countries. But it was done more quickly in BiH than anywhere else showing that it is possible to implement large, technical projects in BiH successfully. It has been operating since 5 January 2001 and is going very smoothly. We have done 11.9 million transactions worth KM 16.8 billion in our new internal payments system over the first year of operation. There have probably been a similar level of intra-bank transactions. Minimum capital requirements: These requirements have been substantially increased through a series of steps from an initial KM 2.5 million to KM 10 million and will increase again this year to km 15 million. This is forcing banks to merge or find strategic partners. Inter-entity banking: It became possible for a bank registered in one entity to operate branches in the other entity. Six banks (three from each entity) are already doing so and more will follow. Foreign banks: A number of foreign banks commenced operations in BiH in the last two years, either by applying for licenses directly or by purchasing an existing BiH bank. Increased foreign competition has already been very good for the BiH economy. It has given depositors more choice and it has forced the local banks to improve the range and quality of the services they provide in order to survive. Deposit insurance: A limited deposit insurance scheme has started which covers deposits in approved banks up to KM 5,000. This is also helping return citizens confidence to the banks that qualify. So far, it is only operational in the federation and seven banks are members. A law is currently before the Entity Parliaments that will introduce a single deposit insurance fund for the whole country. Sixth, most of the state-owned banks (there are still eleven state or mainly-state owned banks in BiH) finally had their opening balance sheets approved last year and they moved into the privatisation phase. But progress in bank privatisation was very slow until quite recently. While this is disappointing, in my view it is no longer critical for the process of bank reform in BiH as the reform process is being largely driven by privately-owned banks, including the recently arrived foreign banks. The citizens actually show a higher degree of trust in privately owned banks as compared to state-owned banks. While at first sight, this may seem to be paradoxical it is completely understandable once one knows a bit of the financial history of the region. As a consequence of all these changes, thee has been considerable consolidation in the banking sector. The number of banks has been reduced quite sharply, particularly in the Federation. But as the chart in my handout shows, when one looks at various types of banking services  deposits, payments, cash handling- the degree of consolidation that has already occurred is much more than appears from the number of banks. What lies ahead in the banking sector for the rest of 2002 and 2003? The degree of foreign ownership will increase; The number of banks will decrease substantially under the combined pressure of higher capital requirements and sharply increased competition; A single deposit insurance agency will be established and more banks will become eligible for insurance; Banking supervision, currently carried out by entity agencies, will come under the umbrella of the CBBH; The range and quality of banking services will continue to improve. Products like mortgages, credit cards and so on will become more available and new products will appear; The degree of state involvement in the banking sector will decrease substantially through the privatisation or closure of state-owned banks. In short, the BiH banking system will start to look more and more like the banking system you see in other European countries. It is probably too optimistic to say that by the end of 2002 the BiH banking system will have completed its transition to becoming a European type banking system. But I think most people will be surprised by how quickly the banking system will continue to change and improve. The main things that will slow down the transition are problems in the legal and regulatory frameworks in BiH that make it difficult for banks to take and use collateral for lending. This is where the reform focus now needs to be concentrated. THE ECONOMIC OUTLOOK: There are two things that make it difficult to predict the economic outlook in BiH with precision. The first is that BiH is going through so many transitions simultaneously that the economic numbers can move through very large ranges. For example, our foreign reserves grew by 127% in the December 2001 quarter alone. Second, the economic outlook depends crucially on an accelerartion of the micro-economic reform process in bih. Forecasts based on the status-quo as compared to those based on an accelerated reform path will be very different. In fact, unless the regulatory, legal and tax systems are changed, and changed quickly and substantially, BiH will have a very difficult future. In my view, these problems are interrelated and have a common core  a lack of understanding of the way in which a private sector economy works and what the investment environment needs to be like to attract the level of investment that BiH needs. The environment for private investment has improved but it is still far too complicated. This applies to local as well as foreign investment. It should be a real wake-up call to policy makers in BiH to discover that the citizens over thelast four months have taken DM 3 billion out from under their mattresses and converted it. That was money that has been in BiH for some time, but the citizens were not prepared to put it in bank or invest it in a business themselves. This is where the attention of BiH politicians and international consultants and advisors needs to be directed. The macroeconomic situation in bih is a stable one. It is the areas of regulatory, tax and legal system reform that will determine the future of BiH. There is not one, quick policy fix that BiH can adopt to get themselves out of the difficult economic situation that has built up over a long period of time. It is not that simple. Continued banking reform, accelerated regulatory reform, legal and court reform, reduction of bureaucracy, lowering of the tax burden, privatisation  there is a long list of things that still need to be completed. In the meantime, the stability given by the Currency Board is the most positive attribute BiH has for attracting foreign investment. Undermining the stability of the KM by adopting some other discretionary form of monetary policy would be the best way I can think of to guarantee that BiH will have an economic crisis. But, I do not believe that will happen. I am an optomist and believe that we will see a combination of continued macro-economic stability and accelerated micro-economic and legal reform. On this basis I would expect inflation to remain stable at around current levels, economic growth rates to be at least 6-7 percent per annum in nominal terms ( 5% real) and bank interest rates for credit-worthy borrowers to decline quite rapidly. There are still risks attached to investing in BiH. But there are also many opportunities. Given the high degree of macro-economic stability in BiH, I believe the balance between risk and opportunity now favours opportunity. I take your presence at this roundtable as a very encouraging sign for BiH.

Title: Welcome and Opening Remarks - The TransTypeion of the Payments System in BiH
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: OPENING REMARKS GRAND OPENING OF NEW BANJA LUKA PREMISES OF THE CENTRAL BANK OF BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA Vuk Karadzic 6 Banja Luka, BiH Wednesday, 15, March 2000 14:30 CBBH Governor Mr. Peter Nicholl I would like to welcome one and all of you to our new offices today in order to help us celebrate its grand opening. This event is a celebration of the success of the Central Bank of BiH and its important role in the economic structure here in Republika Srpska. It is also an opportunity to recognize the role the KM has played in the RS, in giving the people here a monetary unit that they can trust and place their faith in. Our sales of the KM in the RS have been very strong over the last year or so and our net sales of KM in the RS have now reached KM 242 million. Also, commercial bank deposits denominated in Km have risen from only KM 22 million in March 1999 to around KM 110 million today. I would like to thank the RS Government and the people of the RS for their strong support of the KM. The KM is the dominant currency in ALL of BIH these days, and this dominant role has increased the workload of our Banja Luka staff. I have to admit that even before this, our Banja Luka staff has been working in very cramped quarters on Maria Bursach Street. Out of three small rooms, KM was purchased and sold to the commercial banks in the RS, relationships were nurtured between the Central Bank and the various financial institutions of the RS, and market analysis was performed. The CBBH purchased this office space to help alleviate the overcrowding, but also to provide the room required to perform new tasks and better perform the older ones as the KM worked its way into every corner and pocket of the RS. The purchase of this space also shows our commitment to the RS, and its economic future as well as the community. We are no longer renters, perceived as temporary residents and transient. We are here to stay and contribute as much as we can to the community and economic growth and prosperity of the Republika Srpska and BiH as a whole. While I am at it, I would like to thank the staff and management of the Medical Electronics building who have helped us in preparing for this big day, and have allowed us to place the flag of BiH outside, along side the entity flag of Republika Srpska. A symbol to those visiting us here is that the state and entity can work successfully side by side in harmony for the common good of the people. As we look ahead to the common good of all BiH citizens, we are drawn to one of the most important issues facing BiH right now. That of course is the transformation of the payments and clearing systems in BiH. The Payments Bureaus are to be closed by the end of this year. As part of that process, some of their functions, such as tax administration and statistics, need to be transferred to other agencies. Payments functions are being transferred to commercial banks at the moment and it is important that commercial banks move quickly to start doing domestic non-cash payments. Some banks have already received authorisations in the Federation but so far none have done so in the RS. I hope that RS banks will apply for licenses soon and the RS Banking Agency will approve some of them promptly. It is also important that if the BiH economy is to prosper and become more reliant on the private sector, its commercial banking system needs to get banks that are bigger and stronger. Such banks should be able to play a much bigger role in attracting peoples savings and lending to private sector businesses. It is high time that the economic sector of BiH moved out from the shadows of politics and decisions on economic issues were made on economic criteria. For example, it must be realized that BiH is much too small to contain three banking sectors. If the current subdivisions continue, BiH will never create the financial institutions it needs to foster development. In the rest of the world, the overwhelming trend is just the opposite. It is one of mergers, in order to create bigger, more highly capitalized and often cross border institutions. Take for example last weeks announcement in Frankfurt that Deutsche and Dresdner banks were merging creating the largest bank in Europe with more than 1.3 trillion dollars in assets. Two former rivals now married in a union made necessary if they are to survive in the new financial system of globalization. Here in BiH we still dont have even one bank that operates in both entities, other than the CBBH! The second major problem is spawned by the first which I just mentioned. Too many banks, and too little capital to go around. BiH banks at present include many that are too small and under capitalized to play any significant role in attracting savings and financing private sector investment. The news is not all discouraging though. Changes are occurring. The Federation Banking Agency is doing a good job in encouraging smaller yet solvent banks to merge resulting in a decrease in the number of Federation banks from 55 to 42 in the past year. In the RS, good progress is being made in preparing the state-owned banks for privatisation. Much more needs to occur and fast because having so many small banks does not help economic growth and BiH needs to have strong economic growth. On the contrary, small, weak banks hurt the economic and financial systems by fostering a lack of public confidence in the banking sector. One change that needs to occur promptly is an amendment to the RS Banking Law to allow banks authorised in the Federation to operate as branches in the RS. This change would also allow banks authorised in the RS to operate as branches in the Federation. This is necessary if bigger, stronger, state-wide banks are to develop in BiH. The RS Government has told me they will make this amendment and I urge them to do so promptly. But returning to the main reason we are all here this afternoon, the opening of this new office here in Banja Luka, signifies our determination to support the continuing reform and growth of the financial sector, whenever and where ever possible. With the opening of these premises we wish to say, we are not here just for the short term, but for good. As the chief authority on monetary policy in BiH the CBBH will play a large role in this reform and growth of a modern and strong financial system in BiH.

Title: Opening Remarks For The 4Th Financial Forum
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: The BiH Financial System in the Year 2000 & Beyond By Governor Peter W. Nicholl Tuesday, 30th November 1999 Holiday Inn Hotel Sarajevo, BiH This 4th Financial Forum is the last one that we will hold this century. It is therefore appropriate that the theme of the forum is the Bosnian Financial Sector in the Year 2000 and beyond. The year 2000 will be crucial for the Bosnian Financial System and for the Economy. I said in my opening comments to this forum last year, "The Financial Sector in BiH is currently very fragmented and weak. As a consequence, the level of financial savings and lending is very low and the financial sector is incapable of playing the roles it needs to if the economy of BiH is to develop and grow". A year later , this statement is still true. While some progress has been made, the process of reforming the financial sector here and creating institutions that are big enough and sound enough to play a significant role in the economy is still at the very beginning. I am not sure if most people understand just how far from having a viable and useful financial sector BiH actually is. I will give you one example to try and put this into context. The country in which I come from, New Zealand, has the same population as BiH, and income levels which are about 20 times higher. But the level of savings held by New Zealanders in their banks is around 400 times higher than the level of bank savings in the banks in BiH. BiH has a lot of banks--over 60 at present. (New Zealand incidently has five big banks and about 14 banks in all.) But none of the BiH banks operate over the whole country and many of them are extremely small. A lot of the savings of Bosnian people are either held in cash under the mattress or in banks abroad. For other financial institutions and instruments, the situation is generally worse. Many of them dont yet exist in BiH. The process of banking and payments system reform did start in 1999 and some important steps were taken. For example: All banks now have reserve accounts at the CBBH and the framework for an inter-bank market therefore exists. This will be expanded on in 2000. The legal monopoly the payments bureaus had on domestic non-cash payments has been removed and a strategy has been agreed to at the political level which will transfer these functions to the commercial banks gradually over the next year. It is absolutely essential that this process of transferring payments functions to the banking sector occurs next year. The first banks to start providing domestic payments should be authorised shortly. I urge the BiH banks to make their applications for this authorisation quickly. The banks have been telling me for the two years that I have been here that they want to be given this opportunity. Now they have it and the next steps are up to them. A deposit insurance agency has been established in the Federation of BiH, and one should be established in Republika Srpska soon. This should help to restore public confidence in the banking sector. There are some BiH banks trying to commence operations across the whole country. This has to be encouraged by the entity governments and banking agencies. But as I understand it, the Banking Law in the Republika Srpska treats Federation BiH banks as foreign banks, and they would have to set up completely separate banks in in order to operate there. The Federation BiH Law does not have the same requirement, but the Federation Banking Agency sazs that for reciprocity reasons, they would apply the same requirements to an RS bank. This situation must be changed and must be changed quickly if the banking sector in BiH is to develop institutions of any reasonable size and strength. There are some banks from Western Europe that are getting close to commencing operations in BiH. In fact, the first such bank, Volksbank, from Austria, has placed an advertisement announcing their intentions in some BiH papers yesterday--just in time for the forum. The precense of foreign banks in the BiH banking sector should be encouraged as they will quickly help to improve quality and services. The KM as become the dominant currency in all of BiH and is also the main currency in which bank deposits are now denominated. These steps are to be applauded. But they are only the beginning. The reform path has a very long way to go if BiH is to build a financial system that works and contributes to economic development in the way a western European financial system does. It seems to me that there are two important facts that many people forget or ignore in the financial reform discussions and process in BiH. The first is that BiH is a small country. For many of the financial markets and instruments that are planned to be introduced in BiH in 2000 and beyond, it is doubtful if the BiH market on its own is big enough to sustain them. The second fact is that in western Europe, North America, and Asia, the trend is toward creating even larger, more diversified and often cross-border institutions and markets. How does the BiH financial system and reform process look when compared against these three facts? The answer is not very good. BiH essentially still has two banking systems, one in each entity. Proposals to create new markets, such as a securities market and a stock exchange, are being developed at the entity level rather than the state level. When I ask why, I am told that this is what the constitution and politics require. But these issues should not be political if BiH wants to create serious and useful financial instituions and markets. These issues are economic issues. BiH is, as I have said, a small country and to further fragment its financial institutions and markets into smaller units is in my view not sensible and will do little to help the economy develop in the next century. If BiH does not create serious, state-wide financial institutions of its own there are only two possible outcomes. If foreign institutions are allowed to compete freely in the market, they will soon come to dominate it and BiH will get a GOOD financial sector-- but one with few domestic institutions. The second outcome, if foreign institutions either aren't allowed to enter the market or don't want to come, is that the BiH financial sector will remain a minor player in economic events in the country and the economy will suffer as a consequence. I applaud the efforts going onat present to create securities markets and stock exchanges in BiH and the CBBH will cooperate wherever it can. But BiH is a very small country and creating two of such institutions may be a guarantee that neither will be particularly useful as an engine of economic growth. As I said earlier, the international trend is for national institutions and markets to merge or cooperate. At the very least therefore, if any new institutions are set uo in BiH at the entity level, they have to be set up with compatible systems and rules so that during the next few years they can move to working together, then working in unison with neighboring country systems and eventually woring in unison with EU systems. This has to be the vision that drives the reform of the existing financial system in BiH and the creation of new institutions--to create financial institutions and systems that can quickly integrate into the broader financial markets of Europe. The theme of this concerence is the BiH banking system in 2000--and beyond. To create a good banking system in BiH will require a vision and boldness. Tinkering with the present system will not be sufficient. The vision I think is relatively easy--it should be to create a European style banking system; One that meets European standards and provides European services. Such a banking system will contribute to economic development in BiH in ways that the present system is simply unable to do. Boldness--I will look to some of the speakers that follow me to say if they will reach for this vision with boldness. I wish the Finance Forum every success. The challenges before the BiH banking sector are very large. But so are the opportunities for the banks and the country if banking reform is carried out in a successful and meaningful way.

Title: Speech notes on ceremony of the agreement signed with BAMCARD
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: SPEECH NOTES FOR CEREMONY FOR KM 200 BANKNOTE. I would like to welcome everyone to this ceremony to put the new KM 200 banknote formally into circulation. I especially want to welcome our partners in this project, the Presidency of BH. I am delighted that all three me members are able to be present. I also give a special welcome to our invited guests from the Austrian banknote printing company, OeBS and the Austrian Embassy in BH. The first KM banknotes were put into circulation in June 1998, which is a little less than four years ago. The KM has since then been very stable and successful as a currency. It has become the dominant currency everywhere in the country. The Governing Board of the CBBH decided last year that the time had come to add a KM 200 banknote to the structure of the Bosnian currency. There were two main reasons for this. First, the volume of KM banknotes in circulation had risen rapidly from around KM 162 million at the end of 1998 to KM 696 million at the end of 2000. The growth continued in 2001  but at an even more rapid rate and the amount of KM in circulation at the end of last year was KM 1,806 million, 160% higher than the year before. Second, the Deutschemark was going to disappear as a currency at the end of 2001. This meant the high denomination dm banknotes that were being used in BH would also disappear. While the KM 200 continues many of the main themes that were part of our first issue of KM banknotes, there are some significant differences in the process by which the design was decided and in the design itself that I want to highlight. First, it took many months of negotiations to get a decision on the design of the first set of KM banknotes. Though the Presidency of BH at that time came close to agreeing, they were unable to do so and the designs were imposed by the High Representative. This time, the Presidency discussed proposals recommended by the Governing Board of the CBBH, which included single design, and the use of Ivo Andri and bridge on the Drina as the main elements. The Presidency agreed at a single meeting to accept those proposals. In 1998, we had a similar ceremony to this one to introduce the first KM banknotes. I shared the platform with the then High Representative. This time I am sharing the platform with the Chairman of the Presidency and all three members of the Presidency are present. This is a very great pleasure for me and for the Governing Board and staff of the CBBH. I think it is an important example of the progress in decision-making that has been made in BH since 1998. To use the buzzword that has become popular with the international community, it is a good example of local 'ownership.' The first issue of KM banknotes had two variations of each banknote. The two designs were very similar and they have been used interchangeably in both entities virtually from the beginning. The KM therefore quickly became a single currency in all parts of the country. This KM 200 banknote completes that process as it has a single design. We had an international tender for the printing of the new banknote. This tender was won by OeBS, the Austrian banknote printing company. A number of representatives of the Company have come to Sarajevo for this ceremony and I welcome them to CBBH and to Bosnia and Herzegovina. I want to thank their company for the very professional job they have done for us on this KM 200 banknote. The KM 200 banknote continues many of the main design elements of the first KM banknotes, so there are links between the first KM banknotes and this new one. First, it has an author, Ivo Andri, the country's only Nobel Prize winning author, on the front. Second, it has an image related to the author, the bridge on the Drina, on the reverse. Third, it makes equal use of the Cyrillic and Latin script. But the design has been 'modernized'. For this I wish to thank Robert Kalina of OeBS. Mr. Kalina is very famous in the banknote industry as his designs were the ones that were selected for the euro banknotes. So he can say that he has designed banknotes that are now being used by over 300 million people. To that claim he can now add a banknote that will be used by 3 and a half million people in BH. The design has a good balance between classical and modern banknote design. I think it is a very attractive banknote. I hope all of you here today and the citizens of BH when they start to use the banknote will agree that it is an attractive banknote. It is also a very secure banknote. The banknote also incorporates the most up-to-date security elements that are available and we therefore think it will be secure from counterfeiting. The media and the banks and other enterprises have already played an important role by giving good publicity to these security features to the public. We will continue this publicity campaign over the next several weeks and we therefore request your continued assistance in getting this important information to the public. The Governing Board of the CBBH has taken a decision that the KM 200 banknotes will become legal tender and go into circulation as from today, the 15th May. The banknotes have already been distributed to the CBBH's four vaults in Banja Luka, Brko, Mostar and Sarajevo. Commercial banks can buy them from us today. So the citizens of BH should be able to get then from their bank today also  or if not today, tomorrow certainly. This new banknote is very much a Bosnian banknote. All of its elements were decided by CBBH and the Presidency. But it is also a banknote with strong links to the euro. This is very appropriate for BH as Europe is where the future of BH lays. Its value is tied to the euro through the Currency Board arrangements. It is worth euro 102.25. Its design mirrors some important features of the euro  in particular, it has a bridge on the reverse side, as do all euro banknotes. But BH choose to have a bridge on our new banknote before we knew what the winning euro design would look like. Also, our bridge has a name and you can actually go and see it. I think this is a banknote of which BH can feel proud. I again want to thank to the people here who were involved in this process, the Governing Board and staff of the CBBH and the Presidency of BH.

Title: Signing of the protocol of the Eurosystem needs assessment programme to the benefit of the CBBH
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: Protocol Signing Event with the European Central bank and the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina February 16, 2007 at 11am, Central Bank building It is an honor to be here today to represent the European Delegation in the signing of this Protocol with the European Central Bank and the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the one of the first and most successful State institutions of BiH. Under its leadership remarkable successes have been achieved which have resounded in the economy of BiH and in the lives of everyday people; The CBBH's monetary policies have achieved macroeconomic stability in BiH and inflation has been relatively low compared to neighbouring countries. The CBBH has preserved the stability of the Konvertible Marka, which has forged public confidence in the BiH currency, as evidenced by steadily rising KM-denominated deposits. However, as the economy continues to develop and grow, institutions must also evolve. In this regards, the Central Bank is a model for other BiH institutions on how to function as an independent and professional institution that is willing to embrace change. The EC Delegation is therefore pleased to provide its assistance to the Central Bank. We will provide 300,000 EURO to the European Central Bank and Member State National Banks in supporting the BiH Central Bank in moving towards the standards of the Eurosystem Banks; I have to admit that I was pleasantly surprised with the number of the Member State National Banks that have taken a keen interest in supporting this activity: the Deutsche Bundesbank, Eesti Pank, Bank of Greece, Banco de Espana, Banque de France, Banca d'Italia, Banka Slovenije and Osterrerichische Nationalbank. I would like to take this opportunity to thank them and especially the European Central Bank for their leadership role. To the Central Bank, I ask that you fully undertake the necessary reforms to adapt your policies and procedures to those of the Eurosystem central banks. I also ask that you take this opportunity to learn as much as possible from the National Bank and ECB experts. Finally, as part of the SAA, BiH needs to maintain a stable macroeconomic environment. As we all know the Central Bank plays a key role in this and I commend them for their commitment in conducting their tasks and responsibilities. However there are many other challenges that await BiH, if BiH is one day to become a fully fledged member of the EU. Most it is important to realize that the necessary reforms are for the benefit and the prosperity of the country and not just to please the European Union, your success in meeting these challenges does not depend on us in the European Union but on the people and political leaders of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Title: CBBH and USAID international conference "Macroeconomic Imbalances and EU Convergence"
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: Marko skreb Closing remarks at 2nd Annual CBBH Research Conference Macroeconomic Imbalances and EU Convergence 7. November 2019. Dear Mr. Governor, Ladies and gentlemen, It is a great honor for me to give closing remarks at this important Conference. However, it is a tough task after all those interesting presentations, papers, discussions etc. The bad news is I am afraid that despite Einsteins concept of relativity of time I would kindly request your attention for several more minutes of so called absolute Newtonian time. Good news is I will not summarize what has been said so far , but will attempt to give this Conference a broader perspective by answering three questions: 1) When did it all start? 2) Is converging towards EU still a valid goal? and 3) Where do we go from here? When did it all start? I mean when did convergence toward EU start, not macroeconomic imbalances. I guess that since the beginning of time we had imbalances even without being aware of them or being able to measure them. But what about convergence? Convergence towards EU started with the Fall of the Berlin wall. Almost to a day (09. November 1989.), three decades ago a historical event happened for the World, more so for large part of Europe and especially for this part of Europe. The Berlin wall, symbol of divided Europe but Cold war as well has been demolished. This physical and ideological divide which stood from 1961 to 1989 has fallen. Thus, started the process of transition and consequently EU convergence. True, the then Yugoslavia was not part of the Warsaw Pact, it was not strictly speaking behind the Iron Curtain, but it was not a liberal democracy with flourishing and efficient private ownership market economy either. Is EU still a valid goal for countries in South-East Europe? Last political events and I mean not opening negotiations with North Macedonia and Albania1 is a blow to enlargement process of EU. Some speculate that this may weaken the reform momentum not only for them but for other countries in the region, even those that opened negotiations (Serbia, Montenegro) and of course, still potential candidate Bosnia and Herzegovina. Others claim differently that this should strengthen countries willingness to reform toward EU. As if burden of proof is now on the candidate countries. But the question is should those countries still aim towards EU as their strategic goal, or should they seek alternatives? My answer to this question is a big yes. EU is and should remain to be the goal for countries in this region. To quote Winston Churchill: Democracy is the worst form of government except for all those other forms that have been tried from time to time. Based on my own experience, EU enlargement and its achievements have been positive by most accounts. I am convinced that my own home country- Croatia would not be as developed economically nor politically today were it not for the EU. Let me emphasize that EU was and still is a strong magnet that attracts its neighbors into joining this members-only club. A short walk down the memory lane . As the Iron Curtain fell, most former communist countries chose membership of the EU as their ultimate goal. Geographical proximity was an important, but not the only, contributing factor. Most countries wanted to join the EU for its high standards of living, political democracy and more generally a human way of living. Compared to the rest of the world, the EU has the highest quality of life. Therefore, joining the EU has been a bright beacon, helping navigation along the paths of post-communist reforms for many. As I was policy maker for some time in the last century,2 I can testify firsthand that EU membership was the main driving force behind economic reforms. What were the main transmission mechanisms for convergence toward the EU and the Euro? First it was legal framework and the EU rules. Acquis Communautaire is not a menu from which to pick and choose. It is a set of rules and adopting them is a necessary precondition 1 - with-albania-and-north-macedonia-is-a-mistake 2 See my CV at markoskreb.hr for EU membership. If you want to be a member of this club, you must adapt and obey them. This worked very well for Croatia. As a former socialist economy, without those rules we would have endless discussions on how to address a reform. Lets take an example of central bank independence. There is no doubt in my mind that without the EU and the ECB watching changes in our legislation, the Croatian national banks law and its independence would look quite different today. Populism and printing money were very much alive in our country long before it became fashionable in Europe or in the world. In one of his blogs the famous economist Paul Krugman quoted an experienced policy maker who said that bad economic ideas are like cockroaches, you flush them down the toilet but sooner or later they come back. The EU and its rules have been playing (at least partially) the role of flushing bad economic ideas away in Croatia. Let me mention the example of shipyards in Croatia which over the years has received ample taxpayers money. Some of them are still not profitable. Was it not for the EU state aid rules, I am sure this waste would have been even bigger? As a taxpayer, I say thank you EU3! Second transmission mechanism was via set of macroeconomic benchmarks. The Maastricht criteria are the first set of important economic parameters for a country to be considered stable. As Croatia has decided it wishes to join the Euro sooner rather than later, this set of benchmarks helps in guiding policy making and stopping endless discussions with populists on topics such as why do we need low inflation? I am sure that our public debt would continue growing were it not for EUs Stability and Growth Pact, the Macroeconomic imbalances procedure and the Excessive Deficit Procedure. Third transition has been going on through financial system integration. I personally have no doubt that foreign banks contributions to the economic development of Croatia have been and are today positive and relevant. First, following the privatization and sale of some banks to foreign banks, there was no need to bail them out  unlike most banks bailed out by taxpayers money in former Yugoslavia.
