LET ME JUST BRIEFLY MENTION MAJOR CHANGES IN BANKING SECTOR, WHICH ALL HAVE BROUGHT TO CONSIDERABLE CONSOLIDATION IN BANKING SECTOR: THE PAYMENT SYSTEM UNDERWENT FUNDAMENTAL REFORM. IT HAS BEEN OPERATING SINCE 5 JANUARY 2001. AND IS GOING VERY SMOOTHLY WHICH IS THE FACT WE HAVE TO BE PROUD OF. WE WILL CONTINUE TO WORK WITH ALL BANKS TO CONSTANTLY IMPROVE THE PAYMENTS SYSTEM. STATE LEVEL DEPOSIT INSURANCE SCHEME HAS BEEN ESTABLISHED AND PLAYS A VERY IMPORTANT ROLE IN RE-ESTABLISHING CITIZENS CONFIDENCE IN THE BANKING SECTOR. IT IS INTENDED THAT BY AUGUST THIS YEAR, ALL BANKS WILL NEED TO BE MEMBERS OF THE DEPOSIT INSURANCE SCHEME. THEN, THERE HAS BEEN CONSIDERABLE CONSOLIDATION IN THE BANKING SECTOR. THE NUMBER OF BANKS HAS BEEN REDUCED QUITE SHARPLY AND WILL DECREASE FURTHER UNDER COMBINED PRESSURE OF THE HIGHER CAPITAL REQUIREMENTS AND SHARPLY INCREASED COMPETITION. THIS IS FORCING BANKS TO MERGE OR FIND STRATEGIC PARTNERS. BIH IS A SINGLE AND SMALL COUNTRY, AND ALTHOUGH WE HAVE TWO BANKING LAWS, THE BANKING SPACE OF BIH IS ALREADY CONSIDERABLY INTEGRATED. WE ARE VERY CLOSE TO HAVING A SINGLE BANKING SYSTEM. BANKING SUPERVISION WHICH IS CURRENTLY CARRIED OUT BY ENTITY AGENCIES WILL NEED TO BE UNIFIED AT THE STATE LEVEL, PROBABLY UNDER THE UMBRELLA OF THE CBBH. THERE IS ONE MORE ITEM I WANT TO MENTION TODAY AS ALL OF YOU ARE PRESENT. IT IS A SINGLE REGISTRY OF BANK ACCOUNTS. THE NATIONAL PAYMENTS COUNCIL SUPPORTED THE ESTABLISHMENT OF SUCH A REGISTRY AT LEAST TWO YEARS AGO. I UNDERSTAND ALL BANKS ARE IN FAVOUR. THE TASK WAS TO BE CARRIED OUT BY THE ENTITY MINISTRIES OF FINANCE. BUT A SINGLE REGISTRY OF BANK ACCOUNTS IS STILL NOT IN EXISTENCE IN BIH. THERE IS NOTHING TO PREVENT THE BANKS VOLUNTARILY SETTING UP A SINGLE REGISTER OF BANK ACCOUNTS. IF YOU WISH TO DO SO, THE CBBH WOULD BE PREPARED TO MANAGE THE ACCOUNT REGISTRY. WE WOULD MAKE THE INFORMATION AVAILABLE TO ALL PARTICIPATING BANKS. I THINK THE INFORMATION SHOULD ALSO BE AVAILABLE TO THE COURTS AND TO ANYONE ELSE WHO HAS A VALID INTEREST IN THE INFORMATION. THE TWO BANKING ASSOCIATIONS SHOULD DISCUSS THIS IDEA WITH THEIR MEMBERS. IF IT IS SUPPORTED, YOU SHOULD MAKE A FORMAL REQUEST TO THE CBBH. I TAKE YOUR PRESENCE HERE TODAY AS A VERY ENCOURAGING SIGN. ALL OF YOU HAVE PARTICIPATED DIRECTLY IN THE IMPLEMENTATION OF BANKING SECTOR REFORM. NOW WHEN YOU HAVE YOUR OWN INSTITUTIONAL CHANNEL TO SPEAK UP I URGE YOU TO PARTICIPATE ACTIVELY IN FUTURE REFORM THROUGH YOUR ASSOCIATION. ONCE AGAIN I WARMLY CONGRATULATE TO FEDERATION BANKERS ON THEIR EFFORTS AND WISH THEM SUCCESSFUL WORKING PART OF THE SESSION. THE PRESENCE OF GUESTS FROM RS IS CERTAINLY A VERY SUPPORTIVE SIGN FOR FURTHER INTEGRATION OF BANKING SYSTEM OF BIH.

Title: Speech notes for ceremony for KM 200 banknote
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: PETER NICHOLL, GOVERNOR OF THE CENTRAL BANK OF BiH SPEECH NOTES ON CEREMONY OF THE AGREEMENT SIGNED WITH BAMCARD SARAJEVO, 30 MAY 2002 I am very pleased to be signing this Agreement with BAMCARD today on behalf of the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is another step in the developmet of a modern payments system in BiH. When I came to BiH n 1997 the payment system here was very fragmented and undeveloped. There were four currencies being used for cash transactions; there were 76 banks but most were very small and none of them operated over the whole country;ATM machines, credit cards and e banking were non-existant; the payments bureaus had a monoply on domestic non-cash payments  but even here BiH had its own twist because they had split into three separate payments bureaus during the war. We have come a long way over the last five years. The KM is the dominant currency in cash transactions in BiH; the banking system has become much sounder and stronger and, as a consequence, citizens are returning to using the banks; ATM machines and credit cards are becoming quite common and e banking is starting. And last, but not least, a modern payments system based on the banking sector has been operating succesfully for over a year and the old monopoly payments bureaus have been closed. As part of this payments reform, the cbbh built and runs two clearing houses: an RTGS system and a giro system. They are at the forefront of modern clearing house technology and software. They have operational 99.9% of the time since we started. This system has the capacity to clear and settle many more transactions than it is currently doing. this applies both to the volume of transactions and the types of financial transactions. Indeed, the CBBH needs to increase the volume of transactions using our clearing houses or we may be forced to increase our fees to banks in order to cover or costs and allow the system to be continuously upgraded. We believe there is a lot of potential in the BiH financial markets for the volume of non-cash payments to increase. First, BiH is still very much a cash society but many more people have opened bank accounts in the last year and financial products like credit cards are expanding rapidly. So non-cash payments should increase. The development of new financial markets such as securities and stocks will also increase the potential turnover in our clearing houses. So, the Governing Board of the CBBH decided some months ago that we would not increase our clearing house fees. Instead we will look for and support financial market initiatives that will increase the volume of transactions going through our clearing houses. Today is one step in that process. The CBBH of course has to be and will be neutral when it comes to competition between financial service providers so this contract today confers no special priviledgs on BAMCARD that will not be available to any other service provider who can sell their services to the commercial banks. It is the banks that are the members of our clearing house. I congratulate BAMCARD on establishing a successful service and gaining bank customers to use it. We are vey happy to work with tem and wish them every success.

Title: Speech at International Investment Conference: "Role of the CBBH and development of the banking sector "
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: SPEECH OF THE GOVERNOR OF THE CENTRAL BANK OF BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA PETER NICHOLL "Role of the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina and development of the banking sector " International Investment Conference Mostar, 26th and 27th February 2004 PRESENTATION BY THE GOVERNOR OF THE CBBH, PETER NICHOLL I WILL COVER FOUR TOPICS IN MY PRESENTATION. THE FIRST WILL BE THE CENTRAL BANK OF BIH AND THE ROLES IT PLAYS IN MAINTAINING FINANCIAL STABILITY IN BIH. THE SECOND WILL BE THE SIGNIFICANT IMPROVEMENTS THAT HAVE OCCURRED IN THE BANKING SECTOR IN BIH OVER THE LAST THREE YEARS. THE THIRD WILL BE THE CHANGES THAT LIE AHEAD OF THE BIH FINANCIAL SECTOR IN THE IMMEDIATE FUTURE, AND I WILL FINISH WITH SOME BRIEF COMMENTS ON THE ECONOMIC OUTLOOK. THE CENTRAL BANK (CBBH): THE IS A STABLE STATE LEVEL INSTITUTION AND OPERATES OVER THE WHOLE COUNTRY THROUGH FIVE OFFICES. IT HAS 260 STAFF AND I AM THE ONLY FOREIGNER. BUT IT IS NOT TRUE COMPLETELY, BECAUSE I AM ALSO A BOSNIAN. THE CBBH LAW SPECIFIES CLEARLY THE FUNCTIONS THAT THE CBBH MUST CARRY OUT AND ALSO SETS A NUMBER OF LIMITATIONS ON ITS OPERATIONS. SUBJECT TO THESE LEGAL REQUIREMENTS AND RESTRICTIONS, THE CBBH IS COMPLETELY INDEPENDENT OF POLITICAL INFLUENCE. MONETARY POLICY: MONETARY POLICY IS THE CBBHS MOST IMPORTANT FUNCTION. THE CBBH OPERATES MONETARY POLICY THROUGH A STRICT CURRENCY BOARD ARRANGEMENT, WHICH IS STIPULATED IN THE CBBH LAW. THE THREE ESSENTIAL FEATURES OF THE BIH CURRENCY BOARD ARE: A FIXED EXCHANGE RATE SPECIFIED IN THE LAW; FULL FOREIGN EXCHANGE BACKING FOR ALL THE KM LIABILITIES OF THE CENTRAL BANK; FULL CONVERTIBILITY OF THE CBBHS KM LIABILITIES INTO THE ANCHOR CURRENCY. I WILL SAY SOMETHING ABOUT THESE CHARACTERISTICS WHICH ARE IMPORTANT FOR FOREIGN INVESTMENTS. (i) the fixed exchange rate: THE INITIAL EXCHANGE RATE WAS SET AT 1 KM 1 DEUTSCHMARK (THE BOSNIAN CURRENCY IS CALLED THE CONVERTIBLE MARKA). THE CHOICE OF THE DM AS THE ANCHOR CURRENCY FOR THE BIH CURRENCY BOARD WAS AN EASY ONE. THE DM HAD LONG BEEN A VERY STABLE CURRENCY AND IT WAS ALREADY WIDELY USED AND TRUSTED IN BIH. WHEN THE DM WAS REPLACED BY THE EURO, THE CBBH LAW WAS CHANGED TO MAKE THE EURO THE ANCHOR CURRENCY FOR THE BIH CURRENCY BOARD. THE NEW EXCHANGE RATE WAS SPECIFIED IN THE CBBH LAW AT EXACTLY THE SAME RATE AS THE DM HAD BEEN LINKED TO THE EURO, IE, 1KM 0.51129 EUROS. THIS MEANS THAT THE EXCHANGE RATE OF THE KM HAS BEEN UNCHANGED SINCE THE CBBH COMMENCED ITS OPERATIONS IN 1997. THE TRANSITION FROM THE DM TO THE EURO AS THE ANCHOR CURRENCY WENT VERY SMOOTHLY AND THE IMPACTS ON THE KM AND THE CURRENCY BOARD WERE VERY POSITIVE. (ii) full foreign exchange backing: THE KM LIABILITIES OF THE CBBH, WHICH ARE THE KM CURRENCY IN CIRCULATION AND THE DEPOSITS OF THE BIH COMMERCIAL BANKS AT THE CBBH, HAVE TO BE FULLY BACKED IN CONVERTIBLE FOREIGN ASSETS. AS OUR LIABILITIES ARE TIED TO THE EURO, WE HOLD MOST OF OUR RESERVES IN EUROS IN ORDER TO AVOID TAKING ANY EXCHANGE RATE RISK. THE TABLE BELOW SHOWS THAT THE CBBH HAS MAINTAINED THIS FULL FOREIGN EXCHANGE BACKING FOR THE KM SINCE 1998 AND WE HAD FREE RESERVES OF KM 153 MILLION AT THE END OF 2003. IN DECEMBER LAST YEAR WE HAD KM 2, 9 BILLION OF NET FOREIGN RESERVES THAT IS, ACCORDING TO THE INTERNATIONAL STANDARDS, VERY PLEASING. TABLE 1: CBBH FOREIGN RESERVES (End of period in KM millions) DATE NET FOREIGN MONETARY FREE RESERVES RESERVES LIABILITIES Dec 1997 144.1 160.3 -16.2 Dec 1998 283.3 253.9 29.4 Dec 1999 865.7 836.7 29.0 Dec 2000 1021.2 973.2 48.0 Dec 2001 2666.6 2591.6 75.0 Dec 2002 2463.2 2345.1 118.1 Dec 2003 2780.6 2626.3 153.3 (iii) full convertibilty: AS THE FOLLOWING TABLE SHOWS, THE KM HAS BEEN A CONVERTIBLE CURRENCY WITHIN BIH IN PRACTICE AS WELL AS IN NAME. (KM BILLION) KM ISSUED TO BIH KM PURCHASED FROM NET KM BANKS BIH BANKS ISSUED 12.747 10.523 2.224 THIS MEANS THAT WE HAVE ISSUED ALMOST KM 13 BILLION OF KM BANKNOTES AND WE HAVE, WITHOUT QUESTION OR LIMIT, CONVERTED BACK AROUND KM 10.5 BILLION, LEAVING A NET AMOUNT OF KM 2.2 BILLION IN CIRCUALTION AT THE PRESENT TIME. THE SUCCESS OF THE CURRENCY BOARD ARRANGEMENTS: THE CURRENCY BOARD HAS BEEN A VERY SUCCESSFUL TYPE OF MONETARY POLICY FOR BIH: THE KM HAS BEEN A STABLE CURRENCY AGAINST THE DEM AND THE EURO SINCE IT WAS INTRODUCED. INFLATION IN BIH IS NOW LOW, ABOUT ONE PERCENT, AND STABLE. TABLE 3: INFLATION IN BIH. (Retail price index, Annual % growth) YEAR FEDERATION REPUBLIKA SRPSKA BIH ENDED. OF BIH. AVERAGE DEC 2000 4.0 16.1 8.0 DEC 2001 0.3 2.2 0.9 DEC 2002 -0.7 2.4 0.3 DEC 2003 0.3 1.3 0.6 KM USE HAS RISEN STEADILY IN BIH AND THE KM IS NOW THE DOMINANT TRANSACTIONS CURRENCY IN ALL PARTS OF THE COUNTRY (EUROS ARE GENERALLY ACCEPTED TOO, AT LEAST FOR LARGER TRANSACTION). THE STABILITY OF THE KM HAS BEEN AN IMPORTANT ELEMENT IN INCREASING THE LEVEL OF FOREIGN DIRECT INVESTMENT COMING INTO BIH. ACCORDING TO THE INTERNATIONAL STATISTICS, WE HAVE ABOUT KM 6 BILLION OF FOREIGN INVESTMENTS AND THIS DATA WAS SHOWN LAST YEAR. BUT THE OFFICIAL STATISTICS REDUCE THE REAL VALUE. I HAVE STATISTICS RELATED TO THE BANKS, BECAUSE THEY RESPONDED MORE THEN OTHERS. FOREIGN BANKS SAY THEY INVESTED 15 PERCENT MORE THEN THE OFFICIAL STATISTICS SHOWED. MY MESSAGE TO THE DIRECT FOREIGN INVESTORS IS THAT THE SITUATION IN BH IS MUCH BETTER THAT THE OFFICIAL STATISTICS SHOW. MY MESSAGE TO THE BOSNIAN COLLEAGUES IS THAT WE HAVE TO IMPROVE OUR OFFICIAL STATISTICS BECAUSE WE OFFER OURSELEVES TO THE INVESTORS ALL THE TIME. THE CURRENCY BOARD WILL CONTINUE: THE PRESIDENCY OF BIH HAVE ANNOUNCED THAT THE CURRENCY BOARD ARRANGEMENTS WILL CONTINUE AS ONE OF THE MAJOR FEATURES OF MACRO-ECONOMIC POLICY IN BIH. IT IS ALSO SET OUT EXPLICITLY IN THE POVERTY REDUCTION STRATEGY PROGRAM THAT ALL LEVELS OF GOVERNMENT HAVE RECENTLY ADOPTED. THE LONG TERM GOAL OF BIH POLICY IS TO TAKE THE ECONOMY CLOSER TO AND EVENTUALLY INTO EUROPE. THE KM IS ALREADY TIED TO THE EURO. IT IS THEREFORE SENSIBLE TO MAINTAIN THIS LINK. THE EXIT STRTAEGY FOR BIH FROM THE CURRENCY BOARD WILL THEREFORE BE THE EVENTUAL ADOPTION OF THE EURO AS THE CURRENCY OF BIH. BANKING SECTOR: BIH HAS AN IMPROVING BANKING SECTOR. THE REFORM IN THE BANKING SECTOR HAS GONE FURTHER AND FASTER THAN REFORM IN ANY OTHER SECTOR OF THE ECONOMY. CONFIDENCE HAS COME BACK AND DEPOSITORS ARE NOW PREPARED TO PUT THEIR SAVINGS IN THE BANKS RATHER THAN KEEP THEM AT HOME IN FOREIGN CASH UNDER THE MATTRESS. BANK LENDING ALSO GREW VERY RAPIDLY LAST YEAR AND IS CONTINUING TO RISE STRONGLY THIS YEAR, THOUGH AT A SOMEWHAT SLOWER RATE THAN LAST YEAR'S DOUBLING. FOREIGN INVESTMENT IN THE BANKING SECTOR HAS BEEN HIGHER THAN IN ANY OTHER SECTOR IN BIH. 90 PERCENT OF BANKING SECTOR HAS BEEN PRIVATIZED. I WILL BRIEFLY LIST THE MAIN CHANGES THAT HAVE BROUGHT ABOUT THIS IMPROVEMENT IN THE BIH BANING SECTOR: PAYMENTS SYSTEM REFORM: THE CASH PAYMENTS SYSTEM HAS BEEN UNIFIED WITH THE KM BECOMING THE DOMINANT, AND ALMOST THE SOLE, CURRENCY IN USE IN BIH. IN THE NON-CASH PAYMENTS AREA, THE OLD STATE-OWNED CENTRALISED SYSTEM THAT HAD A MONOPOLY WAS CLOSED IN EARLY 2001. IT HAS BEEN REPLACED WITH A MODERN EUROPEAN-TYPE SYSTEM. THE SUPPLIERS WE USED HAD PUT SIMILAR SYSTEMS INTO PLACE IN NINE OTHER EUROPEAN COUNTRIES. BUT IT WAS DONE MORE QUICKLY IN BIH THAN ANYWHERE ELSE SHOWING THAT IT IS POSSIBLE TO IMPLEMENT LARGE, TECHNICAL PROJECTS IN BIH SUCCESSFULLY. MINIMUM CAPITAL REQUIREMENTS: THESE REQUIREMENTS HAVE BEEN SUBSTANTAILLY INCREASED THROUGH A SERIES OF STEPS FROM AN INITIAL KM 2.5 MILLION TO KM 15 MILLION FROM THE BEGINNING OF 2003. THIS HAS FORCED BANKS TO MERGE OR FIND STRATEGIC PARTNERS. INTER-ENTITY BANKING: IT BECAME POSSIBLE IN 2001 FOR A BANK REGISTERED IN ONE ENTITY TO OPERATE BRANCHES IN THE OTHER ENTITY. DEPOSIT INSURANCE: A DEPOSIT INSURANCE SCHEME STARTED IN 2001. IT COVERS DEPOSITS IN APPROVED BANKS UP TO KM 5,000. THIS IS ALSO HELPING RETURN CITIZENS CONFIDENCE TO THE BANKS THAT QUALIFY. INITIALLY, TWO AGENCIES WERE ESTABLISHED, ONE IN EACH ENTITY. BUT IN 2002, THEY WERE MERGED INTO A STATE DEPOSIT INSURANCE AGENCY. AT PRESENT, 20 BANKS HAVE MET THE STANDARDS REQUIRED TO BE A MEMBER OF THE DIA. FOREIGN BANKS: A NUMBER OF FOREIGN BANKS HAVE COMMENCED OPERATIONS IN BIH, PARTICULARLY IN THE LAST THREE YEARS. FUTURE INITIATIVES IN THE BIH FINANCIAL SECTOR: BIH NOW HAS A SOUND CENTRAL BANK AND A STABLE CURRENCY AND A RAPIDLY IMPROVING COMMERCIAL BANKING SECTOR. NOW THAT THE BIH FINANCIAL SYSTEM HAS A FIRM BASE, THE CHALLENGES FOR THE NEXT TWO YEARS ARE TO MAINTAIN FINANCIAL STABLITY AND TO DEVELOP THE CAPITAL AND SECURITIES MARKETS SO AS TO BROADEN THE RANGE OF FINANCIAL SERVICES AVAILABLE TO SAVERS AND INVESTORS IN BIH. I WILL BRIEFLY LIST SOME OF THE INTITIATIVES THAT ARE UNDERWAY OR PROPOSED: SOVEREIGN CREDIT RATING: THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS HAS DECIDED THAT BIH SHOULD SEEK ITS FIRST SOVEREIGN CREDIT RATING AND HAS ASKED THE CBBH TO ADMINISTER THE PROJECT. THE CREDIT RATING SHOULD BE AVAILBLE IN APRIL, 2004. THE PRESENT INTERNATIONAL PERCEPTION OF BIH IS OFTEN VERY NEGATIVE. WE BELIEVE HAVING A PUBLISHED RATING WILL IMPROVE THE KNOWLEDGE ABOUT BIH AND THE PERCEPTIONS MANY POTENTIAL INVESTORS CURRENTLY HAVE. SECURITIES MARKET: WORK IS CURRENTLY UNDERWAY TO DRAFT A SECURITIES LAW AND TO DEVELOP SELLING, REGISTRY AND SETTLEMENT PROCESSES FOR A SECURITIES MARKET IN BIH. I EXPECT THE MARKET TO COMMENCE IN THE SECOND HALF OF 2004. STOCK EXCHANGES: TWO STOCK EXCHANGES HAVE BEEN ESTABLISHED IN BIH BUT BOTH ARE VERY SMALL. THIS IS THE CASE WITH MOST OF THE STOCK EXCHANGES ESTABLISHED IN THE REGION. THERE ARE DISCUSSIONS BEING HELD WITH THE AIM OF MOVING TOWARDS SOME FORM OF REGIONAL STOCK EXCHANGE, WHICH IN MY VIEW IS VERY POSITIVE AND IS THE ONLY FEASIBLE AND SENSIBLE OPTION FOR BIH, AND FOR MOST OTHER COUNTRIES IN THE REGION. THE ECONOMIC OUTLOOK: THERE ARE TWO THINGS THAT MAKE IT DIFFICULT TO PREDICT THE ECONOMIC OUTLOOK IN BIH WITH PRECISION. THE FIRST IS THAT BIH IS GOING THROUGH SO MANY TRANSITIONS SIMULTANEOUSLY THAT THE ECONOMIC NUMBERS CAN MOVE THROUGH VERY LARGE RANGES. SECOND, THE ECONOMIC OUTLOOK DEPENDS CRUCIALLY ON AN ACCELERARTION OF THE ECONOMIC, REGULATORY AND LEGAL REFORM PROCESSES IN BIH. FORECASTS BASED ON THE STATUS-QUO AS COMPARED TO THOSE BASED ON AN ACCELERATED REFORM PATH WILL BE VERY DIFFERENT. THE ENVIRONMENT FOR PRIVATE INVESTMENT HAS IMPROVED BUT IT IS STILL TOO COMPLICATED. THIS APPLIES TO LOCAL AS WELL AS FOREIGN INVESTMENT. THERE ARE MANY IMPORTANT INITIATIVES UNDER ACTION, INCLUDING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A SINGLE INDIRECT TAX AUTHORITY, A PROPOSAL TO SIMPLIFY COMPANY REGSISTRATION, AND THE ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMERCIAL COURTS. I AM AN OPTOMIST AND BELIEVE THAT WE WILL SEE A COMBINATION OF CONTINUED MACRO-ECONOMIC STABILITY AND ACCELERATED MICRO-ECONOMIC AND LEGAL REFORM. ON THIS BASIS, I WOULD EXPECT INFLATION TO REMAIN STABLE AT AROUND CURRENT LEVELS OF 1-2 %, ECONOMIC GROWTH RATES TO BE AT LEAST 6-7 PERCENT PER ANNUM IN NOMINAL TERMS (5% REAL) AND THE BALANCE OF PAYMENTS SITUATION TO GRADUALLY IMPROVE. THOUGH BIH IS A SMALL COUNTRY, IT IS VERY STRATEGICALLY LOCATED WITH FREE MARKET ACCESS TO A VERY LARGE EUROPEAN MARKET. IT HAS A WELL EDUCATED LABOUR FORCE. GIVEN THESE TWO FACTORS AND THE HIGH DEGREE OF MACRO-ECONOMIC STABILITY IN BIH, I BELIEVE THE BALANCE BETWEEN RISK AND OPPORTUNITY NOW FAVOURS OPPORTUNITY. I TAKE YOUR PRESENCE AT THIS CONFERENCE AS A VERY ENCOURAGING SIGN FOR BIH.

Title: Speech at the conferences on investment and trade
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: Bosnia and Herzegovina investment and trade conferences Washington D.C., Tuesday, 17 June 2003 and New York, Thursday, 19 June 2003. Presentation by Peter Nicholl Governor Central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will cover four topics in my presentation. The first will be the central bank of BH and the roles it plays in maintaining financial stability in BH. The second will be the significant improvements that have occurred in the banking sector in BH over the last three years. The third will be the changes that lie ahead of the BH financial sector in the immediate future, and I will finish with some brief comments on the economic outlook. The central bank (CBBH): The CBBH commenced its operations on 11 August 1997 so it is still quite a young organization. It is a state level institution, which means it is the only monetary authority in BH and operates over the whole country through five offices. It has 250 staff. The CBBH law specifies clearly the functions that the CBBH must carry out and also sets a number of limitations on its operations. Subject to these legal requirements and restrictions, the CBBH is completely independent of political influence. Monetary policy: Monetary policy is the CBBHs most important function. The CBBH operates monetary policy through a strict Currency Board Arrangement, which is stipulated in the CBBH law. There were three main reasons for the choice of a Currency Board for BHs monetary policy: It provided a firm nominal anchor in the form of a fixed exchange rate in a situation where there was significant economic instability; It removed discretion in a situation where there was considerable difficulty in establishing institutions and making political decisions; Currency boards had been recently established in some other eastern European countries and were working well. The Currency Board: The three essential features of the BH Currency Board are: A fixed exchange rate specified in the law; Full foreign exchange backing for all the KM liabilities of the Central Bank; Full convertibility of the CBBH's KM liabilities into the anchor currency. The fixed exchange rate: The initial exchange rate was set at 1 KM (the Bosnian currency is called the Convertible Mark) 1 Deutschmark. The choice of the DM as the anchor currency for the BH Currency Board was an easy one. The DM had long been a very stable currency and it was already widely used and trusted in BH. When the DM was replaced by the euro, the CBBH Law was changed to make the euro the anchor currency for the BH currency board. The new exchange rate was specified in the CBBH law at exactly the same rate as the DM had been linked to the euro. I.e., 1KM 0.51129 euros. This means that the exchange rate of the KM has been unchanged since the CBBH commenced its operations. The transition from the DM to the euro as the anchor currency went very smoothly and the impacts on the KM and the Currency Board were very positive. (See table 1 below). Full foreign exchange backing: The KM liabilities of the CBBH, which are the KM currency in circulation and the deposits of the BH commercial banks at the CBBH, have to be fully backed in convertible foreign assets. As our liabilities are tied to the euro, we hold most of our reserves in euros in order to avoid taking any exchange rate risk. The table below shows that the CBBH has maintained this full foreign exchange backing for the KM since 1998 and we had free reserves of KM 137 million at the end of March 2003. Table 1: CBBH foreign reserves (end of period in KM millions) Date net foreign monetary free reserves reserves liabilities Dec 1997 144.1 160.3 -16.2 Dec 1998 283.3 253.9 29.4 Dec 1999 865.7 836.7 29.0 Dec 2000 1021.2 973.2 48.0 Dec 2001 2666.6 2591.6 75.0 Dec 2002 2463.2 2345.1 118.1 Mar 2003 2227.4 2090.0 137.4 This table also illustrates the way in which the KM gradually substituted for the other currencies that were in use in BH thus leading to a steady increase in the CBBH balance sheet from 1997 to 2000. This trend accelerated during the euro conversion period in late 2001 and early 2002. In all, the CBBH sent DM 4.3 billion of DM banknotes back to Germany from Bosnia during this conversion period and the CBBH's foreign reserves more than doubled. Our foreign reserves have fallen from the peak they reached at the end of 2001 and at the end of March 2003 our KM liabilities were KM 502 million lower and our foreign reserves were KM 439 million lower. Most of the fall has been in the level of commercial bank deposits at the CBBH: Table 2: CBBH KM liabilities (KM million) Date KM in circulation bank deposits at CBBH 31 Dec 01 1806.0 758.6 31 Mar 03 1728.7 340.6 Change - 77.3 -418.0 The sharp fall in bank deposits has come about for four reasons: The level at 31 December 2001 was unusually high and had risen very quickly because of the magnitude and speed of the DM conversion process in BH; Bank lending has increased rapidly, Banks made a portfolio shift of some of these deposits to foreign banks as they earned no interest on their surplus deposits at the CBBH and there was no short-term liquidity instrument in BH on which they could earn interest (the CBBH has recently moved to paying interest on all commercial bank deposits at the CBBH and this could help reverse this trend); The large current account deficit has also had some impact but I do not think it has been the major reason. As at 31 March, 2003 the CBBH's net foreign reserves still represented 3.5 months of import coverage and were still more than double the level at the end of 2000. Full convertibility: As the following table shows, the KM has been a convertible currency within BH in practice as well as in name. Table 3: net KM issued from 11/8/97 to 5/6/03. (KM billion) KM issued to BH KM purchased from net KM Banks BH banks issued 11.160 9.308 1.851 The success of the Currency Board arrangements: The Currency Board has been a very successful type of monetary policy for BH: The KM has been a stable currency against the DEM and the euro since it was introduced. Inflation in BH is now low and stable: Table 4: inflation in BH. (retail price index, annual % growth) Year Federation Republika Srpska BH ended. Of BH. Average Dec 2000 4.0 16.1 8.0 Dec 2001 0.3 2.2 0.9 Dec 2002 -0.7 2.4 0.3 Mar 2003 0.0 2.1 0.7 KM use has risen steadily in BH and the KM is now the dominant transactions currency in all parts of the country (euros are generally accepted too, at least for larger transaction). The proportion of bank deposits denominated in KM is also growing, though at March 2003, 52% were still denominated in foreign currency (46% in euros). The KM has remained fully convertible in BH since it was introduced. The stability of the KM has been an important element in increasing the level of foreign direct investment coming into BH: Table 5: foreign direct investment into BH (in KM m.) Period foreign direct investment 117.4 324.5 310.1 274.1 604.3 2002q1 140.8 2003q1 181.7 The Currency Board will continue: The presidency of BH has announced that the Currency Board arrangements will continue as one of the major features of macro-economic policy in BH. This is also the policy of the state and entity governments as set out in the letter of intent they have sent the IMF as part of the stand-by negotiations with the fund. The most important reason for this is that the policy has produced major economic and social benefits. Secondly, the citizens of BH have faced many financial traumas in the past. They therefore value a stable currency and the Currency Board consequently has a high level of public support within BH. Finally, the long term goal of BH policy is to take the economy closer to and eventually into Europe. The KM is already tied to the euro. It is therefore sensible to maintain this link. The exit strategy for BH from the Currency Board will therefore be the eventual adoption of the euro as the currency of BH. Banking sector: The second area i want to focus on in my address is the commercial banking sector. BH has an improving banking sector. The reform in the banking sector has gone further and faster than reform in any other sector of the economy. Confidence is coming back and depositors are now prepared to put their savings in the banks rather than keep them at home in foreign cash under the mattress. For example, commercial bank deposits grew by 25% from KM 3,324 million to KM 4,158 million over 2002. Bank lending also grew very rapidly last year. Table 6: commercial bank lending: Date amount of lending (KM m) growth rate(%) 31.12.00 1652 15.6 31.12.01 2101 27.2 31.12.02 3213 52.9 Competition in the banking sector is real, helped by the arrival of some good foreign banks. Proportionately, foreign investment in the banking sector has been higher than in any other sector in BH. Bank interest rates on lending have fallen substantially under the pressure of increased competition, but are still relatively high. Comprehensive data on interest rates was not collected prior to 2002 but most bank lending rates prior to 2001 would have been over 20%. They have fallen steadily since that time and the average short term lending rate in March 2003 was 11.5% and the average long term lending rate was 10.67%. Prime borrowers can now easily get funds at single digit interest rates. I will briefly list the main changes that have brought this improvement in the BH banning sector about: Payments system reform: the cash payments system has been unified with the KM becoming the dominant, and almost the sole, currency in use in BH. In the non-cash payments area, the old state-owned centralized system that had a monopoly was closed in early 2001. It has been replaced with a modern European-type system with two clearing houses, an RTGS one and a giro one, owned and operated by the central bank. Payments are being conducted by the commercial banks. The suppliers we used had put similar systems into place in nine other European countries. But it was done more quickly in BH than anywhere else showing that it is possible to implement large, technical projects in BH successfully. It has been operating smoothly and effectively since 5 January 2001. Minimum capital requirements: these requirements have been substantially increased through a series of steps from an initial KM 2.5 million to KM 15 million from the beginning of 2003. This has forced banks to merge or find strategic partners. This, plus increased competition, has led to a sharp reduction in the number of banks in BH. In 1997, there were 76 registered banks in BH in 1997 but most of them were extremely small. At present there are 38 registered banks in BH. This number will reduce further over the next year as consolidation continues. Inter-entity banking: it became possible in 2001 for a bank registered in one entity to operate branches in the other entity. Thirteen banks, including most of the larger ones, are already doing so and more will follow. It is interesting that seven banks registered in the Federation have branches in the RS and six banks registered in the RS have branches in the Federation. So the movement has been in both directions. We can say that in the banking sector, BH now has a single economic space. Deposit insurance: a deposit insurance scheme started in 2001. It covers deposits in approved banks up to KM 5,000. This is also helping return citizens' confidence to the banks that qualify. Initially, two agencies were established, one in each entity. But in 2002, they were merged into a State Deposit Insurance Agency. At present, 13 banks have met the standards required to be a member of the DIA but all banks will need to meet these standards later this year or face the risk of losing their banking license. Foreign banks: a number of foreign banks have commenced operations in BH, particularly in the last two years. Increased foreign competition has already been very good for the BH economy. It has given depositors more choice and it has forced the local banks to improve the range and quality of the services they provide in order to survive. Privatization of government owned banks: progress in bank privatization was initially very slow but accelerated markedly in 2002. The process of privatization is now virtually complete. These latter two trends, foreign entry and privatization, have led to a substantial shift in ownership in the BH banking sector towards private ownership and, in particular, foreign private ownership. Table 7: capital structure in BH banking sector (%) 31.12.00 31.12.01 31.12.02 31.5.03 State capital 47 19 10 8 Private capital: 53 81 90 92 Domestic na 25 24 21 Foreign na * 56 67 72 * The data isnt available but the % of foreign ownership would have been low. In short, the BH banking system is looking more and more like the banking system you see in other European countries  or in the USA. The BH banking system has still not completed its transition to becoming a modern European type banking system but it is well on the way and I think most people will be surprised by how quickly the banking system will continue to change and improve. The main things that will slow down the transition are problems in the legal and regulatory frameworks in BH that make it difficult for banks to take and use collateral for lending. This is where the reform focus now needs to be concentrated Future initiatives in the BH financial sector: BH now has a sound Central Bank and a stable currency and a rapidly improving commercial banking sector. Now that the BH financial system has a firm base, the challenges for the next two years are to maintain financial stability and to develop the capital and securities markets so as to broaden the range of financial services available to savers and investors in BH. I will briefly list some of the initiatives that are underway or proposed: National capital markets council (NCMC): I have recently formed a NCMC in order to develop a broadly based and supported strategy for the next stages of financial market development in BH. The council includes representatives from state and entity governments, regulatory authorities and market participants. All organizations that I invited to join have enthusiastically agreed to do so. Sovereign credit rating: The Council of Ministers has decided that BH should seek its first sovereign credit rating and has asked the CBBH to administer the project. The credit rating should be available by the end of 2003. The present international perception of BH is often very negative and we believe having a published rating will improve the knowledge about BH and the perceptions many potential investors currently have. Securities market: Work is currently underway to draft a securities law and to develop selling, registering and settlement processes for a securities market in BH. It has not yet been decided whether the first securities will be issued by the state government, the entity governments or the CBBH. But the legal and administrative work will be done to allow any or all of those organizations to issue securities, hopefully in 2004. Stock exchanges: Two stock exchanges have been established in BH but both are very small. This is the case with most of the stock exchanges established in the region. There are discussions being held with the aim of moving towards some form of regional stock exchange, which in my view is the only feasible and sensible option for BH, and for most other countries in the region. Banking supervision: Banking supervision in BH is based on the Basle principles. Banking supervision is currently carried out by entity agencies, with the CBBH having a coordinating role. There is good cooperation among the three institutions and this was recently formalized by the signing of a memorandum of understanding. The banking system in BH is rapidly moving towards being a single country-wide system with banks registered in one entity operating in both entities. Because of this, banking supervision is likely to move under the umbrella of the CBBH in the near future. Harmonization with the EU standards and regulations: In all areas in financial market developments (as in all other areas), we are trying to ensure that the things we introduce are consistent with EU standards and regulations. The economic outlook: I attach a table of the main economic indicators for BH in order to give you a context for considering future economic developments. There are two things that make it difficult to predict the economic outlook in BH with precision. The first is that BH is going through so many transitions simultaneously that the economic numbers can move through very large ranges. Second, the economic outlook depends crucially on an acceleration of the economic, regulatory and legal reform processes in BH. Forecasts based on the status-quo as compared to those based on an accelerated reform path will be very different. In fact, unless the regulatory, legal and tax systems are changed, and changed quickly and substantially, BH will have a very difficult future. The environment for private investment has improved but it is still far too complicated. This applies to local as well as foreign investment. This is where the attention of BH politicians and international consultants and advisors needs to be directed. The macroeconomic situation in BH is a stable one. It is the areas of regulatory, tax and legal system reform that will determine the future of BH. I am an optimist and believe that we will see a combination of continued macro-economic stability and accelerated micro-economic and legal reform. On this basis, I would expect inflation to remain stable at around current levels, economic growth rates to be at least 6-7 percent per annum in nominal terms (5% real) and the balance of payments situation to gradually improve. There are still risks attached to investing in BH. But there are also many opportunities. Though BH is a small country, it is very strategically located with free market access to a very large European market. It has a well educated labor force. Given these two factors and the high degree of macro-economic stability in BH, I believe the balance between risk and opportunity now favors opportunity. I take your presence at this conference as a very encouraging sign for BH.

Title: Five years of the CBBH
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: FIVE YEARS OF THE CBBH. Presentation for the CBBH Conference The Monetary Policy Role of Currency Boards: History and Practice Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina. 11 April, 2003. CBBH. Introduction: The first two speakers at this conference, Warren Coats and Jure Pelivan, have described for you the development of the CBBH Law that set the legal framework under which the CBBH operates and the process of getting the CBBH established and operating. I arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina in November, 1997 to take up the position of Governor of the newly-established central bank. It quickly became clear to me that the legal framework set out in the CBBH Law was a very good one. This framework has been an important reason why the CBBH has been able to establish itself and operate successfully. I am very pleased that so many people who were involved in the development of the CBBH Law and the establishment of the CBBH are here today for this conference: Serge Robert, the first Governor of the CBBH, Warren Coats, Scott Brown and Kim Rhee from the IMF,and the three local Board members, Manolo Coric, Kasim Omicevic and Jure Pelivan. I want to congratulate and thank them for the sound work they did to get the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina underway. The structure of the CBBH: My paper will focus on the operations of the CBBH during its first five and a half years and the results that have been achieved. But first I will briefly set out the main features of the CBBH structure that have had an important impact on the Banks operations: The CBBH reports to the State Presidency of BiH and to the State Parliament. The setting of strategic directions, establishing policies and procedures, and monitoring performance are all the responsibility of a Governing Board of four members. The members are all very experienced and there has been stability in the Board membership. I joined the Board in November 1997  and I am the newest member. One unusual feature of the governance structure is that for the first six years, the Governor is appointed by the International Monetary Fund, after consulation with the Presidency of BiH and shall not be a citizen of BiH or any neighboring state. The first Governor, Serge Robert, who was Governor-elect from November 1996 and Governor from August to October 1997 is from France. I am from New Zealand. The day-to-day management of the Bank is in the hands of the Governor, who is the Chief Executive Officer, and three Vice Governors. Two of the three Vice Governors have also been working in the CBBH from the beginning. The third Vice Governor joined the Bank from 1 January, 2000. So the senior management team of the CBBH has also been a very stable one (you will find from my presentation that stability is a key word for the CBBH). Independence One other very important feature of the CBBH framework is that it has operational independence. The CBBH Law says that within the limits of its authority established by this Law, the Central Bank shall be entirely independent .. in the pursuit of its objectives and the performance of its tasks. (Article 3) There are two important comments I want to make about this statutory independence. First, we are not independent in the sense that we can do whatever we choose. We must operate within the CBBH Law. The CBBH Law sets very clear definitions in most areas of what we must do and what we cant do. Second, independence needs to be established and maintained in practice. It is not enough for it to be just a word in a law  and then ignored in practice. The CBBH did have to struggle to establish its operational independence in the first 18 months of our operations. Over the last three years, the situation has generally been much improved. But even during this latter period, the CBBH has had to insist on its statutory independence being respected in response to proposals in other laws that would have undermined our independence, such as the Civil Service Law and the Law on Ministries. The Monetary Policy of BiH: The CBBH Law says that the first basic task of the CBBH shall be to formulate, adopt and control the monetary policy of BiH by issuing the domestic currency (Convertible Marka) at a one to one exchange rate with the Deutsche mark with full backing in freely convertible foreign exchange.(Article 2.3.a) That is a long-winded way of saying the CBBH would operate as a currency board. Though the term currency board does not appear in Article 2 of the Law, it does appear in several other articles of the Law (Articles 1, 2.3.h, 11.1.a, 31). The choice of a currency board as the monetary policy of BiH had two main motivations. First, it provided a firm nominal anchor for the countrys monetary policy. This was considered critical for the very uncertain post-war economic environment BiH faced. Second, it took into account the difficulty there would be in making political decisions in the complex political environment in BiH. One other monetary policy choice that was available at the time that would have been consistent with these two motivations would have been for BiH to adopt the DM as its currency. This policy would also have delivered monetary stability to BiH. There have been two additional benefits for BiH from taking the currency board option. First, the KM has become a unifying symbol in the country. Second, the CBBH earns seignorage from issuing KM which would have gone to the Bundesbank if the DM had been adopted as the currency of BiH. For BiH, the choice of the anchor currency was an easy one. The DM had been a sound and stable currency for a long time; the Bundesbank had an unparalleled reputation for strength and stability, and the DM was already widely used in BiH because the people had confidence in it. The DM also played a significant role in the trade of BiH. The decision to set the exchange rate at 1 KM 1 DM ( also equal to 100 Bosnian dinars at that time) proved to be a very sensible and important decision. The Bosnian dinar exchange rate had been BD 100 1 DM throughout the war. So the new KM exchange rate was set at a rate that was already known to many of the citizens of BiH. The 1 KM 1DM exchange rate also allowed the two currencies to be used side-by-side. This is what happened for three years. During this period, the KM gradually substituted for the DM. This substitution process came to a dramatic and successful conclusion when all the remaining DM banknotes in BiH had to be converted at the time of the introduction of Euro banknotes and coins. A second important feature of the currency board arrangements is that the CBBH has to maintain at least 100% backing in foreign exchange reserves for all of its KM liabilities. There were some short-term breaches of this requirement in the first year of the CBBHs operations. This did weaken the initial acceptance of the KM, particularly in some parts of the country. These initial problems were resolved in 1998 and the KM liabilities have been fully covered by foreign exchange reserves since that time. Table 1: CBBH Free Foreign Reserves Date Foreign Exchange Assets KM Monetary Liabilities Free Foreign Reserves KM million KM million KM million 11/8/97 132.6 132.6 0 31/12/97 144.1 160.3 -16.1 31/12/98 283.3 253.9 29.4 31/12/99 865.7 836.7 29.0 31/12/00 1,021.4 973.2 48.0 31/12/01 2,696.5 2,591.6 75.0 31/12/02 2,464.4 2,345.2 118.1 31/3/03* 2,228.5 2,090.0 137.4 * Unaudited The third key feature of the currency board arrangements is that the CBBH has to maintain full convertibility of the KM within BiH. The convertibility was initially into DM and is now into Euro. In order to ensure that we can do this at all times, our policy on the investment of our foreign reserves has been very careful and cautious. No exchange rate risks are taken, credit risks are minimised by holding funds only in banks rated AA- or better, and a high level of liquidity has been maintained. The foreign reserve guidelines have been reassessed from time to time during the last few years and changes made in order to try and increase average returns. But the over-riding principle has remained minimisation of risk. As the following table shows clearly, the KM has been a convertible currency within BiH in practice as well as in name. Table 2: Net KM issued, 11/8/97 to 1/4/03 (KM billion) KM issued to BiH banks KM purchased from BiH banks Net Issuance 10.794 8.924 1.870 Progress of the KM There were early political difficulties regarding the design of the KM currency that delayed its introduction. The Law said that as an interim measure the Central Bank will put in circulation Coupons and that all endeavours should be made to do this within three months of the passing of the Law. This deadline was not met and in the end, the CBBH did not introduce Coupons but went straight to banknotes. Given that the KM had to be convertible at all times, it was not feasible to put the KM into circulation as a coupon. It was necessary to have the security features of a banknote from the beginning in order to avoid the risk of counterfeiting. The first banknotes had, as was specified in the CBBH Law, two different variants for each denomination, one for the Federation and one for the RS. Despite this, the Presidency was unable to agree on the designs and the decision on the designs of the first KM banknotes was imposed by the High Representative in January, 1998. The first KM banknotes went into circulation on 22 June 1998. We initially circulated the Federation design in the Federation and the RS design in the RS. The two designs had most of their main features in common and the two variations were not separated once they were returned to the CBBH. The two variations became intermingled and began to be used as one currency quite quickly. The first coins went into circulation on 9 December, 1998. In contrast to the drawn out discussions on the design of the first banknotes, the coin designs were agreed quickly by the CBBH Board and the Presidency. Also, there was only one design for the coins. This progress has been taken further with the introduction of a single KM 200 banknote in 2002. The decision on the design elements for this banknote was taken by the Presidency at a single meeting and they left the approval of the final design to the CBBH. The main gauge of the acceptance of the KM as the main transactions currency in BiH is the change in the level of the CBBHs KM liabilities. The CBBH started in August, 1997 with a balance sheet of KM 132.6m which it took over from the former National Bank of BiH (NBBH). Just prior to the introduction of the first KM banknotes in June 1998, the level had dropped to KM 118 m. as there had been a switch to increased use of the DM because of problems with the currency board. As Table 1 shows, the requirement to have 100% foreign exchange backing for the CBBHs KM liabilities was breached at the end of 1997 and these breaches continued to occur on occasions during the first half of 1998. These breaches of the currency board requirement had two sources. First, there were transactions related to the former NBBH being conducted through the Payments Bureau that had the effect of putting the CBBH into a situation of lending to the NBBH. These transactions were not under the control of the CBBH. Second, the CBBH was operating without any capital during this early period. The CBBH Law (Article 25.1 and 25.2) said  The initial capital of the Central Bank shall have a value of twenty-five million Convertible Marka and The entire initial capital of the Central Bank shall be fully paid up within two weeks from the date this Law enters into force. This means that the CBBH should have received this capital before it started operating in 1997. But we did not receive this initial capital until June 1998. Prior to that date we were running a strict currency board with no capital. If the CBBH had received its initial capital at the time set out in the Law, the inadvertent, periodic lending to the NBBH would still have been a breach of Article 1.1 of the CBBH Law, which prohibits the CBBH from extending credit. But the CBBH would not have breached the requirement to have full foreign exchange backing for our KM liabilities. Table 3: CBBH KM liabilities Date KM liabilities (KM m) 11/8/97 132.6 31/12/97 160.3 22/6/98 118.0 31/12/98 253.3 31/12/99 836.7 31/12/00 973.2 31/12/01 2,591.6 31/12/02 2,345.2 28/2/03 2,052.5 The downward trend in our KM liabilities was reversed as soon as the KM banknotes were introduced and the problems that had led to currency board breaches were resolved. These two events occurred around the same time in 1998 so it is not possible to isolate the relative significance of each for the improvement in use of the KM. Throughout 1998, 1999 and 2000 a number of events occurred that increased the usage of the KM as the transactions currency of BiH. Some of the main ones were: September 1998: KM became the only currency used in domestic non-cash payments conducted through the Payments Bureaus; December 1998: Low denomination KM coins introduced; April, 1999: KM exchange started in some banks abroad; September, 1999: non-cash payment transaction between RS and FBiH in KM only commenced; October 1999: non-cash payments in the internal payments system in FBiH are done exclusively in KM; July 2000: non-cash payments in the internal payments system in the RS are done exclusively in KM; During 2000, the value of the Yugoslavian dinar fell sharply against the KM; July, 2000: 1KM and 2 KM coins introduced; January, 2001: the new payments system operating through the commercial banks and the Central Bank started and the Payments Bureaus ceased making payments. But the event that had the biggest impact on the growth of KM usage was the introduction of the Euro currency on 1 January, 2002. This required the citizens of BiH to convert the large quantities of DM banknotes they were holding. The timing of the Euro currency introduction was very favourable for BiH. By the time it occurred, the citizens had full trust in the KM and were regaining trust in the BiH commercial banks. As a consequence, a large proportion of the DM 4.3 billion of DM banknotes that the CBBH shipped out of BiH during the period September 2001 to March 2002 were converted either to KM currency or put on deposit in a BiH bank. During that period, the amount of KM in circulation rose from KM 812 milion at 31 August 2001 to KM 1,977 million at the 31 March, 2003, a rise of 143%. The amount of bank deposits in BiH commercial banks rose from KM 2,372 million to KM 3,730 million over the same period, a rise of 57 %. The subsequent decline in 2002 was primarily related to a reduction in commercial bank deposits held at the CBBH as banks began to lend some of the large increase in deposits they had received from the DM conversion process. The declines in early 2003 are, we believe, primarily related to the deteriorating balance of payments situation in BiH. As a consequence, they are a concern and indicate a need to accelerate the pace of economic reform in the country. Nevertheless, the CBBHs KM liabilities at present are still around 110% more than they were at the end of 2000 and are almost sixteen times higher than they were in the opening balance sheet of the CBBH in August, 1997. Based on this, the currency board has been very successful in convincing the citizens of BiH to trust and use their own currency, the KM. Reasons for the Currency Boards Success. In my view there are four main reasons why the currency board has been successful in establishing and maintaining trust in the KM. First, people in BiH have faced many financial traumas. They therefore understand and value a stable currency. The currency board consequently has a high level of public support within BiH. This is evident from the citizens willingness to increasingly use the KM. It is also evident from the opinion surveys conducted for UNDP and published in their Early Warning System documents. These surveys regularly report that the KM is one of the few things the citizens of BiH have much trust in. Second, people in BiH had complete trust in the anchor currency, the DM. The currency board type of monetary policy has allowed the CBBH, a new institution with no track record and operating in an environment where citizens generally didnt trust the institutions of the state to gain some of the of the DM and the Bundesbank. This didnt happen instantly. The CBBH had to show that it would strictly adhere to the currency board principles. Once the citizens believed that, their confidence in and use of the KM grew surprisingly rapidly. There were no adverse impacts on this confidence in the stability of the KM when the DM was replaced by the Euro. Indeed, the conversion of the large amounts of DM banknotes that were in BiH proved to be very positive for the KM and for the banking system in BiH. The CBBH set the exchange rate of the KM to the Euro at exactly the same rate as the DM had been tied to the Euro. This rate is 1 Euro 1.95583 KM ( or 1KM 0.51129 Euros if you prefer to specify it that way). While an exchange rate of 1 Euro 2KM would have undoubtedly been more convenient, the CBBH decided it was much more important for citizens continued confidence in the KM that the exchange rate established in the CBBH Law in 1997 was retained. Third, some people say the CBBH and the currency board have succeeded because the CBBH has a foreign Governor. That is very flattering - but it is only a small part of the story. In my view the major reason the currency board has worked in BiH is the very good legal and institutional framework the CBBH operates under: the goal of the CBBH is simple, clear and specified precisely in the Law; there are very clear roles set out in the CBBH Law for the main participants: the State Parliament, The State Presidency, the CBBH Governing Board, and the CBBH Governor. there are clear reporting lines and reporting obligations between each of these groups of stakeholders set out in the CBBH Law. the CBBH Law limits our activities where there could be any potential conflicts with the currency board requirements; within these statutory goals and limitiations, the CBBH is independent of political direction; the CBBH can be easily held accountable. A breach of the currency board requirements would be quickly obvious to all. In order to make it even easier for people, we publish a line at the bottom of our published financial statement which sets out our net foreign assets minus our monetary liabilities. If this number is negative, the core currency board requirement has been breached. Within the current economic jargon it is a very transparent form of monetary policy implementation. The CBBH has added to this good legal framework by establishing sensible and sound decision making processes within the Bank and by also establishing good monitoring processes that allow the Governor and the Governing Board to be confident that we are operating effectively and efficiently. The benefits of the currency board arrangements. It is important to judge whether or not a policy framework has operated successfully by analyzing its performance against the objectives it is required to achieve by its statute. It is not appropriate to judge the performance of monetary policy framework against objectives it has not been formulated to achieve. Monetary policy is also only one policy instrument and cannot, on its own, be expected to achieve all the economic and social objectives of the government. The goals of BiH monetary policy as set out in the CBBH Law are very clear  to achieve financial stability in terms of the exchange rate and the inflation rate. Judged against these statutory objectives the currency board in BiH has been a very successful type of monetary policy. BiH has exchange rate stability against the countries of the Euro area and against most of its neighboring countries, who have also in various ways linked their currencies to the Euro. Inflation in BiH is now low and stable. The gap between the inflation rates in the Federation and the RS has narrowed significantly. Table 5: Inflation Rates in BiH. (%) Year Federation Republika Srpska BiH 1998 5.8 37.2 16.3 1999 -0.3 15.1 4.8 2000 1.5 13.6 5.5 2001 1.7 6.5 3.3 2002 -0.2 1.7 0.4 Stability in a country's exchange rate and inflation rate are extremely important economic benefits. They allow people to plan their economic decisions ahead with more confidence. This is particulary important for investment as the economic return from any investment is spread over many years. This benefit applies to both local and foreign investors. BiH is a small country; it has a large balance of trade deficit; it has enormous development needs in order to improve the living standards of its citizens. All these characteristics mean that BiH needs substantial investment, including private foreign investment. But foreign investors don't need to come to BiH. In most cases, they can supply the small BiH market from a neighboring country or even from their home country. There is still a considerable degree of political and business risk in investing in BiH. The fact that the currency board has delivered exchange rate stabilty and low inflation are the most positive factors BiH currently has for persuading potential foreign investors to bring their capital to BiH. Stability in inflation and the exchange rate are also extremely important for financial sector development. At present, the main risk the banks need to focus on is the credit risk of their borrowers. This is still a major problem in BiH, particularly in the business sector. This is the major reason why banks are currently lending more to the household sector than to the business sector. They perceive there to be less risk in lending to households. But as credit risk inow the main area of financial risk for bank lending in BiH, it is possible for the authorities, banks, and the business sector to work together to develop policies to progressively reduce it. The banking sector in BiH has made enormous progress over the last three years. The quality of the banks has improved and most of their balance sheets are stronger. The range of services they are offering has increased. Interest rates on loans have declined significantly. As a consequence of these positive improvements in the banking sector, citizens are again trusting their savings to the banks rather than keeping them at home under the mattress. People need to remember that only a little over a year ago, the citizens of BiH still held DM 4 billion of savings in DM banknotes 'under the mattress.' I am sure that if the banks also had to worry about inflation risk and exchange rate risk in BiH we would not have seen any significant improvements in the banking sector and the economic performance in the country would be much worse than it currently is. Financial stability is also an important social benefit because it is more frequently the poor who suffer from the adverse affects of devaluation or inflation. The rich or well-connected can often finds ways around it - or even ways to benefit from it. These economic and social benefits from financial stability are even more valuable in a region that has experienced extreme instability in the past, as BiH has. The Currency Board in the Future: The main reason that the currency board should be retained as the monetary policy of BiH is that it is producing real economic and social benefits. The citizens can see this. There is widespread public support for the currency board because it has provided one of the few elements of stability the people of BiH have had for some time. A second reason for retaining the currency board approach to monetary policy is that most countries in the region now have a high degree of exchange rate stability against the Euro. For BiH to move in the opposite direction would be very risky. A third important reason why the currency board needs to be retained in BiH is that there is no sensible alternative given the present state of the BiH economy and its institutions. It would be extremely risky to change the policy as confidence in the KM would quickly drop as people waited to see how any alternative monetary policy would work. Some people are advocating that BiH should abandon the currency board arrangements but none of them have made their alternative type of monetary policy clear. I do not see how a discretionary form of monetary policy would work at the present time or in the foreseeable future in BiH. The politicians are unlikely to be prepared to give the discretionary monetary policy powers to an official. But given that there is still a considerable lack of trust amongst political groups, I do not see how politicians would be able to make these decisions. Any alternative types of monetary policy are much more likely to generate inflation rather than economic growth or to lead to little action but a lot of confusion and uncertainty. The one thing that financial markets hate the most is uncertainty. The currency board gives them and the people of BiH certainty. The final reason why the currency board should be retained is that the long-term goal of BiH policy is to take the economy closer to and eventually into Europe. The KM is already tied to the Euro. It is therefore sensible to maintain this link. The exit strategy for BiH from the currency board should therefore be the eventual adoption of the Euro. This is probably many years away. But it should still be the medium-term objective to which monetary policy in BiH should be aimed. Some economists in BiH say BiH needs to move to a normal type of monetary policy by which they seem to mean a policy based on active lending by the Central Bank. I think it is this type of thinking about monetary policy that is now old-fashioned thinking. By choosing to adopt a currency board approach to monetary policy, BiH decided that the aim of its monetary policy would be to achieve stability - stability of the value of the value of the KM against the anchor currency and stability in the rate of inflation in BiH. The overwhelming direction that monetary policy around the world has taken over the last fifteen or so years has been to make financial stability the objective of monetary policy. Many countries have adopted explicit inflation targets. The desire for stability has also led to a revival of interest in currency boards in the 1990s when six were established, including the one in BiH. Far from being colonial institutions, the majority of currency boards in the world today are very recent and modern institutions. A number of countries have taken this desire for stability even further by adopting the currency of another country (so-called dollarisation) or by introducing a new common currency for a number of countries, as the Euro area countries have done. It is true that a currency board is a rule-based rather than a discretionary form of monetary policy. That is a major reason why it was chosen and is one of its strengths rather than a weakness. Implementing monetary policy in BiH through a currency board approach is not 'unusual' or 'abnormal'. What would be unusual, and would have a very adverse effect on confidence and investment, would be a return in BiH to the old-fashioned discretionary type of monetary policies that have failed in many countries  and failed spectacularly in this region. It is possible to add additional roles to a Central Bank that is a currency board  with one important condition. These additional roles must not be inconsistent with the currency board objective or put the currency board at risk in any way. The CBBH already does play additional roles in the BiH financial sector: we operate the clearing and settlement system for the domestic non-cash payments system. The new system, which commencedin Janaury, 2001, is operating very well. It has the potential to expand its clearing and settlement role as the BiH financial system develops further; we provide banking services for the State of BiH and for international financial institutions. Some other levels of government have also decided to use some CBBH banking services; the CBBH plays a coordianting role in banking supervision. One reason for this conference is to learn from other currency boards and from international and local economists whether there are other financial sector roles that the CBBH can take on without endangering the currency board. One such role that the CBBH has already considered is the issuing of short-term CBBH securities. We proposed an amendment to the CBBH Law in 2002 which would have allowed us to do this. The securities would have had to be issued under the same currency board requirements that apply to our other KM liabilities, KM banknotes and depsoits. I.e they would have had to have full foreign exchaneg coverage. The amendment was withdrawn because of opposition to it. But I still believe the proposal would be ebneficial for the devlopment of a short-term money market in BiH and could encourage the banks to hold more of their liquidity in BiH rather than abroad. We will therefore reintroduce this amendment to our Law when the time is suitable. Conclusion: The currency board approach to monetary policy has achieved the objective it was asked to achieve: financial stabilty in BiH. This has brought considerable economic and social benefits to the economy and citizens of BiH. The currency board should be continued as it is important that finaicial sector stability is retained. Financial stabilty is not a goal that you achieve once and then move on to some other objective. Financial sector stabilty has to eb maintained through a consistent application of monetary policy. But it is possible for a Central Bank that operates as a currency board to carry out other financial sector roles that will help economic development  with the strong proviso that those other policies must never be able to put the currency board arrangements at risk. The CBBH already does this in the payments system and in banking. We will continue to expand our roles in the BiH financial sector while always remebering that our main goal is to maintain financial stabilty by operating as a currency board.

Title: Speech notes for round table on banking sector: "Is capital in BH expensive?"
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: SPEECH NOTES FOR ROUND TABLE ON BANKING SECTOR: IS CAPITAL IN BIH EXPENSIVE? SARAJEVO, OCTOBER 24, 2002 I WELCOME YOU ALL TO THIS ROUNDTABLE AT THE CBBH. IT IS ONE OF A SERIES OF MEETINGS THAT HAVE BEEN HELD AS PART OF THE PROCESS OF DEVELOPING A POVERTY REDUCTION STRATEGY PROGRAM (PRSP) FOR BIH. AS PART OF THE PRSP, WE HAD A ROUNDTABLE ON MONETARY POLICY IN BIH A FEW MONTHS AGO. TODAY'S ROUNDTABLE FOCUSES ON THE BANKING SECTOR. SO FOR ONCE I WILL NOT SAY ANYTHING ABOUT THE CENTRAL BANK, MONETARY POLICY OR CURRENCY BOARD. WE HAVE CIRCULATED A BACKGROUND PAPER THAT MY STAFF HAVE PREPARED THAT SETS OUT THE PROGRESS THE BANKING SECTOR HAS MADE IN BIH OVER THE LAST THREE YEARS AND DESCRIBES ITS CURRENT STRUCTURE, SIZE AND CONDITION. WE HAVE DONE THAT SO THAT I CAN SPEND MOST OF THE SHORT TIME I HAVE LOOKING AT THE FUTURE, RATHER THAN DESCRIBING THE PAST AND THE PRESENT. BUT I DO WANT TO DRAW YOUR ATTENTION TO A FEW OF THE FACTS IN THE CIRCULATED PAPER: BANKING SECTOR REFORM HAS GONE FURTHER THAN REFORM IN ANY OTHER SECTOR OF THE ECONOMY; BANK PRIVATISATION IS ALMOST COMPLETE. THIS MEANS WE HAVE CREATED A PRIVATE SECTOR MARKET IN ONE SECTOR OF THE BIH ECONOMY, BANKING. I THINK THE IMPROVEMENTS IN THE RANGE AND QUALITY OF BANKING SERVICES SHOWS CLEARLY HOW WELL PRIVATE MARKETS CAN OPERATE IN BIH  TO THE BENEFIT OF THE CITIZENS. THE BANKING SECTOR IN BIH IS GETTING CLOSER TO MODERN INTERNATIONAL BANKING IN THE RANGE OF BANKING SERVICES THAT ARE AVAILABLE TO BANK CUSTOMERS; CONSIDERABLE CONSOLIDATION HAS OCCURRED AND THE BANKS THAT REMAIN ARE BIGGER AND STRONGER; THE SHARE OF FOREIGN CAPITAL IS INCREASING. THERE HAS PROBABLY BEEN MORE FOREIGN INVESTMENT INTO THE BANKING SECTOR THAN INTO THE REST OF THE BIH ECONOMY COMBINED; CONFIDENCE IN THE BANKING SECTOR IS INCREASING RAPIDLY AS EVIDENCED BY THE STRONG GROWTH IN DEPOSITS; BANK LENDING IS ALSO INCREASING RAPIDLY, THOUGH THE GROWTH IS MAINLY IN LENDING TO HOUSEHOLDS RATHER THAN TO THE BUSINESS SECTOR. INTEREST RATES ON BANK LENDING HAVE FALLEN SUBSTANTIALLY OVER THE LAST TWO YEARS BUT THEY ARE STILL QUITE HIGH RELATIVE TO THE LOW RATE OF INFLATION IN BIH. GENERALLY, THIS PICTURE OF THE CURRENT STATE OF THE BANKING SECTOR IN BIH IS A POSITIVE ONE, PARTICULALRLY IF YOU COMPARE IT TO THE SITUATION IN MOST OTHER SECTORS OF THE ECONOMY. THE BANKING SECTOR IN THE FEDERATION STARTED ITS PROCESS OF RAPID IMPROVEMENT ABOUT TWO YEARS AGO. THE PROCESS STARTED MUCH MORE RECENTLY IN THE RS AND HAS NOT YET GONE AS FAR. BUT ALL THE SAME TRENDS THAT HAVE BEEN EVIDENT IN THE FEDERATION FOR TWO YEARS ARE NOW EVIDENT IN THE RS TOO  AND FOR THE SAME REASONS. I AM CONFIDENT THAT THE IMPROVING TRENDS IN THE BANKING SECTOR WILL CONTINUE. I DO NOT THINK THAT IS AN ISSUE THIS ROUNDTABLE NEEDS TO DEBATE. WHAT WE SHOULD FOCUS ON IS WHAT ARE THE FACTORS THAT WILL INFLUENCE HOW RAPIDLY THE IMPROVEMENTS WILL OCCUR AND ARE THERE MEASURES THAT CAN BE TAKEN TO HELP SPEED THE PROCESS UP AND INCREASE THE POSITIVE DEVELOPMENT ROLE THE BANKING SECTOR CAN MAKE. CONSOLIDATION IN THE SECTOR HAS ALREADY GONE FURTHER THAN SHOWN BY THE REDUCTION IN THE NUMBER OF BANKS, WHICH HAS FALLEN FROM 61 TO 45 OVER THE LAST TWO AND A HALF YEARS. FOR EXAMPLE, OUR PAPER SHOWS THAT ALREADY OVER 80% OF CITIZENS DEPOSITS ARE IN 10 BANKS. UNDER THE COMBINED PRESSURE OF INCREASED MINIMUM CAPITAL REQUIREMENTS AND INCREASED COMPETITION, THE NUMBER OF BANKS IN BIH WILL DROP FURTHER OVER THE NEXT YEAR EVEN WHILE THE OVERALL SIZE OF THE SECTOR GROWS. BANKING IN BIH IS RAPIDLY MOVING TO BE A SINGLE BANKING SYSTEM. ALREADY SEVEN OR EIGHT BANKS OPERATE IN BOTH ENTITIES, INCLUDING MOST OF THE BIGGEST BANKS. THIS TREND WILL ALSO CONTINUE. REFLECTING THIS TREND, A STATE DEPOSIT INSURANCE AGENCY HAS BEEN SET UP RECENTLY TO REPLACE THE TWO ENTITY AGENCIES. I AM CONFIDENT THAT THE NEW DEPOSIT INSURANCE AGENCY WILL BE SUCCESSFUL. WE ALSO HAVE A WORKING GROUP OF THE CBBH, THE ENTITY BANKING AGENCIES, AND THE ENTITY MINISTRIES OF FINANCE THAT IS WORKING ON INCREASING THE DEGREE OF COOPERATION AND COORDINATION IN BANKING SUPERVISION. I THINK THE TYPE AND QUALITY OF REGULATION IN THE BANKING SECTOR IN BIH IS NOW GOOD AND THIS WIL PLAY A POSITIVE ROLE IN THE FUTURE DEVELOPMENT OF THE BIH BANKING SECTOR. MOST OF THE MAIN PROBLEM AREAS THAT WILL SLOW DOWN THE FURTHER DEVELOPMENT OF THE ECONOMIC ROLE OF THE BANKING SECTOR ARE NOW OUTSIDE THE BANKING SECTOR ITSELF. THE FIRST KEY ONE IS THE LEGAL AND COURT SYSTEM. IT IS STILL DIFFICULT FOR BANKS TO GET CLEAR AND SOUND COLLATERAL FOR BANK LENDING. I THINK THIS IS A BIGGER PROBLEM IN THE BUSINESS SECTOR THAN IN THE HOUSEHOLD SECTOR AND THIS IS ONE REASON WHY BANKS CURRENTLY PREFER TO LEND TO HOUSEHOLDS. BANKS FREQUENTLY TELL ME THAT THEY DO NOT BELIEVE THEY CAN RELY ON THE COURT SYSTEM TO RESOLVE PROBLEMS IF A BORROWER DOES DEFAULT ON THE LOAN OBLIGATIONS. FOR ONE THING, THE COURT CASES CAN TAKE YEARS. THERE IS A SAYING THAT JUSTICE DELAYED IS JUSTICE DENIED. WHETHER THAT IS TRUE OR NOT, JUSTICE DELAYED DOES BECOME VERY EXPENSIVE FOR THE BANKS. SECOND, BANKS FIRMLY BELIEVE THAT THE COURTS OFTEN FIND IN FAVOUR OF THE BORROWER RATHER THAN THE BANK. THESE LEGAL PROBLEMS ARE ANOTHER REASON WHY THE BANKS ARE CURRENTLY MORE WILLING TO LEND TO HOUSEHOLDS THAN TO BUSINESSES. FIRSTLY, HOUSEHOLDS DO NOT DEAULT ON THEIR OBLIGATIONS AS MUCH AS BUSINESSES SO THERE ARE FEWER LEGAL PROBLEMS. SECONDLY, THE BANKS SEEM TO BE ABLE TO EXERCISE THE COLLATERAL THEY HAVE MORE EASILY WITH HOUSEHOLDS THAN WITH BUSINESSES. THIRDLY, BUSINESS BORROWERS, PARTICULARLY LARGE BORROWERS, ARE MORE LIKELY TO USE DELAYING TACTICS IN COURT PROCESSES. ALL OF THESE PROBLEMS MAKE THE BANKS LESS WILLING TO LEND TO THE BUSINESS SECTOR AND KEEP THE LEVEL OF INTEREST RATES FOR ALL BORROWERS, INCLUDING THE HONEST ONES, HIGHER THAN THEY OTHERWISE NEED TO BE. THERE IS WORK UNDER WAY TO REFORM THE COURT SYSTEM. THESE EFFORTS SHOULD BE STRONGLY SUPPORTED BY THIS ROUNDTABLE. BUT THEY WILL TAKE TIME AND MAY STILL LEAVE SOME PROBLEMS IN THE COMMERCIAL LAW AREA. I THINK THERE IS A ROLE FOR A SPECIALISED COMMERCIAL COURT TO DEAL WITH FINANCIAL CASES, INCLUDING CASES INVOLVING BANKS AND THEIR CUSTOMERS. HOPEFULY, SUCH A COURT COULD HAVE SIMPLIER AND QUICKER PROCEDURES. SUCH A COURT WOULD ALSO BE ABLE TO HAVE MORE EXPERTISE AMONGST THE JUDICIARY BECAUSE OF ITS SPECIALISED ROLE. I WOULD BE INTERESTED TO HEAR THE VIEWS OF OTHER PARTICPANTS ON THIS PROPOSAL. THE SECOND PROBLEM IS THE CREDIT CULTURE IN BIH. MOST CITIZENS DO SEEM TO FEEL AN OBLIGATION TO REPAY THEIR BANK LOANS. BUT FOR REASONS I DON'T FULLY UNDERSTAND, THE BUSINESS SECTOR IS MUCH MORE MIXED. I CANNOT OVERSTATE THE DAMAGING IMPACT LOAN DEFAULTERS HAVE ON THE WILLINGNESS OF BANKS TO LEND AND ON THE COST OF CREDIT FOR EVERY OTHER BORROWER IN THE COUNTRY. I HAVE CIRCULATED A SIMPLE EXAMPLE TO ILLUSTRATE THE IMPACT. SO ONE ANSWER TO THE QUESTION WHY BANK INTEREST RATES IN BIH STILL APPEAR TO BE HIGH IS VERY CLEAR TO ME  THE COUNTRY IS PAYING A HIGH PRICE FOR THE PEOPLE AND COMPANIES WHO HAVE DEFAULTED ON THE LOANS THEY HAVE TAKEN FROM BANKS. THE CITIZENS, THE POLITICIANS, THE POLICE, THE COURTS AND THE MEDIA IN BIH SHOULD HAVE NO SYMPATHY FOR THESE PEOPLE. YOU ARE ALL PAYING THE COST OF THEIR IRRESPONSIBILITY OR CRIMINAL BEHAVIOUR. A THIRD PROBLEM IS THE LACK OF CAPITAL MARKETS IN BIH. DEVELOPING EFFICIENT AND EFFECTIVE CAPITAL MARKETS IN BIH WILL HAVE MANY POISITIVE BENEFITS FOR THE BIH ECONOMY. I DON'T HAVE TIME TO GO INTO ALL OF THOSE TODAY. TODAY I WILL FOCUS ON THE IMPACT THIS HAS ON THE COST AND AVAILABILITY OF BORROWING IN BIH. THE LACK OF SUITABLE INSTRUMENTS IN BIH IN WHICH BANKS CAN INVEST THEIR LIQUID FUNDS HAS TWO EFFECTS. FIRSTLY, THEY HOLD SOME OF THEIR LIQUIDITY IN DEPOSITS AT THE CBBH ON WHICH THEY EARN NOTHING. THEY THEREFORE HAVE TO EARN MORE ON THE REST OF THEIR ASSET PORTFOLIO, OF WHICH THE MAIN ELEMENT IS LOANS. SECONDLY, THEY HOLD A LARGE PART OF THEIR LIQUID FUNDS OUTSIDE BIH IN ORDER TO EARN AN INCOME. THIS IS SENSIBLE BANKING BEHAVIOUR. BUT THE LACK OF SUITABLE INSTRUMENTS IN BIH, SUCH AS TREASURY BILLS OR CBBH BILLS, DOES HAVE NEGATIVE EFFECTS ON BOTH THE AVAILABILITY AND COST OF BANK CREDIT IN BIH. SO WE NEED TO CREATE URGENTLY A SHORT TERM CAPITAL MARKET IN BIH. THE CBBH DID PROPOSE AN AMENDMENT TO OUR LAW LAST YEAR THAT WOULD HAVE ALLOWED US TO START THIS PROCESS, WHILE FULLY PROTECTING THE CURRENCY BOARD. THIS PROPOSED AMENDMENT WAS NOT SUPPORTED BY THE RS PARLIAMENTARY DELEGATES OR BY THE IMF. I THINK BOTH OF THEM WERE WRONG IN THEIR OPPOSITION TO THIS PROPOSAL. I WILL THEREFORE ATTEMPT TO REINTRODUCE THE PROPOSAL NEXT YEAR. THE NEXT TOPIC I WANT TO TALK ABOUT IS A POSSIBLE ROLE FOR A CREDIT GUARANTEE AGENCY. BIH DOES NOT HAVE THE PROBLEM OF A SHORTAGE OF AVAILABLE BANK FUNDS AT PRESENT. THIS MEANS THAT THERE IS NO CASE THAT CAN BE MADE FOR NEW DEVELOPMENT BANKS TO BE ESTABLISHED. THAT WOULD ONLY BE SENSIBLE IF THE PROBLEM WAS A SHORTAGE OF AVAILABLE FUNDS. THE PROBLEM IS THAT BANKS PERCEIVE THERE TO BE A SHORTAGE OF CREDIT-WORTHY BORROWERS, PARTICULARLY IN THE BUSINESS SECTOR. IT IS THEREFORE LIKELY THAT A PROPERLY DESIGNED CREDIT GUARANTEE AGENCY COULD PLAY A POSITIVE ROLE IN ACCELERATING THE BANKS WILLINGNESS TO LEND BY SHARING THE RISK. SUCH AN INSTITUTION MAY ONLY BE NEEDED IN BIH FOR A FEW YEARS SO IT SHOULD NOT BE SET UP AS A LARGE, ELABORATE INSTITUTION. MY FINAL POINT IS RELATED TO THE LAST ONE. ONE REASON THAT THERE IS A SHORTAGE OF CREDIT-WORTHY BUSINESS BORROWERS IN BIH IS THAT THE ENVIRONMENT FACING PRIVATE SECTOR BUSINESSES IN THIS COUNTRY IS STILL HOSTILE. I USE THAT WORD DELIBERATELY. THE ENVIRONMENT IS CERTAINLY NOT ENCOURAGING. IT IS NOT EVEN NEUTRAL. IT IS HOSTILE: INTRUSIVE AND MULTI-LEVEL REGULATION, HIGH, COMPLEX AND INEFFICIENT TAXES, THE DIFFICULTY OF OPERATING IN BOTH ENTITIES, AND INSPECTORS/INSPECTORS/INSPECTORS. IF THE BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT IN BIH WAS REALLY IMPROVED, MORE COMPANIES WOULD BECOME CREDIT-WORTHY. BANKS WILL WILLINGLY LEND TO SUCH COMPANIES, AS THAT IS HOW BANKS MAKE THEIR INCOME. THEY WOULD EVEN LEND AT LOWER INTEREST RATES TO SUCH COMPANIES. IT IS IN THIS AREA THAT THE REAL SOLUTION TO THE ISSUE BEING DISCUSSED BY TODAY'S ROUNDTABLE, THE HIGH COST OF CAPITAL IN BIH, LIES. IT IS ALSO WHERE THE REAL SOLUTION TO ALLEVIATING POVERTY IN BIH LIES. THE AIM SHOULD BE TO FREE UP THE ENERGY, INITIATIVE AND WILLINGNESS TO WORK THAT EXISTS IN YOUR PEOPLE.

Title: Presentation at the Second business roundtable with governments of BH
CentralBank: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
text: Second business roundtable with the governments of Bosnia and Herzegovina Sarajevo, September 22-23 Central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina I would like to welcome all of you to this roundtable and thank you for attending. I will cover four topics in my presentation. The first will be the Central Bank of BH and the roles it plays in maintaining financial stability in BH. The second will be the significant improvements that have occurred in the banking sector in BH over the last three years. The third will be the changes that lie ahead of the BH financial sector in the immediate future, and I will finish with some brief comments on the economic outlook. The Central Bank (CBBH): The CBBH commenced its operations on 11 august 1997 so it is still quite a young organization. It is a state level institution, which means it is the only monetary authority in BH and operates over the whole country through five offices. It has 250 staff. The CBBH law specifies clearly the functions that the CBBH must carry out and also sets a number of limitations on its operations. Subject to these legal requirements and restrictions, the CBBH is completely independent of political influence. Monetary policy: Monetary policy is the CBBHs most important function. The CBBH operates monetary policy through a strict Currency Board arrangement, which is stipulated in the CBBH law. There were three main reasons for the choice of a Currency Board for BHs monetary policy: It provided a firm nominal anchor in the form of a fixed exchange rate in a situation where there was significant economic instability; It removed discretion in a situation where there was considerable difficulty in establishing institutions and making political decisions; Currency boards had been established in some other eastern European countries and were working well. The Currency Board: The three essential features of the BH Currency Board are: A fixed exchange rate specified in the law; Full foreign exchange backing for all the KM liabilities of the central bank; Full convertibility of the CBBHs KM liabilities into the anchor currency. The fixed exchange rate: The initial exchange rate was set at 1 KM 1 Deutschmark (the Bosnian currency is called the Convertible Marka). The choice of the DM as the anchor currency for the BH Currency Board was an easy one. The DM had long been a very stable currency and it was already widely used and trusted in BH. When the DM was replaced by the euro, the CBBH law was changed to make the euro the anchor currency for the BH Currency Board. The new exchange rate was specified in the CBBH law at exactly the same rate as the DM had been linked to the euro. I.e., 1 KM 0.51129 euros. This means that the exchange rate of the KM has been unchanged since the CBBH commenced its operations.
